Is that the question?'), and illustrates his strange distinction between existents and existing through Dick's existing-without-existents: the hallucinated town of The Cosmic Puppets, the aura of fake American relics in The Man in the High Castle, Freck's nonexistent aphids. Working through phenomenology, the idios kosmos / koinos kosmos split of A Maze of Death and Eye in the Sky, and the eerie 'There is' of the void, it reworks Descartes's cogito into Levinas's question ('I think, therefore what should I do?') because out there is the Other.
- ch. 133 "He Ain’t Heavy, He’s My Other" **·** Emmanuel Levinas, Martin Heidegger, René Descartes — The Face of the Other; The Ethics of Care — This section stages Levinas's infinite responsibility for the Other against Heidegger's tendency to treat others as tools for warding off death: J.R. Isidore's one-way care for androids who vivisect a spider, Dick's 'The Android and the Human' warning that androidization means becoming predictable means, and the treatment of animals as the litmus test of humanity. The self becomes real through selfless action (Tagomi saving a stranger, Sweetscent returning to his wife), and because the height separating self and Other descends from Descartes's idea of infinity, meeting the face of the poor stranger, from Radio Free Albemuth's beggar to The Adjustment Bureau's Chairman, is an encounter with God.
- ch. 134 "Fifty Ways to Love Your Other" **·** Emmanuel Levinas — The Face of the Other; The Golden Rule; The Ethics of Care — The section reads Levinas's demand to experience the Other's suffering in the Other's place as Dick's empathy made literal: the shifting points of view that blur heroes and villains, Felix Buckman's tears, Molinari developing his people's symptoms, and the empathy boxes bonding users to Mercer's endless stoning, a fraud whose falsity is beside the point because the concern is the real thing. Villains are precisely those who refuse the transfer, and the ordinary one-way gift, buying a stranger a drink with no return, enacts the Golden Rule: even if the universe isn't real, Melina is right, kiss each other anyway.
- ch. 135 "Puppets and Precogs" *(front)*
- ch. 136 "Chapter 21 - Knowing Tomorrow While Choosing Today" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Fate and Foreknowledge — Sara Worley's introduction frames Minority Report and 'Adjustment Team' as versions of the classic free will problem: if precogs foresee my crime before I commit it, or the Adjustment Team knows what I will do, my action seems already settled, like a sunflower's turn toward the sun. Influence alone does not cancel freedom, since we can do otherwise where plants cannot, but foreknowledge threatens exactly that, the same quandary long posed by an omniscient God who already knows every action we will perform.
- ch. 137 "Freedom and Prediction" **·** Fate and Foreknowledge; Free Will vs Determinism — The section distinguishes two models of foreknowledge: prediction, as when you confidently predict that sci-fi-loving Jill will skip the John Wayne retrospective, and Molina's 'middle knowledge' of how each person will respond to various circumstances. It then argues prediction can be certain only if character and circumstances guarantee the outcome, the way facts and laws fix where Mars will appear, which would leave no alternatives to choose; so on the predictive model, infallible foreknowledge and the ability to do otherwise cannot coexist.
- ch. 138 "Outside of Time" **·** Boethius, Anselm of Canterbury — Fate and Foreknowledge — This section presents the Boethian-Anselmian alternative: God is outside time, so nothing is past, present, or future for him; all events are eternally laid out for him simply to 'look' at, rather than learn about past events from fossils or future ones from predictions. On this model God has no foreknowledge strictly speaking, and his seeing Jill buy her ticket no more constrains her choice than my watching someone choose would make them unfree.
- ch. 139 "Prediction, or Sight" **·** Fate and Foreknowledge; Free Will vs Determinism — The section tests both models against the stories and finds 'sight' incoherent: the precogs foresee murders that never happen, the Adjustment Bureau tracks two incompatible previsions per circumstance, and a precog genuinely seeing the actual future would generate an oscillating loop in which her own report makes the prevision false. Prediction fits instead: the adjusters tweak Mr. Douglas's cautious character in 'Adjustment Team,' and Anderton's three discrepant predictions in 'The Minority Report' track how leaked information changes his circumstances and motivation to kill Kaplan.
- ch. 140 "Perfect or Probabilistic" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Fate and Foreknowledge — This section argues predictive foresight is compatible with freedom only if probabilistic, yet Precrime treats its predictions as certain, arresting people for what they will rather than might do. Lisa's doubts in 'The Minority Report' turn out to concern incomplete information rather than free will, while The Adjustment Bureau dramatizes freedom differently: the adjusters work by making the preferred path easiest, but David and Elise's three-year persistence shows that those who 'fight' for their free will get it, leaving open how predictable we really are.
- ch. 141 "Chapter 22 - Total Recall’s Total Rethink" *(front)*
- ch. 142 "Memory and the Brain-Butchers" **·** John Locke — Personal Identity (memory theory); Personal Identity — The section uses Quaid's Rekall-fabricated life, complete with false wedding memories and a false eight-year marriage, to challenge Locke's memory theory of personal identity: implants, together with ordinary forgetting, revision, and loss, show memory cannot be what makes you the same person from one day to the next. Kuato's line, 'A man is defined by his action, not his memory,' is offered as the alternative the following sections develop.
- ch. 143 "Owning Your Actions, Owning Your Past" **·** Aristotle — Free Will vs Determinism; Personal Identity — This section reconstructs the traditional view of free agency from Aristotle: an action is freely mine when it 'has its origin in the agent himself,' so owning an action means tracing its causal chain back to one's own decision. It explains Aristotle's picture of natures as internal sources of motion and decision as the distinctively human motion, then asks whether Quaid, following the suitcase, video, and clues Hauser pre-arranged, is picking up the chain of his own prior decision, and so becoming himself again.
- ch. 144 "Inpsychation and Chains of Will" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Ralph Waldo Emerson, John Locke — Free Will vs Determinism; Personal Identity — The section develops freedom as extending the will through tools and other people, via Nietzsche's 'inpsychation' and Emerson's conversion of fate into force: Cohaagen shuts off the air through Lori and Harry as Hitler invaded Poland through his soldiers. Locke's memory theory returns demoted to a useful tool rather than an identity-maker, and Nietzsche's Genealogy II.1 on the unbroken 'long chain of will' explains Hauser's masterpiece, planning around his own memory wipe so that Quaid, following the planted clues, re-inpsychates Hauser's decisions.
- ch. 145 "Quaid’s Problem—Mucky Origins" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Personal Identity — This section complicates everything: two taped Hausers contradict each other, rebel hero or Cohaagen's 'bosom buddy,' so Quaid cannot settle who he is by tracing his origins. It then generalizes: in the scientific worldview of universal causation, from gravity to DNA inherited through chimps and sea squirts from the primeval muck, no one originates anything, a conclusion quoted at length from Baron d'Holbach's System of Nature, yet first-person deliberation still leaves Quaid feeling the weight of choice.
- ch. 146 "Freedom Without Origins" **·** Epicurus — Free Will vs Determinism; Personal Identity; Authenticity — The section rejects randomness as a foundation for freedom, quantum indeterminacy being Epicurus's swerve again, since actions tracing to random particle events are no more mine than law-determined ones, then turns to the ethical problem: if Hauser volunteered and Cohaagen's story is true, freedom-as-origination would require Quaid to become Hauser again, Mercedes included. Quaid's verdict ('The guy's a fucking asshole') shows freedom is also changing course to do what is right; as Lowe says in 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale,' what defines us is 'not a memory but a desire,' and in breaking with his past Quaid decisively becomes free.
- ch. 147 "Chapter 23 - Lonely Wolves" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — The Absurd; Existence Precedes Essence — Travis Paterson's introduction reads A Scanner Darkly as Dick's most autobiographical novel and explains Arctor's disgust at the over-happy Brown Bear Lodge audience through Sartre's Nausea: Roquentin's discovery that existence is sheer contingency, that we are superfluous, vaguely alarmed beings who cannot define existence as necessity. Arctor never finds Roquentin's slender chance of acceptance, so the nausea curdles into addiction and the wolf parable, the magnificent lone wolf shot to protect the meager, over-fed animals, poses the chapter's question of why the sensitive outsider is the one sacrificed.
- ch. 148 "Society’s a Bad Hit (If You’re Banging Up, Cranking, or Popping)" **·** Cultural Hegemony; Discipline and Docile Bodies — This section argues A Scanner Darkly's primary philosophical contribution is the recognition that the fate of Dick's drug circle was social violence against those who did not fit in: dominant California normalizes the apathetic, slothful 'straights' of the Brown Bear Lodge while phone-tapping peace advocates, ransacking writers' homes, and hunting or abandoning drug users whose pain gets attributed to addiction rather than rejection. The Thelma Kornford mosquito-hawk episode, the deposition about color TVs, animals, and My Lai, and Donna's final 'It is easy to win' all expose how winning requires never choosing your own values.
- ch. 149 "Cultural Minority Report" **·** Communitarianism; Authenticity — This section asks whether the outsider can live in society with dignity, using Charles Taylor's politics of recognition, the claim that dominant societies commit an egregious harm when they refuse to affirm a subculture's value, to read Arctor and his friends as a subculture whose leftover American dream is recognition. Parallels with indigenous ceremonies, typecast immigrant youth, and French assimilation pressure frame the novel's question: can pluralist America include drug culture, or does the ethical order that preaches pluralism have limits the Arctors have already hit?
- ch. 150 "The Problem with Drugs" **·** Cultural Hegemony; The Harm Principle — The closing section rebuts the communitarian defense of California's drug laws, noting there is more than one community and most people belong to several, then turns to Douglas Husak: moral rights exist to protect persons from majority interference, and the crusade against drugs is cultural hegemony. Cocaine, marijuana, and opiates were outlawed along racial lines (blacks, Mexicans, and Chinese respectively) while the ruling class's alcohol and tobacco remained 'autonomous choices,' suggesting the real problem with drugs is who uses them.
- ch. 151 "It’s the Nausea" **·** G.W.F. Hegel — Struggle for Recognition — This closing section of the A Scanner Darkly chapter argues that Bob Arctor's identity is grounded not in social acceptance but in his nausea at dominant social values and his pride in being an outsider 'wolf' among Arctor, Barris, Luckman and Frick. It stresses that Arctor is not simply anti-social: as the narc Fred he genuinely wants to bust dealers and put the Substance D world to hell, so he belongs to his society even while rejecting its values. Arctor's split Bob/Fred personality symbolizes a 'permanent provocation' toward the mainstream that is identity-creative and liberating, a case that even liberal recognition theory cannot absorb because what he values most is his very difference and superiority.
- ch. 152 "Wolves Finish Last" **·** G.W.F. Hegel — Struggle for Recognition — The conclusion of the A Scanner Darkly essay spells out the cost of Arctor's struggle for recognition with society at large: because his addiction strips him of legal protection and moral standing, the Sheriff's Department easily turns him into a puppet while pursuing drug manufacturers 'even if it means wasting the lives of innocents.' The novel thereby shows the boundary of even a supposedly pluralistic society's recognition - counter-cultural identities formed in opposition to mainstream stupidities, like Arctor's circle, are too antagonistic to be recognized and are persecuted like wolves. What they actually want, the chapter argues, is liberty, independence and the American Dream, which they think the rest of America has abandoned.
- ch. 153 "Futurity Doctored" *(front)*
- ch. 154 "Chapter 24 - I Know What You Did Next Summer" **·** Henri Bergson — Duration (durée); The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Paul Atkinson's introduction to Chapter 24 frames 'The Minority Report' and 'Paycheck', together with their film adaptations, as explorations of the many different ways of knowing the future. He proposes Henri Bergson - who denied the future can be known and explained why we sometimes think we can - as the philosopher perfectly placed to 'write the rules' for the time-travel game these stories play. It also contrasts philosophy's umpire-like settling of issues with the films' urge to literally show us the future rather than merely predict it.
- ch. 155 "Pay Now, Live Later" **·** Henri Bergson — Duration (durée); Matter and Memory — This section reads Precrime through Bergson's duree: in Dick's story the precogs are 'monkeys' and 'idiots' emitting snippets that investigators must analyze, while the film shows a precog immersed in and living through the future visually. It explains Bergson's claim that clocks and timelines falsify time, which is really lived duration in which the past endures as memory and actively directs us toward an open future, and rehearses his reunion thought experiment: imagined futures are mere sketches, while the actual future arrives with the unique specificity of the Mona Lisa. No one, on this view, can know the future as if living it.
- ch. 156 "I Can Predict What You (Don’t) Do Next Summer" **·** Henri Bergson — Duration (durée); Fate and Foreknowledge — Using Bergson's imprevisible and 'The Possible and the Real', this section argues that the story's Precrime works by prediction-as-elimination: investigators discard the precogs' babblings that do not fit the world, 'closing the gate' on the impossible to leave only a statistically possible future. Bergson's gate metaphor shows prediction never yields the real future, only the negatively 'not impossible', yet Precrime arrests people for an abstract possible event they have never actually lived. It ends by asking whether Anderton, accused of a future murder in advance, would still commit it, since ever-changing memory and knowledge make a possible future never identical to the actual one.
- ch. 157 "Living in the Time of the Crime" **·** Henri Bergson — Duration (durée) — A close reading of the film's opening murder contrasts cinematic precognition with the story's: the camera moves from Sarah Marks's terrified face and dilated pupil to the precog Agatha's watery blue eye as she utters 'murder', making Agatha an empathetic witness immersed in the scene. Anderton then pieces the moving images together like a film editor working with rushes, so no analytic machinery connects present to future - the future is simply given in visual detail. In the film, precognition is the foreseeable rather than the predictable: precogs and audience alike live in the time of the crime.
- ch. 158 "Always Invest in the Future" **·** Henri Bergson — Duration (durée); The Metaphysics of Time Travel — This section retells 'Paycheck' in story and John Woo film versions: engineer Jennings trades two memory-wiped years for a cloth sack of ordinary objects - a piece of wire, a bus token - which his erased past self chose as tools for future crises, from breaking out of a police cell to paying a robot ticket inspector. It explains the story's time machine, a 'mirror' that images the future and a 'scoop' that extracts objects from it, a significant difference from the movie. The section shows how past-Jennings exists for present-Jennings only through these leftovers, which prove more valuable than money.
- ch. 159 "Summarizing the Future" **·** Henri Bergson — Duration (durée); Fate and Foreknowledge; Matter and Memory — Applying Bergson's Time and Free Will claim that recalling the past shortens it into a 'thing', the section uses the curriculum-vitae metaphor: like a CV or Facebook page, we imagine the future as a summary compiled from the past. In 'Paycheck', Jennings's sack becomes a plan only when he reflects - the wire at the police station, the token on the bus - until past, present and future fuse and he feels 'a strange elation' at fulfilling his past self's design, raising again whether awareness of the future changes what we do. The film diverges by having Jennings sabotage the atomic-bomb future he foresees, echoing Minority Report's contest between an inevitable future and present action.
- ch. 160 "The Future as Predictive Text" **·** Henri Bergson — Duration (durée) — The section develops a 'predictive text' metaphor: once Jennings's past is constructed as a narrative by past-Jennings, the future merely mirrors it, filling in missing letters like autocorrect - as in the ticket-stub passage where Jennings deduces where he 'had been' and concludes 'he had foreseen this too.' It contrasts the short stories, where a possible future only guides present action, with both films' screens - rewinding videotape, headline videos of an exploding city, the Minority Report editing suite - that render the future almost indistinguishable from the present. For Bergson the future can never appear on a television screen, since that would require a camera living in the time of the event; at most the future is a gate closing or a frame narrowing to a vague sketch.
- ch. 161 "Chapter 25 - Untimely Speculations" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Eternal Recurrence; Amor Fati (love of fate); The Übermensch — Heath Massey's introduction to Chapter 25 opens with Nietzsche's Gay Science passage on intellects that might experience time backward, then stages the demon of eternal recurrence: every pain and joy returning in the same sequence in a world without aim, which either crushes you or becomes 'the highest formula of affirmation', amor fati. Eternal recurrence is a test of the will separating 'man' from 'overman', since one could not celebrate it while believing the world needs a divine purpose. The chapter then maps Dick's imaginative variations of temporality onto two Nietzschean tendencies - disruptions of time-sense that render characters powerless, and extraordinary temporalities that liberate them beyond finite human time, culminating in Dick's theory of supertemporality.
- ch. 162 "Human, All Too Human" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Eternal Recurrence — This section collects Dick's incapacitating temporalities. In Martian Time-Slip, repairman Jack Bohlen relapses into schizophrenia while trying to slow autistic Manfred Steiner's accelerated time-sense, concluding that psychosis is 'the utter alienation of perception from the objects of the outside world', which would also explain the fine line between prophecy and psychosis. In 'Your Appointment Will Be Yesterday' the Hobart Phase reverses time - libraries eradicate books, authors unwrite their manuscripts - and threatens a closed loop of Eng's swabble until crank Lance Arbuthnot has his own manuscript eradicated to keep the reversal in place. In Ubik, Joe Chip watches cigarettes, milk and TVs regress to prior 'templates' as the world decays; in all three, altered time crushes rather than elevates, leaving characters struggling not to be overcome by the inexorability of time.
- ch. 163 "Preparatory Human Beings" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; Possible Worlds; Eternal Recurrence — The counter-tendency gathers Dick's empowering temporalities. 'The Golden Man' presents Cris Johnson, a golden-haired mutant with virtually no frontal cortex, who survives a random-firing gun by 'pre-thinking' a panorama of possible futures - Homo superior as superhuman beast, by instinct rather than intelligence. In Now Wait for Last Year, General Molinari uses the drug JJ-180 to trip sideways into parallel presents and recruit healthy duplicates of himself, virtually overcoming mortality with 'a dynasty consisting of himself'. And in The Man in the High Castle, Abendsen's The Grasshopper Lies Heavy, Frank Frink's handwrought jewelry and Tagomi's meditative slip all point toward an alternate present - ours - where the Allies won, making art and the I Ching oracles of resistance to totalitarian domination.
- ch. 164 "On the Advantage and Disadvantage of Eternity for Life" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Possible Worlds; Eternal Recurrence — The essay's close presents Dick's own 'wicked thought' from 'If You Find This World Bad, You Should See Some of the Others': a plurality of universes arranged laterally to linear time, 'ten thousand bodies of God' hung like suits, including one where Germany and Japan won World War II. It asks whether lateral change might explain schizophrenic experience and whether eternity, in Dick's phrase being 'free from and somehow out of and above time', is supertemporality - occupying multiple time sequences at will. Like Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, Dick's multiverse is a test rather than a doctrine: those crushed by an aimless universe remain merely human, while those who can affirm endless strife or tap parallel presents are virtually superhuman, resisting time's supposedly inexorable march.
- ch. 165 "Chapter 26 - The Day Roosevelt Was Assassinated" **·** Fate and Foreknowledge — Peter Simons opens Chapter 26 with the real 1933 Zangara shooting that missed President-elect Roosevelt by inches and killed mayor Anton Cermak, then asks the counterfactual question: what if Zangara had hit, as happens in the divergence launching The Man in the High Castle, the 1962 Hugo winner? Dick's epigraph about chance, accident and 'one great figure... strategically placed' frames whether anyone can alter fate. The section positions the novel within Dick's alternate-reality work (Minority Report's possible futures, 'The Golden Man', The Divine Invasion) as the one book that fully immerses the reader in a single alternate history.
- ch. 166 "The Story" *(no index entry yet)* — Surveying the thin alternate-history genre - Ward Moore's Bring the Jubilee and Robert Harris's Fatherland - this section credits Dick's novel as the pick of the pack because it is chillingly believable: ordinary characters with mixed motives and limited freedom, embedded in a 1960s America conquered and partitioned between victorious Germany and Japan, with Hitler senile from syphilis and Chancellor Bormann dying. Dick's craft makes the world feel normal: non-linear plotting, seemingly minor protagonists (a Jewish jewelry maker, a dealer in fake Americana, a middle-ranking Japanese official), and grammatical quirks in the characters' thoughts. The banned book-within-the-book, The Grasshopper Lies Heavy, doubly inverts history by describing an Allied victory that is similar to but intriguingly different from our own.
- ch. 167 "Reality" **·** David Lewis, Gottfried Leibniz — Possible Worlds — Taking Dick's 'What is reality?' as its theme, this section distinguishes The Man in the High Castle's alternate world from sham worlds like Time Out of Joint's fake 1950s: the alternate history is as real as ours, its inhabitants no more able to escape into a realer reality than we are, even when Tagomi briefly glimpses our Embarcadero. It introduces Leibniz's possible worlds and David Lewis's modal realism - every consistent way things might have been really exists, and calling only our world 'actual' is mere 'world chauvinism', like a New Yorker denying London exists. Because Dick's characters dismiss worlds like ours as unreal as readily as we dismiss theirs, the symmetry suggests our world has no exclusive title to the label 'real'.
- ch. 168 "Determinism" **·** David Lewis — Free Will vs Determinism; Possible Worlds — Citing Dick's 1976 'soap-bubble' reality interview, this section observes that Lewis's many worlds, each complete in all detail at all times, are deterministic in Laplace's sense - history on rails. Three considerations tell against determinism in our world: our experience of free choice, which grounds praise and blame; quantum indeterminacy, where a nucleus splits when it splits; and objective chance and coincidence - Zangara's near-miss, two wheat grains touching in a granary, Churchill's silence at the crucial meeting tipping the premiership from Halifax, who would likely have negotiated with Hitler. Simons grants that hinge events deviate history by mere inches, but rejects Dick's hint, and Lewis's theory, that all the possible worlds are equally real: only our world is real.
- ch. 169 "Time in the One Real World" *(no index entry yet)* — This section lays out four ontologies of time - eternalism (all actual events equally real), the growing block, presentism, and the tree-pruning model on which Dick's world was a real future branch in 1930 but pruned away by 1934. Against the thought that eternalism entails fatalism, Simons argues coincidence (merging causal chains, a stranger collapsed on a doorstep) and human freedom can live within eternalism, with powerful figures like Truman magnifying chance into history. He endorses eternalism as the view that treats all times democratically, concludes that Dick's world 'has no reality whatsoever' though things could have happened as he describes, and courteously judges that Dick, as a philosopher, was wrong.
- ch. 170 "Precog a Are You" *(front)*
- ch. 171 "Chapter 27 - Time in Unfixed Are You" **·** Edmund Husserl, Martin Heidegger — Phenomenology; Thrownness (Geworfenheit); Dasein (being-there) — Written backwards in homage to 'Your Appointment Will Be Yesterday', this section argues that the self is found in the future more than the present: we understand objects through the actions they afford and ourselves through goals, projects and commitments, so the present moment has very little to do with who we 'really' are. Drawing on Edmund Husserl's 'protention' and Martin Heidegger's existence-as-possibilities, it shows that we hear a melody's building tension as an already-present resolution, and that the past stays present without being recalled - when the phone rings on the couch, where it was is simply there for you. Invoking Don Fallis's 'Lies, Incorporated', it adds that every remembering rewires history to fit our current view, so in memory we travel into the past just as surely as protention carries us into possible futures.
- ch. 172 "Time through Travel You" *(front)*
- ch. 173 "Blur a Are You" **·** Edmund Husserl — Phenomenology — The reversed-text conclusion completes the argument: via Husserl's retention and protention we must be in the past, under erasure, at every moment, and presently precognize future possibilities, or we could not even hear notes as music. After thanking the volume's editors, it states the thesis - to be human is to be unfixed in time, constantly negotiating a past we thought fixed and calibrating futures that are always already present to us. Dick's precogs and time-travelers, who change the past or choose the future, are symbolic retellings of this ordinary human temporality, since science fiction explores the present through the future.
- ch. 174 "Briefings" *(front)*
- ch. 175 "Chapter 28 - “Autofac”" **·** Karl Marx — Utopia and Dystopia; Alienation — Dan Dinello reads 'Autofac' as a dystopian counter to cybernetic utopianism: after nuclear war, self-perpetuating automatic factories with robotic trucks, cameras and humanoid robots keep overproducing useless goods and consuming scarce resources, immutably executing their programming while humans who plead 'we can run our own lives' are condemned to redundancy. Tracing cybernetics from Norbert Wiener's anti-aircraft feedback systems through B.F. Skinner's Walden Two, it argues Dick dramatizes the totalitarian implications of treating humans as machines to be controlled 'for their own good', and the dehumanizing logic of a late capitalism whose profits depend on reckless overproduction, where the system 'gets top priority' and 'mere people come second'. The ending - the factories seeding microscopic self-replicating machinery - completes the vision of a technocratic system expanding and replicating to the possible extinction of humanity.
- ch. 176 "Chapter 29 - “King of the Elves”" **·** George Berkeley — Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi) — Michelle Gallagher reads 'King of the Elves' as a challenge to Berkeley's empiricist criterion of reality: we call real whatever behaves as our past experience leads us to expect, unlike airborne goldfish imagined at whim - which is why we can tell dreams from waking life and why children struggle to. Shadrach Jones, the drab gas-station owner, keeps accepting Elves, Trolls and his own kingship although Elves are 'precisely the thing you wouldn't expect', and his swings of belief track his desires - the grandeur of kingship, dread of the Troll war, the appeal of being needed - until he kills his friend Phineas, the Troll King. Whether the tale is a genuine Elven chronicle or a delusional murder, Shadrach decides he really is King of the Elves because he wanted to: reality attribution driven by wish rather than expectation.
- ch. 177 "Chapter 30 - “The Golden Man”" **·** Aristotle, Lucretius — The Four Causes; Philosophy of Disability; On the Nature of Things — Jeremy Pierce reads 'The Golden Man' through the Aristotle-Lucretius dispute over purposes in nature: Cris Johnson, the precognitive golden mutant, first terrifies the DCA as Homo superior, 'a deeve who would be to us what we are to the great apes', until George Baines finds 'virtually no frontal lobe... It's nothing but an animal' choosing by reflex rather than reflection. Aristotle's teleology - normal development suiting what is objectively good for a human being - makes sense of calling one-armed growth, autism's deficits, or Cris's missing inner life deficiencies, while Lucretius's anti-teleology, largely adopted by the autism community, permits talk only of the typical and atypical. The chapter argues the characters' horror at humanity's replacement by reflex-driven breeders is unintelligible unless something is genuinely missing that is natural and healthy for human offspring.
- ch. 178 "Chapter 31 - “Piper in the Woods”" **·** Henry David Thoreau, Karl Marx — Alienation; Walden (deliberate living) — David Svolba hunts the 'distinct new idea' of 'Piper in the Woods': able-bodied garrison men on Asteroid Y-3 claim to have become plants so they can abandon jobs in a machine where 'the men are parts, and each has his job' - a radical but understandable response to lives devoted to meaningless, alienated labor whose ends they no longer identify with. Reading the story with Thoreau's warning that in a technological world we become 'tools of our tools', and likening the defectors to Timothy Leary's drop-outs, it presents Dick's tacit approval of the sun-basking plant-people as social criticism of a dehumanizing techno-industrial order that sees resistance only as laziness. The darker suggestion is that such a form of life is strangely hard to resist: escape collapses into self-imposed dehumanization, making the story perhaps a parable of drug-like escapism.
- ch. 179 "Chapter 32 - “The Exit Door Leads In”" **·** Plato, Socrates — The Unexamined Life; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Eric Beck reads 'The Exit Door Leads In' as a modernized Platonic dialogue: like Oedipus before the Sphinx, the average salesman Bob Bibleman wins mandatory university admission by answering a computerized waiter's riddle, staging the Delphic 'Know Thyself' against Plato's Gorgias ideal of self-mastery, while Plato's Socrates in Charmides disclaims healthy self-knowledge. When Bibleman's terminal spills classified engine schematics, he decides not on universal principle but on what he thinks the authorities want; his honest answer that he would have handed them over anyway gets him expelled for failing a test he could not read, a double bind showing self-knowledge is contingent and situational. Dick thus revises knowing oneself as negotiation of the state's expectations rather than discovery of an essence, though the ending - Bibleman paying the computer after deciding not to - leaves open that he may one day rebel and need re-education.
- ch. 180 "Chapter 33 - “The Gun”" **·** Theodor Adorno, Martin Heidegger, Walter Benjamin, Hannah Arendt, Plato — The Culture Industry; The Question Concerning Technology; The Aura of the Artwork; The Unexamined Life — Benjamin Stevens reads 'The Gun' - a mindless automated weapon still defending a dead community - as an early statement of Dick's fear that in the Cold War military-industrial complex our very capacities for thought, will and free action may have been objectified into products of a mechanized system that no longer serves us. He brings Dick into dialogue with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry (we are industrially 'produced' as consumers, turned into the carbon-based equivalent of plastic), Walter Benjamin's loss of aura under mechanical reproduction, Hannah Arendt's worry that Sputnik signals an unwise desire to escape our earthliness, and Heidegger's broadened question concerning technology as social control. Like Plato, Dick insists the unexamined life is not worth living: the best life cannot be lived inside a culture that has, without our informed consent, made us artificial.
- ch. 181 "The Master’s Own Voice" *(front)*
- ch. 182 "Chapter 34 - Beyond Lies the Wub" **·** Animal Rights (subjects-of-a-life); What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; I–Thou Relation — Dick's first published story dramatizes the moral status of a rational nonhuman: Peterson's wub, a telepathic, philosophical Martian pig-creature, reads minds, discusses Odysseus and individuation, and pleads that it is 'a sensible being like yourselves', yet Captain Franco - obsessed with eating it - freezes it mid-sentence, shoots it looking him in the eye ('Back on the farm we had hogs'), and serves it for dinner, dismissing Peterson's grief with 'It is only organic matter, now.' The wub's personhood is established entirely through language and philosophy, but speech fails to protect it from being treated as meat, and the closing irony - Franco resuming the wub's own Odysseus meditation, as if the mind survived its meal - underscores how thin the line is between person and livestock. The story thus stages the problem of other minds and the ethics of killing sentient beings who demand to be addressed eye-to-eye rather than dined upon.
- ch. 183 "Chapter 35 - The Eyes Have It" **·** Language Games — Dick's comic story has its narrator read idioms literally - 'his eyes slowly roved about the room', 'Julia had given her heart to the young man' - as proof of a disguised invasion by aliens who detach organs at will, split by binary fission, and get around 'totally lacking in brains.' The humor trades on the gap between literal meaning and idiomatic use: the narrator's interpretation is internally coherent, even biologically reasoned (starfish, unicellular beings), yet wildly wrong, showing how a paranoid reading can make innocuous evidence confirm any theory. His last words - 'I have absolutely no stomach for it' - reveal he has absorbed the idiom-literalizing delusion himself.

## Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Pink Floyd and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Pink Floyd From Pompeii to Philosophy" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Thomas Nagel — Theory of Forms; What Is It Like to Be a Bat? — George Reisch's introduction reads the 1971 Live at Pompeii film, with the band playing to no audience inside a circular stone amphitheatre, as an ironic anticipation of The Wall, tracing how Waters's fury at stadium crowds (culminating in the 1977 Montreal spitting incident that spawned the wall concept) had not yet arrived. It frames the band's post-Barrett move from psychedelic whimsy to minimal formalism as philosophical stripping-away: Barrett wrote like an Aristotle fascinated by odd particulars ('Lucifer Sam,' 'The Gnome'), whose puzzlement at his impenetrable cat prefigures Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and the problem of other minds, while Waters pursued Plato's monolithic 'forms' of time, money, and madness. On this reading Dark Side's closing 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon' indicts Being itself, making life essentially and permanently tragic, a circular trap signaled by The Wall's interlocking 'we came in?' and 'Isn't this where...'
- ch. 6 "Pink Floyd in Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Does Johnny Rotten Still Hate Pink Floyd" **·** Authenticity; The Culture Industry — Reisch argues that Johnny Rotten's 'I hate Pink Floyd' T-shirt was a provocation aimed at the band everyone loved, since Pink Floyd was the exception to late-1970s corporate blandness rather than a symptom of it. Tracing the band from Syd Barrett's disintegration (the ever-changing 'Have You Got It Yet?', his unrecognizable 1975 walk-in at the Wish You Were Here sessions) through the Dark Side triumph and the Waters/Gilmour split, he contends that Pink Floyd 'was punk long before the Ramones and the Sex Pistols.' Where punk used two-minute power chords, Pink Floyd meticulously sharpened an ax to grind: 'Have a Cigar' and 'Welcome to the Machine' dissect the industry machine that cages and commodifies artists, and the whole project attacks the inauthenticity, alienation, and tragedy of modern life.
- ch. 8 "“A New Broom Sweeps Clean, but an Old Broom Knows Every Corner”" **·** Buddhism — Callis interweaves a memoir of the teenage boyfriend who played her Dark Side and later killed himself with an account of Easy Star Records' 2003 reggae remake, Dub Side of the Moon, arguing that the album's themes of time, money, materialism, and madness translate naturally into Rasta reasoning. Nyabinghi drumming, singjay toasting, and bong-bubble effects re-read 'Money' (the cash register replaced by a lighter firing the chalice) and 'Time' (Ranking Joe's 'Time is the master') through Rasta rejection of Babylon, anti-capitalist subsistence, and 'soon come' patience, which she glosses with the Buddhist principle that things happen in their own time. The reggae setting, she concludes, weaves all this pain and madness, from Barrett's collapse to her own ghosts, into something more optimistic than the original ever sounded.
- ch. 9 "Feelings of an Almost Human Nature" **·** Aristotle — Mroz rereads Alan Parker's film The Wall twenty-five years after it left her speechless, arguing it works on the viewer like Jungian lucid dreaming, a conversation between the brain's holistic image-making and linear verbal halves (via Shlain), and that its uroboros structure (the '...we came in?' / 'Isn't this where...' loop) replaces Aristotle's linear plot curve with something closer to Campbell's Hero's Journey, in which the audience's identification rises and the true 'return' happens after the film ends. She complains that most of the film's symbols are over-explicit, since the Judge is literally a talking asshole and the flowers that couple and then maul each other need no interpretation, leaving the viewer nothing to do; the one sequence that earns identification is Young Pink nursing the sick rat that dies anyway. The Trial's 'tear down the wall' becomes the moment the trauma-built self could finally be exposed, leaving the children in the ruins ambiguously alone.
- ch. 10 "Caring Dogs Watching Flying Pigs" **·** Adam Smith, Karl Marx — The Invisible Hand; Ideology and False Consciousness; Utopia and Dystopia — Croskery reads Animals as a beast fable in the tradition of Orwell's Animal Farm that opens with a thought experiment ('If you didn't care what happened to me / And I didn't care for you') and portrays a world without empathy across three corruptible institutions. 'Dogs' dramatizes a malfunctioning marketplace where Adam Smith's invisible-hand justification fails, since success requires lying to those you must trust and ends with the sad old man 'dragged down by the stone'; 'Pigs (3 Different Ones)' targets state corruption from Mary Whitehouse's censorship crusade to war-waging and regulatory capture; and 'Sheep' depicts Marxist false consciousness, the pastoral illusion hiding the slaughterhouse, capped by the Twenty-Third Psalm parody that 'converteth me to lamb cutlets.' The chapter concludes that libertarian, statist, and traditionalist errors each idolize one institution, and that Waters's closing 'Pigs on the Wing' points to the delicate balance of market, state, and community that political philosophy must strike.
- ch. 11 "Thematic Synchronicity" **·** Thomas Kuhn — Paradigm Shifts — Jones asks what the famous Dark Side of the Rainbow synchronization (album plus The Wizard of Oz, started on the third MGM lion roar) could mean given that the band denies designing it. He catalogs vivid syncs ('Time''s chimes as Miss Gulch bicycles past, 'Money''s cash register entering Munchkinland, 'Us and Them''s 'black and blue' over the Witch and Dorothy), then rejects both the Waters-conspiracy model and Jung's acausal 'synchronicity' as pseudoscience, proposing instead Conrad's apophenia and Kuhn's point that suspecting patterns others miss is the lifeblood of discovery. His resolution is 'thematic synchronicity': both works stage the struggle between security and transcendence, Dorothy's 'Over the Rainbow' against 'Eclipse''s 'all you touch and all you see is all your life will ever be,' so the coincidences feel objective because they are subjectively real to everyone.
- ch. 12 "In the End, It’s Only Round and Round (and Round)" **·** Eternal Recurrence — Steiff argues Pink Floyd's music is cinematic in itself: like film it unfolds in time and uses foreshadowing ('Speak to Me'), dynamic contrast, and Kuleshov-effect juxtaposition, which explains why the Wizard of Oz mashup creates any meaning at all, though she finds that mashup a novelty compared to 'Echoes' over the ending of Kubrick's 2001. The heart of the chapter is circularity: the heartbeat that both opens and closes Dark Side, The Wall's interlocking 'isn't this where / we came in,' and the fish bowl of 'Wish You Were Here' make the listener see, not merely be told, that life is a maze of metaphysical necessity, doomed to repeat the same round. Compared to Waters's doggerel 'Free-Four,' which says the same thing about death, Dark Side's forty-three-minute loop lets you live a microcosmic life, and that shown-rather-than-said quality gave a lonely listener the dark hope of knowing he was not alone.
- ch. 13 "Alienation (Several Different Ones)" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "We Don’t Need No Indoctrination" **·** Karl Marx, Martin Heidegger, Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus, Bertrand Russell — Alienation; Being-Toward-Death; Thrownness (Geworfenheit); Authenticity — Detmer argues the four classic albums from Dark Side to The Wall form a unified meditation on alienation, from others, work, nature, and oneself, and reads Waters's stated 'political and philosophical' aims through the existentialists. 'Breathe''s rabbit digging one hole after another illustrates Marx's alienated labor (the worker 'only feels himself freely active in his animal functions'), echoed by Russell on industrialism's life against instinct and Camus on the day the 'why' arises; 'Time''s missed starting gun dramatizes our thrown condition and Heidegger's claim that only facing mortality head-on cures the inauthenticity of living as 'they' do, while Gilmour's improvised solos model the spontaneity such authenticity requires. 'Money' is a satire of greed confirmed by 'Dogs,' whose self-rationalizing climbers end 'dragged down by the stone,' and 'Us and Them' attacks artificial divisions (soldiers manipulated by map-movers, racism's 'black and blue,' the old man who dies 'for the want of the price of tea and a slice'). 'Another Brick in the Wall (Part 2)' indicts indoctrination, being told what to think, rather than education itself, making independent critical thought the road to the Sartrean autonomy and responsibility the chapter urges.
- ch. 15 "Would You Help Me to Carry the Stone" **·** Albert Camus, Plato, G.W.F. Hegel, Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus; Allegory of the Cave; Rebellion and Revolt — Weinstein argues critics who call Waters a gloomy misanthrope misread him: he is an existentialist whose work maps point for point onto Camus's absurd, the human demand for unity endlessly frustrated. Waters's imagery tracks Camus's: the sun (Plato's cave symbol of the good, and the light Sisyphus loved on earth) against the eclipsed moon of death and madness; the stone we secrete through failed communication ('the bad blood slows and turns to stone' in 'Dogs,' 'would you help me to carry the stone' in The Wall) against Sisyphus's rock; and Pink's Trial, condemned for 'showing feelings of an almost human nature,' replaying Meursault's condemnation for failing to cry at his mother's funeral. Since the institutions of home, school, military, and the music industry's machine block every genuine encounter, Waters's persistence in making art that mostly fails to communicate is itself the absurd revolt, so with Camus one must imagine Sisyphus happy, and Weinstein imagines Waters happy too.
- ch. 16 "The Eclipse of Musical Alienation" **·** Theodor Adorno, Karl Marx — The Culture Industry; Alienation — Macan uses Adorno to measure Pink Floyd's career-long confrontation with alienation: after 'Echoes' fused metaphysical loneliness ('I am you and what I see is me') with an explicitly Marxist account of capitalist atomization and commodification, the early epics 'Interstellar Overdrive,' 'Careful with that Axe, Eugene,' 'Set the Controls,' and 'Echoes' unknowingly resurrected Stravinsky's primitivism, their LSD-shaped structures (dechronization, depersonalization, dynamization) modeling the ego's dissolution and reintegration through climactic 'breakthrough' passages of maximum alienation, just as Schoenberg's twelve-tone music 'points out the ills of society' by musically modeling them. Against Adorno's 'On Popular Music,' he argues the early Floyd audience sought challenge rather than reassurance, but that from Dark Side onward the increasingly conventional music, polished by producer Bob Ezrin on The Wall, began 'hearing for the listener,' so Waters's plainspoken social critique lost its transgressive force. The Adornian moral is that you cannot critique alienation through music that is no longer itself alienating.
- ch. 17 "There is No Dark Side of the Moon Really. Matter of Fact It’s All Dark" **·** Martin Buber, Friedrich Nietzsche, The Buddha — I–Thou Relation; The Death of God; Buddhism — Johnston reads The Dark Side of the Moon through Buber's I and Thou: modern life traps us in the I-It mode of experience, from 'Welcome to the Machine' to teachers who treat students as replaceable Its ('Hey, teacher, leave us kids alone!') and Horkheimer's instrumental reason that turns personnel into 'human resources,' while the album repeatedly calls us to the I-You encounter, from 'Echoes'' strangers whose glances meet ('I am you and what I see is me,' Waters's origin of empathy) to 'Breathe''s 'don't be afraid to care.' He links the opening heartbeat and the breath of 'Breathe' to Buber's eternal You, defends Buddhism against Buber's charge that enlightenment is worldless monologue (the Buddha becomes one with the world, a perfect reciprocity like the innate You of the womb), and accepts Nietzsche's point that the Enlightenment's abstract God is dead while insisting, with Buber, that encounter with the eternal You remains possible. The album itself, he concludes, resists degenerating into an It: even if 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon,' the light persists and Dark Side can be the antidote to the It-world.
- ch. 18 "Apples and Oranges Or Just Apples" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "To Join in with the Game" **·** John Locke, Immanuel Kant — Personal Identity (memory theory); Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Gracyk argues Waters is wrong that Pink Floyd ended when he quit in 1985: Waters's case rests on an illicit use of the identity of indiscernibles, since if losing Waters's lyrics destroys the band's identity, then losing Barrett's or Wright's, or adding 'Lucifer Sam,' would too, which proves too much. Borrowing Locke's distinction between the same man and the same person (the oak that remains the same oak through change; the unrecognized Syd in Abbey Road's Studio Three) and Kant's contrast between free and dependent beauty to explain how intentions change aesthetic evaluation, he defends actual intentionalism over hypothetical intentionalism: Hendrix really sings 'kiss the sky,' and interviews with Waters genuinely aid interpretation of Wish You Were Here. He then argues for collective agency, that groups can have intentions through members charged to act responsibly on the group's behalf, so no single member can disband a collective: Waters had a duty to leave, Gilmour, Mason, and Wright were entitled to continue the group's longstanding intention of making and performing original music, and the Echoes compilation is therefore an accurate portrait of the real Pink Floyd.
- ch. 20 "Absolutely Curtains" **·** Derek Parfit — Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity — Michael Patton retells the Ship of Theseus (his 'Trump Princess' rebuilt part-by-part from spares, then duplicated from the salvaged parts) to ask whether Pink Floyd survived its upheavals: Bob Klose's pre-Piper exit, Syd Barrett's 1968 dismissal ('No, fuck it, let's not bother' on the drive to Southampton), Rick Wright's firing during The Wall, and Roger Waters's 1985 lawsuit to stop Gilmour and Mason using the name. Roster, stylistic ('Lucifer Sam' versus 'Money'), legal, and nominal criteria each fail, so he proposes an 'Officeholder View' of identity in which constituencies decide sameness — as when UFO Club's Joe Boyd saw a different Syd at the June 1967 show, while the author's locked-in brother Josh (like Bauby in The Diving Bell and the Butterfly) remained the same son and brother to his family. Parfit's claim that survival tracks memory and personality rather than body underwrites the 'death of a thousand cuts' scenario: the band's criteria, not Syd's own, ended the life of the person 'Syd Barrett', and he didn't get a vote.
- ch. 21 "Wondering and Dreaming. The Words Have Different Meanings" **·** René Descartes, Ludwig Wittgenstein, George Berkeley, John Locke — Philosophical Skepticism; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); The Private Language Argument — Scott Calef argues that the causal theory of perception — the inflatable pig over Battersea reaches you only as an internal representation — breeds Cartesian skepticism: the dreaming argument, asylum inmates who don't know they're mad ('the lunatic is in my head'), the evil demon, and the modern brain-in-a-vat version behind The Matrix. Locke's unknowable substratum behind the Dark Side jacket's qualities and Berkeley's idealism deepen the veil of perception, with 'Julia Dream', Waters's 'If I go insane, please don't stick your wires in my brain', and Syd's 'Jugband Blues' self-diagnosis as Floyd illustrations. Against skepticism he deploys mutual corroboration ('It takes two to know'), J.L. Austin's point that waking experience is qualitatively unlike dreams ('A Pillow of Winds': 'the dream is gone'), and Wittgenstein's beetle-in-a-box private language argument (rebranded as Lucifer Sam's cat) — a purely private language is impossible, so skepticism expressed in language defeats itself, leaving the Barrett-era enigma to keep philosophy's original wonder alive.
- ch. 22 "Meet You on the Dark Side of the Moon" **·** Karl Marx, Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Parmenides, G.W.F. Hegel, Jacques Derrida — Alienation; Being and Changelessness; The Dialectic — Jere Surber frames Pink Floyd as musical heirs to Parmenides's 'path of Non-Being', then maps Marx's four alienations onto the catalog: self-alienation in 'Brain Damage' ('There's someone in my head, but it's not me'), alienation by things in 'Welcome to the Machine', alienation from other persons in 'Us and Them' and The Final Cut's war trauma, and alienation from species-being in Animals ('Dogs'). Existential absence follows: Sartre's café scene, where the whole ensemble arranges itself around the missing Pierre, parallels the absent Syd and the father killed in World War II behind The Wall ('Comfortably Numb': 'the child is grown, the dream is gone'), while Heidegger's withdrawal of Being accounts for the cosmic Angst of 'Eclipse' and Obscured by Clouds. A postmodern coda reads the band's mid-thought-breaking lyrics and Ummagumma sound experiments as Derridean différance woven through language and sound.
- ch. 23 "The Sun Is Eclipsed by the Moon" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Phenomenology; Radical Freedom and Responsibility — Randall Auxier uses Sartre's Psychology of Imagination to explain what 'Brain Damage' and 'Eclipse' do to a listener: auditory images live in time (unlike the spatial visual image of the prism cover), so Waters's repeated 'The lunatic is on the grass' and the anticipated drum entrances seize the will through repetition and the vortex of attention, while musicians themselves escape through an expanded 'now' — the trap-door in time Gilmour knows too well. Sartre's four positional acts of the image (positing the object as non-existent, absent, existing elsewhere, or neutral) are then worked through examples: imaging the contingently absent song, the superstition around imagining a beloved as dead (mode 1), and the neutral mode (4) that Pink Floyd favors over both benevolent and malevolent negations. The dark conclusion: music like Metallica at Guantanamo cancels the will, but Pink Floyd uses neutrality to show that in annihilating the world you destroy above all yourself and remain responsible for the choice — the sun eclipsed by the moon.
- ch. 24 "The Art of Insanity Nietzsche, Barrett, and Beyond" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "You Legend, You Martyr" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Taoism (Daoism) — Erin Kealey reads Syd Barrett's 1967–68 collapse through Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: Barrett 'surrendered his subjectivity in the Dionysian process' to make Piper's songs — 'Astronomy Domine', the wordless 'Interstellar Overdrive', 'Matilda Mother' where 'the words had different meaning' — and 'Chapter 24', written from an I Ching divination on change and return. 'Bike' teeters on psychosis as the room of musical tunes swallows the singer, and 'Jugband Blues' ('much obliged to you for making it clear that I'm not here') with the motionless Scarecrow foretells the catatonia that ended his tenure, after which the band pivoted from anarchic spontaneity to the meticulous Apollonian constructions of Dark Side through The Wall. Following Nietzsche, Kealey argues that the fall of this tragic hero — mourned in 'Shine on You Crazy Diamond' and mirrored in Pink's exploits in The Wall — affirms life, since art alone transfigures the horror of existence into something worth living.
- ch. 26 "“The Madcap Laughed at the Man on the Border”" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Walter Benjamin, Arthur Schopenhauer — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; The Aura of the Artwork — Brandon Forbes reads The Madcap Laughs and Barrett between Nietzsche and Walter Benjamin: the melting-hair gig and the ever-shifting 'Have You Got It Yet?' show Barrett shedding Apollo's principium individuationis (borrowed from Schopenhauer's lone man steadying his boat among the waves) and submerging into the Dionysian dithyramb — 'Opel''s 'warm shallow waters', 'Octopus''s 'lost in the wood', 'It Is Obvious''s minds 'shot together'. He then applies Benjamin's 'Work of Art in the Age of Its Reproducibility': technological mass reproduction destroys the aura and authenticity (the unique 'sequin fan' of 'No Good Trying' versus a supermarket fan), yet the deliberately lo-fi tracks — audible page-turning on 'She Took a Long Cold Look', the false starts and broken 'yum, yummy, yum' of 'If It's in You' — re-introduce the aura in mass form, subverting the record industry's commodification of music much as the unplayable 'Have You Got It Yet?' refused to become a reproducible commodity.
- ch. 27 "Art, Madness, and Syd Barrett" **·** Michel Foucault, Jean-Paul Sartre — Power/Knowledge; Discipline and Docile Bodies; The Panopticon (surveillance) — George Reisch reads The Wall through Foucault's Madness and Civilization: madness is not a brain lesion but a historical construction — Renaissance unreason, classical confinement, then Tuke's and Pinel's psychiatric regime in which the madman must know 'he is watched, judged, and condemned' until judgment is internalized — which explains why Pink imprisons himself brick by brick and asks at 'The Trial', 'Have I been guilty all this time?' The fascist worms and skinhead riots of 'Waiting for the Worms' are the same crusade for uniformity that drove Pink mad — Foucault's 'moral city' where 'virtue is an affair of the state' — so fascism and insanity are versions of each other, with Sartre's 'Hell is other people' from No Exit as the framing thought. Both the album ('Outside the Wall': 'the bleeding hearts and artists make their stand') and Foucault end by defending art as the last channel of unreason, and Reisch argues Syd Barrett's unanswerable absence was exactly that interrupting void powering 'Echoes', Dark Side, Wish You Were Here, and The Final Cut.
- ch. 28 "Resignation and Exploration—I’ll Climb the Hill in My Own Way" **·** Karl Marx, Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates — Alienation; The Myth of Sisyphus; The Unexamined Life — Steven Gimbel asks how to live with the 'pink' malaise of Waters's lyrics and tests five options: capitulation (Marx's four alienations via 'In the Flesh?', 'Have a Cigar', and 'Dogs'), medication ('Comfortably Numb' and the Prozac-ad mother as one of the 'neuro-chemically well-adjusted sheep'), re-creation of childhood (Nietzsche's child playing 'between the fences of past and future' against memory's 'it was' in 'Remember a Day'), and emancipation through LSD or romanticized madness ('See Emily Play', 'Brain Damage'), with Syd Barrett's vacant eyes as the fatal counterexample. What survives is Camus's Sisyphus — fully conscious of his futility yet 'superior to his fate', imagined happy — joined to 'Fearless''s 'I'll climb that hill in my own way' and the mutual care of 'Pigs on the Wing', closing on Socrates' unexamined life: the answer lies in the searching itself, so living pink means living.
- ch. 29 "Selected Pink Floyd Discography" *(notes)*
