## Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Acknowledgements" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "Let’s Go to Woik" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction argues that Tarantino makes the most aggressively self-reflexive films in mainstream cinema, from the Madonna and tipping talk of Reservoir Dogs to Death Proof's Seventies retro pastiche, and asks whether such films possess real philosophy or merely generate the illusion of depth with a canny wink. It identifies three recurring preoccupations across his work—the irony of ethical standards in criminal society, the difficulty of sorting received information from direct experience, and language as a determinant of identity and value—illustrated by Vincent Vega's pontifications in Pulp Fiction. Because Tarantino's characters knowingly recall similar characters from earlier films, the introduction warns that interpreting their ethics requires engaging the films' play of cinematic surfaces, not just their overt content.
- ch. 8 "PART I - “Everybody Be Cool, This Is a Robbery”" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "What of Philosophical Relevance Is there in Tarantino’s Films" **·** David Hume, John Stuart Mill, Socrates — On Miracles; Reason Is the Slave of the Passions — Bruce Russell argues that Tarantino's films share a pattern—a cruel man's life goes awry, violence erupts, and glimpses of compassion appear, like Mr. White comforting the shot Mr. Orange—but that fiction can raise philosophical questions without justifying general philosophical theses. He uses the Pulp Fiction exchange over the bullets that missed Jules and Vincent to raise Hume's problem of miracles (divine intervention versus a 'freak occurrence'), and applies the accounts of Mill, Gibbard, Hare and Hume to show that even Vincent's twisted code—balcony drops for foot massages, execution for keying a car—counts as having a morality. His conclusion: the films raise, but never answer in depth, the questions of what a miracle is and what it is to have a morality.
- ch. 10 "Freeze-Frame Ending" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Gilles Deleuze — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Aaron Anderson reads Death Proof through Baudrillard's hyperreality: Tarantino's references to Vanishing Point and Dirty Mary, Crazy Larry become simulations that feel more real than their originals, at times collapsing into simulacra that reference nothing but other references. He analyzes Stuntman Mike with Deleuze's account of sadism and masochism—the death-proof car as an extension of his murdering body where pleasure fuses with pain—and argues the finale invites the audience to share Kim, Zoë and Abernathy's own sadism. The repeated, slow-motion car crash is where simulation, technology and the human body collide.
- ch. 11 "The End of the Leash" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Arthur Schopenhauer, Immanuel Kant — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; The World as Will — Travis Anderson unleashes Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy on Reservoir Dogs, reading the color-coded aliases as an Apollonian dismemberment of a primordial unity and the pop soundtrack ('Little Green Bag', 'Stuck in the Middle with You') as the Dionysian music structuring the film from within. He defends the ear-cutting scene's excess as creative Dionysian expression rather than gratuity, answering Ella Taylor's charge of 'frighteningly pure art'. Mr. Pink's survival—professional, anonymous, untouched by compassion—marks the reconstituted Dionysus: all but one color must die for the gang to be rejoined in the redemptive orgy of Greek tragedy.
- ch. 12 "PART II - “I Bet You’re a Big Lee Marvin Fan”" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "An Amoral Universe" **·** David Hume — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Reason Is the Slave of the Passions — James Spence rejects the DVD's profile of the Dogs as amoral psychopaths, arguing instead that Reservoir Dogs is filled with morality of just the kind Hume describes: natural sympathies plus artificial virtues constructed to manage conflicts among self-interested people. The tipping debate shows Mr. Pink reasoning with desert and fairness; Mr. Blonde's excuse that the clerks 'touched the alarm', White's 'Just cops' dehumanization, and the professional code restricting violence all display exactly the moral identity-management human psychology predicts. The film thus indirectly supports a third view on which morality grows from human nature and social interaction—criminals cannot actually think outside it.
- ch. 14 "Are We Going Too Far" **·** Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates — Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Forgiveness; Karma and Rebirth; Ressentiment — David Kyle Johnson distinguishes revenge (personal, emotional, unlimited) from retribution and argues that 'Tarantino's view'—mercy should be common practice yet revenge can be justified—is consistent: Jules buys Pumpkin and Honey Bunny's lives but never waives a right of vengeance, since they never wronged him. He tests the view against Bushido, showing Beatrix's revolt against her lord Bill violates the samurai code, and against karma, which makes revenge unnecessary. After finding that Hobbes, Locke, Nietzsche and Socrates all leave revenge's justification open, he defends it—citing Budd's 'that woman deserves her revenge'—so long as the punishment fits the crime and spares innocents, as when Beatrix refuses to make herself even by killing Vernita's daughter Nikki.
- ch. 15 "The Virtues of Superhumans" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Golden Mean; The Categorical Imperative; Utilitarianism; Humanity as an End in Itself — Rachel Robison tests the Deadly Viper Assassination Squad against three ethical theories. Act and rule utilitarianism condemn killing Vernita in front of Nikki and revenge in general; Kant's categorical imperative condemns Elle's black-mamba betrayal of Budd (contradiction in conception), O-Ren's beheading of a dissenter (contradiction in will), and Buck's selling of comatose women (treating persons as mere means). She concludes the Squad instead follows a bastardized Aristotelian virtue ethics—Bill's Superman speech, contempt for Budd's shotgun bushwhack and Elle's poisoning of Pai Mei define courage as the mean between cowardice and rashness—so Beatrix would be cowardly not to seek revenge.
- ch. 16 "The Finder of Lost Children" **·** Thomas Aquinas, Aristotle — Forgiveness; The Golden Rule; Doctrine of Double Effect — Timothy Dean Roth reads Kill Bill as a modern Divine Comedy: Tarantino punishes by contrapasso like Dante—O-Ren dies by Japanese steel, Budd by snake, Elle by blindness, Bill by a broken heart—and both treat vengeance as a form of truth-telling and an act of love. Hattori Hanzo's warning that revenge 'is a forest' echoes Aristotle on how hard it is to set the limits of anger, while the stories-within-stories of orphaned Nikki and O-Ren enact the cycle of violence vengeance perpetuates. Against this, Aquinas's doctrine of double effect shows every one of the Bride's killings is defensive self-preservation, and the film ends where Jules's arc ends: in mercy, mutual forgiveness and a whispered 'thank you' of grace.
- ch. 17 "Mr. Rawls and the Decision Procedure" **·** John Rawls, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; The Veil of Ignorance; The Harm Principle; Justice as Fairness — Joseph Ulatowski uses Mr. Blonde's torture of Marvin to test theories of punishment. He argues Blonde is not a mere psychopath but a retributivist within his social code—punishing clerks who 'touched the alarm' and cops who violated Mill's harm principle—while distinguishing acting on a principle from merely acting in accordance with one, since Blonde acts from sadistic urges. After reviewing Kant's lex talionis and the utilitarian theory's flaws, he asks whether Hart and Sterba's Rawlsian 'retributivism as fairness', whose principles are chosen behind a veil of ignorance, could justify Blonde's actions, concluding Blonde could not by his own lights have done otherwise than punish.
- ch. 18 "PART III - “Why Don’t You Tell Me What Really Happened ”" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "“You Rationalize” Jackie Brown’s Pragmatism" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Socrates — Language Games; Pragmatism; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — K. Silem Mohammad argues Jackie Brown is a study in aporia and Wittgensteinian aspect perception: Ray Nicolette's purple/white bag paralysis, Ordell's 'Is that Rutger Hauer?' mistake, Jackie on the LAX moving walkway, and 'Across 110th Street' turning diegetic all force a re-description of experience within particular language games. The thrice-repeated Del Amo money switch-off adds no information but displays the characters' differing aspects of one event. Against Ordell's mind-fucking 'logical chains', Jackie's 'that's what you do to go through with the shit you start, you rationalize' embodies a pragmatist view of reason as context-bound use, matched by Max's calmly uncertain 'I think I do. Good enough?'
- ch. 20 "Le temps de me laver les mains, or Bathroom Loyalties" **·** Aristotle — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Randall Auxier reads Pulp Fiction's scrambled sequence through Bergson's distinction between clock time and lived, experienced time and through Aristotle's Poetics: Tarantino toys with the three unities to make viewers attend to every character, and only when the film is re-sequenced does it become 'Vinnie's Very Bad Day'. Vincent's fatal flaw is Aristotle's incontinence—weakness of will—signaled by the running bathroom gag and his unwashed hands, while Jules and Butch pass the same moral test of loyalty, whether delivering the briefcase or saving Marsellus from Zed. The moral: be loyal, don't be weak-willed, and wash your hands thoroughly, since in Tarantino nothing lacks perceptible difference.
- ch. 21 "Zed Is Dead" **·** David Hume — On Miracles — Keith Korcz applies Hume's 'Of Miracles' to Jules's survival of the hand cannon: a genuine miracle would suspend a law of nature, but as Vincent says, 'It's a freak, it happens'—and the testimony establishing laws of nature always outweighs miracle reports, while lucky coincidences (cats surviving four-story falls) are selectively reported. He answers objections from revised laws of nature (the 1919 eclipse confirming general relativity) and from prior belief in a miracle-working god, concluding with Hume that a wise man proportions his belief to the evidence. Jules's transformation is real, but would occur regardless of whether his belief in the miracle is true.
- ch. 22 "Don’t Get Into One" **·** Plato — The Social Contract; The State of Nature — Richard Greene renames the Tarantino standoff the 'ex-convict's dilemma' and models it as a special case of the prisoner's dilemma, running from Ordell and Louis's separate interrogation rooms to the White–Pink, Joe–White–Eddie and True Romance shoot-outs. He argues the standard group-rationality solution fails because ECDS participants have conflicting goals—Eddie protecting his father, White protecting Orange, Joe wanting revenge—and his survey of Tarantino's six cases shows escapes come from luck (Mr. Blonde's entrance, Nikki coming home) or shared interests (Beatrix's pregnancy), never group rationality. Tracing the dilemma back to Glaucon's contract argument in Plato's Republic, he concludes the only reliable solution is: don't get into one.
- ch. 23 "PART IV - “God Will Be Cut”" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Kill Bill Volume 2 Mommy Kills Daddy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Death of God — Mark Conard reads the two Kill Bill volumes as Tarantino's Oedipal play and self-therapy: Volume 1 fuses the movie genres of his childhood with women in the lead roles while Bill lurks as the absent, godlike father, and the Bride's empowerment is traced from the Pussy Wagon through the Hanzo sword—a transformation from 'pussy to cock'. In Volume 2, Pai Mei teaches her that her strength lies in her own hands, freeing her from a masculine conception of power, while Bill is humanized—sandwiches, flute-playing, a heart that can break—so that killing him means killing the father's God-like hold, explicitly glossed through Nietzsche's death of God. The final duel's sheathed sword lets the woman, as woman, defeat the man, and the Oedipal act succeeds where Oedipus himself had to go blind.
- ch. 25 "Like Caine in Kung Fu" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; The Death of God; Perspectivism — Bence Nanay and Ian Schnee argue Pulp Fiction is genuinely Nietzschean, but not by celebrating violence: the film stages the crisis of meaning after God's death through two reactions to chance. Vincent is the passive nihilist—dogmatically insisting the six bullets mean nothing, inheriting gangster values unquestioned, modeling himself on Elvis—while Jules's 'moment of clarity' makes him a Nietzschean free spirit who creates perspective-relative meaning and breaks the cycle of violence by buying Ringo and Honey Bunny's lives. His plan to 'walk the earth, like Caine in Kung Fu' reworks Zarathustra's wandering, and the running toilets gag marks Vincent's blindness to the significance of events, which is why only one of them survives.
- ch. 26 "Sudden Enlightenment" **·** The Buddha — Karma and Rebirth; Zen Buddhism; The Four Noble Truths; Emptiness (sunyata) — Luke Cuddy and Michael Bruce ask whether Beatrix Kiddo could reach enlightenment, reading Kill Bill's nonlinear plotting as a Buddhist interconnected web of causes: Pai Mei's Five Point Palm technique causes both the coffin escape and Bill's death, and Budd's degraded trailer life is karma catching up. Beatrix grasps the structure of suffering and its cause—she locates it in Bill and the squad and eliminates them—but mistakes that for ending suffering itself, and her declared lack of 'mercy, compassion, and forgiveness' blocks the compassion enlightenment requires, while Bill's 'natural born killer' story contradicts impermanence and no-self. The chapter closes on her bathroom-floor ecstasy as a candidate case of Zen sudden enlightenment, left to the reader to judge by how she would one day treat a vengeful Nikki.
- ch. 27 "Our Names Don’t Mean Shit!" *(notes)*
- ch. 28 "Any of You Fucking Pricks Move, I’ll Index Every Motherfucking Last One of You!" *(notes)*
- ch. 29 "Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 30 "Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "Copyright Page" *(front)*

## Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Radiohead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Radiohead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "1 Step" **·** Martin Heidegger, Karl Marx, Aristotle — Phenomenology — The editors' introduction argues that Radiohead succeeded The Clash as 'the only band that matters' partly for philosophical reasons: rather than stating abstractions, their music points toward analyses of our actual historical situation, showing 'how it should be possible for pop music to incarnate a particular historical situation' (Greif's question). It reads the laser-data 'House of Cards' video as proof that in our world only the underlying data matters, with Radiohead releasing the source code so fans can re-image it themselves. It then previews the volume's encounters: Heidegger's phenomenology and the manipulation of Yorke's voice on Kid A, Marx on the pay-what-you-want release of In Rainbows, and the pathos of Aristotelian tragedy running through the sad songs.
- ch. 6 "Anyone Can Play Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Where Pink Floyd Ends and Radiohead Begins" **·** Martin Heidegger, Herbert Marcuse, Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Phenomenology; The Question Concerning Technology; One-Dimensional Man — Reisch asks whether Radiohead is the Pink Floyd of the twenty-first century and answers that the comparison misleads: where Barrett-era Floyd used electronics to escape into psychedelic fantasy, Radiohead's apparent space-rock is phenomenological, giving voice to pre-reflective experience of technological modern life. He reads 'No Surprises' (Yorke singing with his head in a filling glass sphere) as a study in the political infantilization of commuters, and OK Computer's car crash ('Airbag'), 'Let Down', and 'Lucky' as registering the feel of a fragile, technology-saturated world. Quoting Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and Chomsky on manufactured consent, he argues we can see no alternative to the technologically rational system, and then, against Descartes' priority of the isolated 'I', invokes Heidegger's Being-in-the-world and Merleau-Ponty's embodied subject to suggest that our deepening immersion in technology may be changing the self itself — the truth the collapsing pedestrians of the 'Just' video cannot face.
- ch. 8 "2. - Radiohead, or the Philosophy of Pop" **·** Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Greif asks how pop music could ever 'incarnate a particular historical situation' and answers with Radiohead's portrait of broadcast culture around 2000: an environing, objectless dread in which each person lives at a knot of shouted messages no one sent and complaining only marks you as a crank. The band's turn to electronica was not avant-garde innovation but the discovery of the sound of that second nature, with Yorke's sampled-and-broken voice alternately absorbed into the machine and reasserting the human, and the lyric 'we' sliding between a scared individual lying that he is not alone, a wished-for collectivity, and the ventriloquized tyrant (as with Brecht's Pirate Jenny). Radiohead's church-tinged sublimity observes the storm from inside it — an internalized, inhuman sublime rather than the tradition's safe vantage on crushing power. Pop, he concludes, neither mirrors us nor preaches: it lets us retain and reactivate knowledge social speech forbids, and its deepest effect is not revolution but defiance — the retention of a private voice, a politics of re-created privacy — epitomized by 'There There' warning 'just 'cause you feel it doesn't mean it's there' inside an art form devoted to making you feel.
- ch. 9 "You’re Living in a Fantasy World, This Beautiful World" **·** Aristotle, Robert Nozick — The Experience Machine; Utilitarianism; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Sylvia argues that the split-screen 'All I Need' video made for MTV's anti-trafficking EXIT project — an American child's comfortable day intercut with a child laborer finishing the very shoes the American takes off — argues against child labor more powerfully than a standard utilitarian argument, because it joins Aristotle's ethos, pathos, and logos instead of relying on logos alone. Using the cognitive/expressive distinction, he claims the song also argues by turning listeners back on themselves ('I only stick with you because there are no others'). He then deploys Nozick's experience machine: we are all plugged into a Baudrillardian, Matrix-like media hyperreality that can make exploitation fade into background images, and the video's slap in the face 'punctures the hyperreality', showing how emotion can do argumentative work that rigorous argument cannot.
- ch. 10 "Are Musical Experiences Universal" **·** David Hume — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Slowik uses Radiohead's evolution — from the standard pop structures of Pablo Honey and The Bends to the layered, quasi-classical textures of Kid A and Amnesiac ('In Limbo''s independent melodic lines, the wordless climax of 'Pyramid Song') — to introduce the philosophy of music. He weighs what a musical work is, testing nominalism, idealism, and realism against 'Like Spinning Plates' and its live versions, then pits the emotion theory against formalism in explaining how songs like 'Like Spinning Plates' move us. The chapter closes on whether musical experience is universal and on Hume's 'Standard of Taste': if the test of time validates greatness, then the argument over whether OK Computer or In Rainbows is the better album might actually have an objectively right answer.
- ch. 11 "Art and Belief" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "Rise and Shine It’s On Again Off Again" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — The Look (hell is other people); Existentialism — Surber proposes Kristeva's 'abject aesthetics' as the new pair of shades that makes Radiohead legible: 'Creep' expresses abjection (the creep excluded even from recognition by the beautiful people), the android of 'Paranoid Android' is a borderline phenomenon neither human nor machine, and the bodily imagery of 'Bones', 'My Iron Lung', and the corpse in 'Knives Out' enacts the eruption of the pre-linguistic, formless abject, as do Donwood's dissolving Kid A letters. He contrasts the Beatles' aesthetics of psychedelic transcendence and Pink Floyd's existentialist aesthetics of alienation — built on Sartre's 'Hell is other people' gaze and the being-for-itself/being-in-itself split — with Radiohead's fluid, boundary-less world where meanings never come into focus and no existential revolt is possible because the embodied self is part of the world. Against the charge of nihilism, he reads Hail to the Thief and In Rainbows ('How come I end up where I started?') as postmodern reconstruction: if boundaries and meanings are fluid, they can also be remade.
- ch. 13 "Where Tragedy Ends and Community Begins" **·** Aristotle, Augustine of Hippo — Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Lott takes up Augustine's puzzle about why we enjoy watching sufferings we would flee, and answers for Radiohead with Aristotle's theory of tragedy: songs like 'Karma Police', 'Exit Music', and 'Fake Plastic Trees' sketch fragmentary characters in breakdown whose undeserved yet partly self-inflicted sufferings — 'Just'''s 'you do it to yourself' is hamartia — evoke pity and fear and then catharsis. Singing along makes identification uniquely intense in pop ('for a minute there, I lost myself' blurs the listener into the character), while music's 'natural sweetness' and its dynamics of build, climax, and release carry the purgation, from the terror of 'Climbing Up the Walls' to the slow ache of 'Videotape'. Because tragedy, unlike history, deals in universals, songs like 'The Bends' and 'High and Dry' open onto reflection on happiness, vulnerability, and the culture that fosters isolation, ending in the thin but real community of listeners who recognize their shared fragility.
- ch. 14 "There Are No Unrelated Phenomena" **·** Jacques Derrida, Albert Camus — Deconstruction — Dark reads Thom Yorke's solo album The Eraser as an experiment in bearing witness — from Donwood's King Canute 'Gold Cnut' cover to 'Harrowdown Hill', which eulogizes David Kelly, the UN weapons inspector whose inconvenient fact-checking of the Iraq WMD dossier preceded his death ('we think the same things at the same time / we just can't do anything about it'). Drawing on Derrida — religion is responsibility or nothing, a poem is nothing without the risk of meaninglessness, words remain under erasure — he argues that Yorke's pub-table 'collating information' ('Analyze', 'And It Rained All Night'''s 'a million engines in neutral') is a sacred, self-undermining act of attention against officialdom's insistence that this has nothing to do with that. Camus's line that crushing truths perish from being acknowledged frames the witness, and the chapter closes by hearing 'Reckoner' ('dedicated to all human beings') as the communal fulfillment of that witness.
- ch. 15 "Radiohead and the Music Industry" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "This Is Really Happening (So Do Something)" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Climate Ethics — Milsky argues that Radiohead practice what environmental virtue ethics preaches, organizing the chapter around Aristotle's akrasia (Nicomachean Ethics VII): Sting, who champions rainforests while advertising Jaguar and topping the 'dirtiest band' carbon table, acts against his own better judgment, whereas Radiohead — confronted with an audit showing their 2003 and 2006 tours emitted roughly 11,368 tons of CO2, mostly from fans driving — changed their actual practice (venues near public transit, car-pool lots, sea freight instead of air, LED lighting and auxilary power units). He reads the King Canute imagery of The Eraser and lines from 'The Clock' and 'And It Rained All Night' as environmental narrative in the tradition of Thoreau's Walden and Leopold's Sand County Almanac, obligating listeners to act or risk akrasia themselves, and presents the band's Friends of the Earth 'Big Ask' commitment as linking environmental virtue to human flourishing. 'Idioteque'''s 'this is really happening' becomes the wake-up call to the akratic fan driving to Lollapalooza with a bottled water.
- ch. 17 "C-M-C Music Factory" **·** Karl Marx — Alienation — Tate reads Radiohead's career through Marx: the band's standing tension between what they would make of themselves and what their record company would make of them is the worker's plight, and 'We Suck Young Blood' — with its fake 'we want sweet meats' recruitment campaign — literalizes Marx's vampire imagery of capital that 'lives only by sucking living labour'. Yorke's documented unease about money, from the 'six fluffy wee rabbits' mock-interview to 'Meeting People Is Easy'''s confession that money gets a band 'by the balls', maps onto Marx's account of labour degraded into 'a fragment of a man', whose Amnesiac echo is 'Dollars and Cents''' 'we're going to crack your little souls'. The pay-what-you-want release of In Rainbows is then read as Marx's C-M-C circuit — selling music to live and make more music rather than M-C-M' accumulation for its own sake — a move that removes the exploitative capitalist middle-man instead of becoming one, and frees the band to make their most human-sounding album, fingers on strings.
- ch. 18 "Go Slowly" **·** John Rawls, Theodor Adorno — Justice as Fairness; The Culture Industry; The Difference Principle — Wittkower frames In Rainbows' pay-what-you-want release with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry: music is expressive communication awkwardly trapped in commodity form — even 'Happy Birthday' has an owner until 2030 — and digital distribution is finally tearing that frame down. He then applies Rawls's justice as fairness to music distribution: the first principle now supports everyone's liberty to listen, rip, and share, because viable alternative models mean restricting listeners can no longer be justified as necessary to artists; and the difference principle, with the sadists-objection to utilitarian aggregation, shows that how benefits are distributed among persons matters, which he extends to racial wealth gaps and the affirmative-action dilemma. His conclusion is that we must 'go slowly': listeners' rights to their culture outweigh labels' legitimate profit expectations, the way emancipation outweighed plantation business models, and labels must adapt into service providers rather than gatekeepers.
- ch. 19 "Radiohead’s Existential Politics" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Brush the Cobwebs from the Sky, Let the Genie Out from the Bottle" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Last Man; The Übermensch; The Death of God; Eternal Recurrence — Lougheed reads OK Computer, Kid A, and Amnesiac as portraits of Nietzsche's Last Humans: passive, resentful denizens of the world after the death of God, from the 'No Surprises' narrator begging for his quiet life of carbon monoxide to the 'Everything in Its Right Place' man sucking a lemon over the loss of objective right and wrong, whose isolated malice ('when I am king you will be first against the wall') is perspectivism collapsed into passive nihilism. Hail to the Thief then breaks from this landscape: its protagonists risk transcendence as Over Humans who create new, life-affirming values ('2 + 2 = 5'''s 'don't question my authority', 'Backdrifts''' 'nothing more to lose'), keep a critical distance from society's nihilistic sickness ('Where I End and You Begin'), and test their lives against eternal recurrence ('Sail to the Moon'''s 'know right from wrong', '15 Step'''s ending up where you started). The chapter closes by weighing Nietzsche's over-human project against critics who prefer gradual, generational self-overcoming for everyone.
- ch. 21 "How to Misunderstand Politics Completely" **·** Albert Camus, Maurice Merleau-Ponty — The Absurd; Rebellion and Revolt; The Myth of Sisyphus — Melançon argues Radiohead's real politics lie not in the overt content of Hail to the Thief but in a Camusian movement from absurdity to revolt: 'Exit Music'''s violent shift from Romeo's tender 'you' to the distorted 'we hope that you choke' enacts revolt against imposed rules and wisdom, while the android of 'Fitter Happier' ('a pig in a cage on antibiotics') and the wished-for alien of 'Subterranean Homesick Alien' dramatize absurd life under others' dictates. Following The Myth of Sisyphus and The Rebel — 'I revolt, therefore we are' — he shows how the songs' 'I' becomes a collective 'we' ('Karma Police', 'Lucky', 'Dollars and Cents') whose revolt, like Sisyphus's conscious walk back down the mountain, affirms life without ever justifying murder. Merleau-Ponty's philosophy of expression then explains why the songs are political anyway: artists express a still-unspoken 'fever' (it took years before 'Nude' could be said), creating a public and a common world — politics as unveiling rather than governing, down to 'Electioneering'''s admission that the band too campaigns for our vote.
- ch. 22 "Hope at the Door" **·** Utopia and Dystopia — Sean Burt argues that despite its Orwellian dystopian surface — the internalized mind control of "2 + 2 = 5" ("I'll stay home forever, where two and two always makes five"), the commands of "Sit Down. Stand Up.," the hunted domesticity of "A Wolf at the Door" — Hail to the Thief is genuinely utopian thought in Ernst Bloch's and Fredric Jameson's sense: imagining any different world, even a repressive one, breaks capitalism's "eternal present" and keeps the future open. He traces fleeting glimmers of hope in "Sail to the Moon" and in "I Will"'s move from bunker to "I will rise up," each quickly shut down again by "Backdrifts" and "Where I End and You Begin" yet never fully renounced. The band's denials that the album is political matter because the album rejects both effective protest music (Against Me!'s ironic meta-protest) and ironic critical distance: we are not in on the joke, the joke is on us.
- ch. 23 "Rising Up" **·** Hannah Arendt — Totalitarianism; The Banality of Evil — Brandon Forbes uses Hannah Arendt's distinction between power (people acting in concert, rooted in plurality and natality) and violence (instruments that ape power, one against all) to read Radiohead's violent imagery. The "Just" video shows that power lies not in what the prone man says but in everyone's collective act of lying down; "Sit Down. Stand Up." and "2 + 2 = 5" dramatize command backed by weapons and the revolutionary moment when a king's violence breeds the dissent that undoes him; "Life in a Glass House" and "Where I End and You Begin" depict totalitarian terror, the stage where violence has devoured power entirely. "I Will" ("I will rise up," "little babies' eyes") closes the chapter as Arendt's natality — the capacity of new political beginnings the gun can never defeat.
- ch. 24 "Thinking in Rainbows" **·** Michel Foucault, Martin Heidegger, René Descartes — The Problem of Evil; Mind–Body Dualism — Jason Lee reads Hail to the Thief as a metaphysics of evil anchored in blurred boundaries between self and other: the "radiohead" conceit (Descartes' inert matter vs. thinking souls, Bowie's Thomas Newton) makes the sentient android of "Paranoid Android" the emblem of a self porous to signals and control, while "Where I End and You Begin" ("I will eat you alive") locates evil in the feared Other, glossed through Heidegger's das Nichts (evil as lack, not a thing) and Foucault's account of Enlightenment reason classing unreason as inhuman. He hears "Sit Down. Stand Up." as Auschwitz ("the raindrops could be gas") and "Go to Sleep" via The Wicker Man's human sacrifice, then argues The Most Gigantic Lying Mouth of All Time and Yorke's turn to Friends of the Earth and pay-what-you-want In Rainbows show philosophy is no longer sovereign: discourse with the Other is "responsibility, the call to respond ethically" — you have not been paying attention, so act before it's too late.
- ch. 25 "Radiohead, Heidegger, and Technology" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "At Ease" **·** Martin Heidegger — The Question Concerning Technology; Dasein (being-there) — Adam Koehler reads Kid A's disfigured, barely intelligible vocals through Heidegger's account of how enabling technology withdraws into an invisible backdrop of everydayness: Pablo Honey hides its studio machinery behind "natural" rock, but Kid A — the cycled voice of "Everything in Its Right Place," the unintelligible vocoded "Kid A," "How to Disappear Completely" — forces the artifice itself into view, and with it the withdrawn world technology ordinarily conceals. The song is beautiful, he argues, because its willful failure to communicate feels human, enacting the anxiety of living in an information age that traps as much as it connects; John Mayer's lyric-clearing acoustic cover misses the point, since making sense now means risking not making sense, and the album's demand is that we listen to, and understand, everything withdrawn in the background.
- ch. 27 "If You Think that You’re Strong Enough . ." **·** Martin Heidegger — The They-Self (das Man); Authenticity; The Question Concerning Technology — Matthew Lampert argues that Radiohead's stock theme of "alienation" is exactly Heideggerian inauthenticity: das Man's platitudes made audible in "Fitter Happier," the falling into the world's "uninhibited hustle" of "Ripcord" and "Let Down," and the tranquility that hides both the problem and any exit. He traces the band's arc from the punk-romantic fix of "Anyone Can Play Guitar" (choose and win yourself, form a band) to a deeper diagnosis on The Bends and OK Computer, where Heidegger's Ge-stell and standing-reserve show that in a technological framework only further technological solutions to technological alienation are available. Following "Why Poets?" and Holderlin's question, he concludes that Kid A makes Radiohead the poets in a desolate time: by risking disappearance itself ("How to Disappear Completely," "Idioteque") and singing alienation in its fullness rather than offering false hope, they stare into the abyss where "the more brightly do the ways into the saving power begin to shine."
- ch. 28 "Knives Out" **·** Martin Heidegger, Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Phenomenology; Embodiment (the lived body) — Michael Thompson argues that the much-debated rhythm of "Pyramid Song" — 4/4 with syncopation, 3/3/4/3/3 groupings, or shifting signatures; Yorke says it is only "felt" — is philosophically pointed: by violating ordinary temporal expectations it forces an awareness of time itself, just as Chopin's nocturnes used time-signature changes to voice the nostalgia and melancholy of his Polish exile. Drawing on Gadamer's historically affected consciousness and the embodied, rhythmic daily life described by Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty, he reads the lyrics' row-boat to heaven ("all my past and futures") as a synoptic flash in which one sees past, present, and future as one organic whole. Because Yorke's heaven echoes Talking Heads' "Heaven" as a place where nothing happens, the song's consolation is that nothing lies outside our temporal embedding — with past and future united "there was nothing to fear and nothing to doubt."
- ch. 29 "A Large Rock Saved My Life" **·** Albert Camus — The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus; Rebellion and Revolt — Lindsey Fiorelli reads OK Computer as Camus's absurd universe: "Subterranean Homesick Alien" and "Fitter Happier" portray a technological world drained of meaning, where to belong you must become a robotic "pig in a cage on antibiotics" and "Let Down" offers only the "emptiest of feelings." She stresses that Camus demands revolt, not escape — Sisyphus and Meursault embrace the absurd and thereby become happy — whereas Yorke's lyrics keep longing to flee (spaceships, growing wings, the resigned "No Surprises"). Yet the music itself embraces the technology the lyrics curse, and this, she concludes, is Radiohead's real Camusian move: like Camus writing novels about an alienating world, they carve Sisyphus's rock — modern technology, synthesizers and computers — into new and marvelous sounds, overcoming alienation by working within it.
- ch. 30 "Radiohead and the Postmodern" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "Today I Woke Up Sucking a Grammy" **·** Jean-François Lyotard, Jean Baudrillard — The End of Grand Narratives; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Bradley Kaye reads Kid A as an album made under Lyotard's postmodern condition: "Everything in Its Right Place" ("what was that you tried to say?") and the murmured title track bear witness to the differend, something that must be put into phrases but cannot yet be; "The National Anthem" dramatizes incredulity toward the grand narrative of nationalism in favor of little narratives and local justice; "Treefingers" is the painful silence of the inexpressible, and "Optimistic" an ironic micro-political hope. The epigone problem (Yorke to Coldplay, Travis, and Muse: "Good luck with Kid A") and the closing Baudrillard turn — "In Limbo"'s "you're living in a fantasy world," the Marcus Welby and Perry Mason hyperreal, "it's not like the movies" — explain why even labeling the album "Best Alternative Album" Grammy presumes exactly the stable categories Kid A dissolves.
- ch. 32 "How to Reappear Completely" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Tim Footman asks whether a rock band inside the media machine can avoid becoming a simulacrum of itself, tracing Radiohead's attempts to pierce Baudrillard's hyperreality: "Fake Plastic Trees" as the chain from plastic plants to plastic people, "Fitter Happier" as a simulacrum made of training-manual words, the no-singles Kid A campaign and leaked album, and the In Rainbows pay-what-you-want release that stripped away marketing — only to congeal into a new story about the band's anti-commercial perversity, since the free download was really advance publicity for a conventional for-sale album. Even seemingly authentic moments ("How I Made My Millions" recorded at home, the fabled Glastonbury 1997 set, Yorke's Dublin dissociation that became "How to Disappear Completely") are packaged slices of reality, so the band's melancholia is less a defeat of the simulacrum than a way of manifesting within it — "the best you can is good enough."
- ch. 33 "How Come I End Up Where I Started" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Perry Owen Wright applies Baudrillard's Seduction to In Rainbows track by track: the Enlightenment reduced sex to anatomical biology and Natural Law, pornography is its hyperreal simulacrum (the HDTV of sex, played out in "Bodysnatchers"' "pale imitation with the edges sawn off"), and what re-enchants sex is seduction — an endless game of reversible signs, appearance and disappearance, aleatory suspension, and the trompe l'oeil's hypersimulation. "Weird Fishes/Arpeggi" shows the mortal risk of entering the game (the anglerfish's dangling false eyes), "All I Need" personifies Death itself as a stalker-seducer drawn into the loop of signs, "House of Cards" reads infidelity as leaving the game for the Law, and "Jigsaw Falling into Place" reduces seduction to production ending at the orgasm. "Videotape" closes the album at the pearly gates where even death becomes a sign to be seduced — the home movie "in red, blue, green" is the immortal sign we always leave behind.

## Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!

- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Red Rising and Philosophy" **·** Class Struggle; The Meaning of Life — The editors' introduction argues that Red Rising grips because it mirrors our own world of class struggle, where a Gold-like elite lives in luxury on the backs of oppressed laborers kept distracted by games and propaganda. It traces Darrow's arc from resigning himself to death after Eo's execution, through his carving and campaign of destruction, to the discovery that friendship with Sevro, Mustang, Victra, and Ragnar—not revenge—is what actually pulls him out of life's mines. It closes by previewing the volume's questions: whether enhancement could doom humanity, whether Darrow is the same person after the carving, love versus vengeance, how society should be structured, and the meaning of life.
- ch. 8 "I. Conundrums for the Quality Control Board" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "1. When Evolution Strikes Back" **·** Social Darwinism; Class Struggle — Tim Jones argues the Golds misread Darwin: they take themselves to be the perfected endpoint of natural selection and use the Passage and Institute to 'help Nature along' by culling weaker Golds, justifying the subjugation of lower Colors—the same social-Darwinist logic Hitler and Stalin used to dress up atrocity. Using Darwin's own contrast between natural selection and man-made selective breeding, he shows the Institute is an artificial arena and the Golds' shaping of Reds and Pinks is self-serving husbandry, not nature's work. The twist is that the very traits the Golds bred into lowReds—Helldiver knuckles, miner's endurance, drill-floor courage—are what win Darrow the Institute, the Iron Rain, and the fight against the Jackal, so their manipulated evolution becomes the tool of their own extinction, just as Quicksilver's case against the static Color hierarchy implies.
- ch. 10 "2. Not So Human After All" **·** Aristotle, Peter Singer — Speciesism — Brendan Shea takes the Jackal's claim that Golds and Reds are separate species (Homo flameus versus Homo sapiens) seriously and tests it first against Aristotle's essentialism—species fixed by necessary properties, complete with the doctrine of natural slaves—and then against three modern species concepts (Mayr's interbreeding criterion, the phylogenetic common-ancestry view, and the ecological-niche view), showing each gives the Jackal ambiguous or inconvenient verdicts, from sterile Pinks to horizontal gene transfer. He concludes with Peter Singer that moral equality never depended on equal intelligence or strength: Reds have interests just as Golds do, so enslaving them would be wrong even if Adrius were right about the biology. The deeper lesson is that the Jackal reasoned backwards from his commitment to Gold rule, finding whatever differences his prejudice needed—a warning against 'discovering' biological support for pre-existing biases.
- ch. 11 "3. Hero or Villain" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, Jeremy Bentham — Consequentialism; Virtue Ethics; Humanity as an End in Itself — Kevin McCain asks whether Darrow the hero and Nero au Augustus the villain can really be told apart, noting both hold noble goals (Eo's dream versus preserving humanity) and share brutal means. Consequentialism fails to separate them: Darrow's sacrifice of dockworkers and Sons of Ares to Romulus mirrors Nero's 'I do what I need to do to protect the greater good,' and Harmony's sacrificing Evey shows the same ends-justify-means reasoning. Kantian ethics condemns both, since each lies to people and sacrifices them without consent, treating them as mere means to an end. Virtue ethics finally offers grounds: Aristotle's requirement of proper motivation, developed through Michael Slote, distinguishes Darrow, who acts from love for Eo, his friends, and the Colors and is wracked by guilt, from Nero, who is fueled by inhuman pride and feels nothing at Eo's hanging—so motivation may be what makes one forgivable and the other a villain, though the chapter ends wondering if good intentions pave the road to Hell.
- ch. 12 "4. Raising Darrow" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The Problem of Evil; The General Will; Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society — Trip McCrossin reads Darrow's storyline as an engagement with the problem of evil in both its theological form (Harmony dubbing him Lazarus, the parables of John and Luke) and its secular form, which Susan Neiman traces to the Rousseau-Voltaire dispute: must evil be made intelligible or not? Darrow begins Voltairean—incredulous before the rigged Laurel and Eo's hanging ('She left me')—but his resurrection and political awakening on the surface remake him Rousseauian: evil is the misalignment of individual and general wills, and humans are corrupted by society, not born bad. The chapter reads Darrow's 'Man was born free' broadcast in Morning Star, his new social contract with Victra, and the education of Pax (with Lysander left to Cassius to 'raise him right') as Rousseau's Social Contract and Emile program—break the chains, then educate each generation so its contracts align ever closer with the general will.
- ch. 13 "5. The One, the Only, Darrow" **·** John Locke, Plutarch — Personal Identity; Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity (memory theory); Teleporter Paradox (personal fission) — Kevin McCain uses Darrow's transformations—Helldiver of Lykos, carved Gold lancer, Reaper of Mars—to ask what makes him numerically the same person, warming up with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus replayed on the Pax and the Quinn trading parts. Same-matter and animalist views (Eric Olson) struggle with Mickey's near-total carving and Darrow's restarted heart, and Locke's prince-and-cobbler example, run as a carver swapping Darrow's and the Jackal's psychologies, sinks all physical-continuity views. The simple memory theory breaks transitivity across Darrow's childhood, and Sydney Shoemaker's psychological-continuity fix then fails when a carver splits Darrow's brain into two surviving bodies—a fission case where both new Darrows continue him—while the soul view cannot be verified; the chapter ends with Trenton Merricks's suggestion that there may be no criteria of identity over time at all.
- ch. 14 "II. Searching for Eo’s Dream" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "6. Driven by Love to Go to War" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Aristotle — Philosophy of Love; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society — John Karavitis deploys Alain Badiou's account of love as a contingent encounter founding the 'Two scene'—seeing the world from the perspective of difference—to argue that Darrow and Eo were never truly in love: their glade conversation, his 'nobility of obedience' against her 'live for more,' was two monologues, and you cannot love a memory. He then diagnoses Darrow as a narcissist in Rousseau's sense of amour-propre—self-love turned vanity that lies to itself—whose quest serves to manage his shame at failing to protect Eo, citing Erich Fromm on narcissism's path to fascism and Aristotle on habituation into Gold ways. Only the Jackal's stone-table imprisonment shatters the narcissism ('Man is no island'), letting Darrow embrace agape, with Ovid's Echo and Narcissus and the haemanthus framing the trilogy as a warning against self-love.
- ch. 16 "7. Being for Red" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, David Hume, René Descartes, Plato, Sigmund Freud — Bad Faith; Existence Precedes Essence; The Look (hell is other people); Bundle Theory of Self — Courtland Lewis asks who Darrow is—Red, Gold, hybrid, savior—and surveys theories of the self: Plato's immortal soul ruling the body, Descartes's cogito as thinking thing, and Hume's denial that introspection ever reveals more than a stream of perceptions (we never experience a soul, only thinking). Freud's id-ego-superego offers a secular soul, but Sartre carries the chapter: Darrow is being-for-itself, perpetually projecting what he is not, tortured by the Look of others—Eo seeing a savior, Mustang holding him at gunpoint, Roque's betrayed friendship—and prone to bad faith through 'guardrails' like the Vale, excuses about Eo and Uncle Narol, and pining for Mustang instead of owning his choice. Since existence precedes essence, Darrow is nothing but the sum of his free choices, and to live otherwise is to choose slavery.
- ch. 17 "8. Living for More" **·** Susan Wolf, Albert Camus, Thomas Nagel — The Meaning of Life; Meaning in Life; The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus — Kevin McCain separates meaning of life—why humans exist at all, with no creator-God found in Gold nihilism ('the Golds have no God'), the Obsidians' manufactured Norse religion, or the Reds' Vale and Old Man—from meaning in life, following Susan Wolf's distinction. After rejecting supernaturalism and pessimistic naturalism (Nero's universe that 'does not notice us,' met by Karnus's Camus-like defiant pride and Thomas Nagel's ironic stance), he rejects Richard Taylor's subjectivism via the Sisyphus story: Karnus and the Boneriders enjoy their cruelty, but enjoying it does not make their lives meaningful. Wolf's objectivism wins—a meaningful life is actively and lovingly engaged in projects of worth—which is exactly Darrow's living for more, contrasted with the Jackal's loveless, self-loathing pursuit of mattering.
- ch. 18 "III. To Live or Not to Live in the Society" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "9. Pierce’s Republic" **·** Plato — Allegory of the Cave; The Noble Lie; The Philosopher King; Justice in the Republic — Randall Jensen maps the Society onto Plato's Republic (Brown has said he drew on it): the Color hierarchy parallels the Myth of the Metals' gold, silver, and bronze souls, the Golds' scorn for Demokracy echoes Book VIII's account of degeneration into tyranny, and Leto's 'We are Plato's philosopher kings' claims a mantle Plato himself doubted anyone could ever fill. Darrow's story is the Allegory of the Cave run from below—a Helldiver literally raised in a mine, blinded by surface light, whose return to a shrunken, grayer garden mirrors the philosopher's homecoming—except Plato never imagined the prisoner carved into a Gold. The Noble Lie survives as the terraforming myth fed to lowReds while the surface has been habitable for centuries, and the chapter weighs Darrow's gospel ('we choose who we are') against Plato's caveats: you can choose who to be only within limits, if you are lucky and greatly helped.
- ch. 20 "10. Virtue Rising" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Aristotle on Friendship (philia); The Noble Lie — Darci Doll argues the Rising exposes the Society's intellectual oppression—each Color denied education and fed 'noble lies' about its role—and that lifting it sparks an 'Intellectual Reformation' proving Color does not dictate potential: Darrow out-performing Golds, Orion the un-carved Blue, Ragnar and Sefi exceeding their station. She uses Plato's Republic (producers, auxiliaries, guardians, the lower orders kept obedient by Noble Lies like the Reds' terraforming myth) as the Society's blueprint, then turns to Aristotle: potential is realized only through the right environment, instruction, and habituated character, and Darrow's practical wisdom—testing himself, reassessing after Titus and Cassius, doing what makes him his best self—lets him flourish and lead. Aristotle's critique of utility-only relations explains why the Society's alliances expire (Antonia executed once useless) while Darrow and Mustang's virtue friendships and just rule endure, opening a society where everyone, including women and lowColors denied opportunity rather than ability, can maximize potential.
- ch. 21 "11. Beautiful Colors and Unjust Societies" **·** Plato — Utopia and Dystopia; Justice in the Republic — Devon Brickhouse-Bryson asks whether the Society, plainly dystopian with respect to justice, might nonetheless be utopian with respect to beauty. Treating a society as an abstract object—a system of persons ordered into a community, not reducible to its members or its gravBoots and razors—and beauty as harmoniousness, the ordering of parts into a unified whole in the tradition of Aristotle, Aquinas, and Hutcheson, he shows the Color system straightforwardly instantiates that definition, each caste an organ of one well-functioning clock. But the harmony holds only if the castes are genuinely teleologically distinct; if that is mere Gold propaganda, the Society is not beautiful but a cacophony. Either way the chapter's real lesson stands against Plato: identifying justice with each part fulfilling its role conflates beauty with justice, and the Society shows how radically the two can come apart—possibly beautiful and radically unjust at once.
- ch. 22 "12. The Law of Red Rising" **·** Antonio Gramsci, Thomas Hobbes, Thomas Aquinas, John Locke, Jeremy Bentham — Cultural Hegemony; Natural Law; The State of Nature; The Social Contract — Christopher Ketcham frames the Society through jurisprudence's debate between natural and positive law, opening with Gramsci's hegemony: Reds have internalized the Golds' message that their slave toil is heroic terraforming service, becoming 'enabled martyrs' who hate rival clans rather than their rulers. He deploys Hobbes's state of nature versus state of laws (Reds live in a state of war against Mars while Golds legislate in a state of law), Locke's suggestion that a sovereign can leave some people in the state of nature, Aquinas-style higher law, and H.L.A. Hart's positivism with Bentham and Austin—a law need not be moral to be law—to argue the Golds' caste statutes are valid yet ungrounded. His coda casts Darrow as Homer Plessy: Goldness, like whiteness in Plessy v. Ferguson, is inheritable property Reds cannot claim, and because Reds who speak are hanged, the law excludes the very voices Hart himself said keep laws from becoming terrible.
- ch. 23 "IV. The Rising and Beyond" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "13. Mustang’s Future Generations" **·** Derek Parfit, John Rawls — The Veil of Ignorance; Justice as Fairness; Utilitarianism; The Difference Principle — Courtland Lewis asks what Mustang owes future generations when rebuilding the Society, first showing that standard moral theories stall: nonexistent people lack rationality, cannot contract, cannot be treated virtuously, and utilitarian forecasting fails since we cannot know whether the Jackal's nuking of Luna might have led, in the deep future, to prosperity. Derek Parfit's Reasons and Persons then strikes: any policy choice creates a different future generation, total utility drives the Repugnant Conclusion (a maximally populous world of barely-worth-living lives, uncomfortably like the Society's Reds), and average utility yields the mere addition paradox (Mustang's Society is both no worse off and worse off when Andromeda's low-pleasure civilization is added). The chapter's solution is Rawls: the original position behind the veil of ignorance—where the Sovereign would not know she is a Gold—yields justice as fairness and maximin reasoning for the just savings problem, choosing to save more than is consumed; against Tim Mulgan's objection that this loops back to the Repugnant Conclusion, Lewis answers that real carrying capacities make the repugnant world impossible.
- ch. 25 "14. Guns Don’t Kill Colors—Colors Kill Colors" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Thomas Aquinas, Augustine of Hippo — Doctrine of Double Effect; The State of Nature; The Ethics of Political Violence — Robert Arp argues from Hobbes's right of nature—self-preservation as the first law found out by reason—that individuals, and by extension oppressed peoples, have a right to the means of lethal defense, so arming the lowColors of the Society is justified. He weighs pacifist counterpoints (Augustine on self-defense as inordinate self-love, the Buddhist first precept, Camus's refusal to kill) and answers with Aquinas's principle of double effect: Darrow destroying the flagship to save Luna, intending the good while foreseeing the deaths, is justified, as is killing in defense of innocent children the Institute rapes and eats. The Society then illustrates why disarmament enables tyranny—Hideyoshi's Sword Hunt, Stalin's weapons bans, the Golds' razor monopoly—so that when lowColors finally receive weapons in Morning Star they become the means by which the police state falls: guns equalize the weak against aggressors and the people against the state.
- ch. 26 "15. Death Begets Death" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant — Forgiveness; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Tripartite Soul; The Golden Mean — The Bocks trace Darrow's education out of vengeance: in Plato's tripartite soul the spirited part (anger) must obey reason, and Aristotle's virtue of mildness—anger at the right things, toward the right people, for the right length of time—is the golden mean between slavish and irascible that Darrow has not yet reached. Darrow learns the difference when he hands Titus over to Cassius's vendetta and admits 'That wasn't justice': retribution in Kant's lex talionis tradition must be dispassionate and proportional, while vengeance is past-oriented and insatiable, and Darrow's own bombing of the Ganymede docks shows how troubling even his 'justice' remains. Against Darrow's violent justice-in-love the chapter sets Martin Luther King Jr.'s agape and loving-forgiveness—Sevro hanging and then forgiving Cassius, Darrow forgiving Tactus, Mustang pulling her brother's legs for a merciful death—closing with King's warning that constructive ends can never justify destructive means, and Darrow's own admission that 'the war is not over.'
- ch. 27 "16. Can We All Get Along" **·** John Locke — Forgiveness; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Natural Rights — Courtland Lewis tackles transitional justice after atrocity: with the Rising won, what is to be done with millions of Golds complicit in slavery, rape, and torture? He tests Peter French's virtuous vengeance—punishment that fits the wrong, grounded in Locke's natural rights—and finds Darrow's destruction of Gold society fails it (disproportionate, unsober, punishing young Julian for his ancestors' crimes), then turns to Jessica Wolfendale's argument that declaring anyone unforgivable adopts the wrongdoer's own devaluing outlook, exactly as Darrow becomes what he despises. The working model is South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission—confession, conditional amnesty, truth-telling, reparations, Tutu, Mandela, Beth Savage hoping to meet her bomber—applied to Mars through Mustang-style dignified engagement on Adam Michnik's model and Slavenka Drakulic's lesson that every Color inherits responsibility for rejecting the Society's past.
- ch. 28 "Guide to the World of Red Rising" *(notes)*

- ch. 30 "Howlers, Helldivers, and Peerless Scarred" *(notes)*

## Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Rick and Morty and Philosophy In the Beginning Was the Squanch" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Rick and Morty and Philosophy In the Beginning Was the Squanch" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Rick and Morty and Philosophy In the Beginning Was the Squanch" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Scientifically, Introductions Are an Idiot Thing" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates — The Meaning of Life; The Death of God; The Unexamined Life — The introduction frames the whole book through the Rick/Jerry opposition: Rick is a Nietzschean artist-creator who insists the world is objectively meaningless and Godless yet keeps choosing his family, while Jerry is the herd-animal chasing socially approved values. It claims the show, like Nietzsche's deliberately difficult writing, sorts its audience into Jerrys who enjoy the dick jokes and Ricks who do the hard philosophical work of finding microscopic meaning in a meaningless cosmos. It closes with Socrates's 'unexamined life is not worth living' to justify submitting to philosophy's perplexity even if the Eyehole Man kicks the shit out of you.
- ch. 10 "I So We Bailed on That Reality and We Came to This One" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "1. The Genuine Article" **·** Robert Nozick, Plato — The Experience Machine; Personal Identity; Truth as What Works — Written in the voice of a non-C-137 Rick, the chapter argues that whether the Beth at the end of 'The ABCs of Beth' is a clone doesn't matter, because our reverence for 'the genuine article' (like the original US Constitution) is romantic packaging, and a functional clone is as good as the original. It tests Robert Nozick's experience machine, whose three objections supposedly show we value genuine reality intrinsically, against Rick's pragmatism of believing what is useful, and reads 'The Wedding Squanchers' (Rick turning himself in to the Federation) as proof that his family is both instrumentally and intrinsically valuable to him. Your answer to the clone question, it concludes, is a Rorschach test revealing what you place intrinsic value on.
- ch. 12 "2. The Unimportance of Identity When You Have a Portal Gun" **·** Derek Parfit, John Locke — Teleporter Paradox (personal fission); Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory) — The chapter argues Rick C-137 is already dead: the Brainalyzer body-hops in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' and the Operation Phoenix swap in 'Big Trouble in Little Sanchez' copy psychological states rather than transfer a consciousness, so each post-transfer Rick is a new psychological clone, exactly as in Parfit's Teletransporter. Building from Locke's memory theory of personal identity to Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, it reads the dimension-hop in 'Rick Potion #9', the Morty voucher, and the ambiguous clone Beth of 'The Rickchurian Mortydate' as the show itself endorsing psychological continuity over numerical identity. What matters is that someone carries on Rick's desires and relationships, so nobody noticed the protagonist's death.
- ch. 13 "3. The M. Night Sh-imulation Hypothesis" **·** Nick Bostrom, Plato, René Descartes, William Paley — The Simulation Hypothesis; Allegory of the Cave; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Philosophical Skepticism — The chapter runs Bostrom's simulation argument against 'M. Night Shaym-Aliens!', where the Zigerions trap Rick in simulations-within-simulations to steal his concentrated dark matter formula, and reads their cheap shortcuts ('My man!' NPCs, human music, Jerry's Appley award) as the glitches and shadow-people Bostrom predicts. It presses the epistemological problem that any evidence for the simulation equally supports its denial, an underdetermination that devastates the theory, and traces the lineage of 'the real world isn't real' through Plato's summoners and allegory of the cave, Descartes's dream doubt, and Paley's design analogy (Morty as the beautiful machine), ending with the microverse battery of 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy': this is the universe we live in, so get used to it.
- ch. 14 "4. Could a Divine Creator Turn Out to Be a Selfish Jerk" **·** William Paley, Alvin Plantinga, Plato, David Hume — The Watchmaker Argument (design); Euthyphro Dilemma; The Ontological Argument — Using 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy', where Morty discovers Rick's car battery is a microverse of gooble-box workers ('slavery with extra steps'), the chapter asks whether a universe's designer must be a perfect God or could be a clever jerk like Rick. It lays out Paley's watchmaker teleological argument, Hume's point that even a real designer need not be morally perfect, the Euthyphro dilemma against Divine Command Theory (would Rick's commands for middle-finger greetings become morally good?), and Plantinga's modal ontological argument recast across the show's multiverse of possible worlds like the one where Hitler cured cancer. It concludes that Rick's advice to just not think about it is exactly what Socrates refused to do.
- ch. 15 "5. Who’d Rick Kill Or, Who Killed Rick" **·** David Lewis, Gottfried Leibniz — Possible Worlds; Personal Identity — Framing Rick's massacre of the Council of Ricks in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' as a crime-scene investigation, the chapter asks whether killing qualitatively identical Ricks is murder or suicide. It contrasts Leibniz's abstractionism (possible worlds as mere descriptions, pictured as the Palace of Fates in the Theodicy, allowing transworld identity via essential properties) with David Lewis's concretism/modal realism (all worlds really exist but are causally isolated, with world-bound individuals and counterpart theory instead of transworld identity). The show, it argues, is a modified concretism: portals let people interact across worlds, so Rick C-137 murdered distinct cosmic doppelgangers, not himself, as the interdimensional cable channels of 'Rixty Minutes' confirm.
- ch. 16 "6. Truth in a Multiverse" **·** David Lewis — Possible Worlds — Expanding outward from Rick's garage to define a 'world' as everything spatiotemporally connected, the chapter explains truth via the correspondence theory (claims are true when they match actual events, like the 2016 election) and the coherence theory (for truths like googol arithmetic that correspond to nothing). It argues that in Rick and Morty's world possible worlds are not abstract tools but real alternate timelines: Beth really could have been a human doctor and Jerry really could have been on DiCaprio's yacht, as 'Rixty Minutes' shows, and the Cronenberg timeline's brave Jerry proves a non-weenie Jerry is possible. Yet infinite timelines may still miss possibilities (Jerry's favorite even number), so abstract possible worlds keep a role, with David Lewis the lone real-world philosopher who took them as actually existing.
- ch. 17 "II Come Watch TV" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "7. Rick and Morty as Socratic Television" **·** Socrates, Plato — Socratic Method (elenchus); Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); The Unexamined Life — The chapter argues Harmon and Roiland write the show as Socratic dialogue: in 'Mortynight Run' Morty's confident moral position (saving Fart from Krombopulos Michael is right) is dismantled until Morty himself pulls the trigger, leaving him in aporia; in 'Auto Erotic Assimilation' Summer's faith in freedom is razed by Unity's happy paternalist hive and the nipple-shaped race war it unleashes; and 'Look Who's Purging Now' refuses to choose between liberalism and conservatism when the post-purge town instantly re-founds the Festival. Like Socrates in Plato's Meno, the show's goal is not to teach lessons but to reduce viewers to confusion, because doing philosophy begins there.
- ch. 19 "8. Neither the Hero You Deserve Nor the Hero You Need" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Master and Slave Morality; The Übermensch; Will to Power; The Death of God — Reading 'Vindicators 3' through Nietzsche, the chapter argues the superhero team are slave-morality charlatans whose duty to protect the weak is the herd's imaginary revenge, while Rick, who defeated Worldender drunk, embodies master morality and honest will to power, against Jerry's dishonest version in the Pluto-not-a-planet fight of 'Something Ricked This Way Comes'. Rick's casual destruction of Worldender becomes Nietzsche's death of God, the collapse of the value-source that gave the Vindicators' lives meaning, which Vance Maximus denies at the cost of his life. The chapter then tests Rick against the Ubermensch via the camel-lion-child metaphor and concludes he is at best Nietzsche's lion, tainted by resentment over his lost family rather than the value-creating child, leaving Morty and Simple Rick as long-shot candidates.
- ch. 20 "9. The Fallacy of the Many Heads" **·** Philosophical Skepticism — The chapter uses Headism in 'Get Schwifty' as a case study in illusory correlation: Principal Vagina walks out to pray just as the Cromulons approve of Rick and Morty's song, so the town builds a false cause-and-effect religion from coincidence, compounding false positives until Beth and Jerry are nearly sacrificed to the Giant Heads. Drawing on Daniel Kahneman's System 1/System 2 model and Peter Wason's confirmation-bias studies, it argues the characters reason rationally on the information available but never check whether their information is sufficient, the same lazy thinking that sustains religious faith, ghost photos, and the Loch Ness Monster. The cure is effortful skepticism, stopping to ask whether we might be wrong, lest we end up shooting Mr. Poopybutthole.
- ch. 21 "10. On Being and Meeseeks" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Existence Precedes Essence; Bad Faith; Existentialism — The chapter asks what kind of being Mr. Meeseeks is and answers with Sartre: despite being 'created to serve a singular purpose', Meeseeks exhibit subjectivity, from the self-assertion of 'I'm Mr. Meeseeks!' to transcendence in envisioning Jerry's fixed golf swing and the anguish, forlornness, and despair of 'Meeseeks and Destroy' ('Your failures are your own, old man!'), so they must be beings-for-itself whose existence precedes essence, freely choosing accomplishment as their meaning. Along the way it glosses Sartre's facticity with Morty's hopeless crush on Jessica, essence-precedes-existence with the butter-passing robot, and bad faith with Jerry's assumed mediocrity and Beth's shrinking of herself into horse surgeon, wife, and mother until Mr. Meeseeks reminds her she is still an individual.
- ch. 22 "11. Are You Imagining That Poopybutthole" **·** René Descartes, Thomas Aquinas — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Cogito; Philosophical Skepticism — Reading 'Total Rickall' as an evil-genius scenario, the chapter treats the memory parasites (Uncle Steve, Sleepy Gary, Reverse Giraffe) as Descartes's deceiving demon lodged in the Smiths' reconstructive memories, with Rick's written headcount an empirical defense that methodical doubt undermines. Morty's formula that parasites implant only good memories is shown to be merely inductive rather than certain like the cogito, so Beth's shooting of Mr. Poopybutthole becomes the test case: applying Aquinas's three kinds of ignorance, the chapter argues she remains morally responsible despite genuine remorse because she neglected the chance to reconsider Morty's probabilistic rule. The upshot is Descartes's advice to restrain the will beyond what the intellect certifies: shoot for the arm, not the head.
- ch. 23 "III I Have No Code of Ethics, Just Love Killin’" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "12. Jerry’s Dick" **·** Peter Singer — Utilitarianism; The Drowning Child (obligation to aid) — Twin essays by two dimension-swapped Wayne Yuens debate whether Jerry owes Shrimply Pibbles his penis in 'Interdimensional Cable 2'. Yuen H-232 defends supererogation: like donating blood or a kidney to a Peter Singer figure, giving up the organ would be Good-Samaritan praiseworthy but beyond duty, since it would derail Jerry's life-plan and autonomy, and the artificial-heart alternative makes it optional, while utilitarianism has no room for such acts. Yuen U-964 replies that the life-plan excuse would absolve every shirked duty up to Evil Morty's massacre of the Citadel, that Singer-style obligation to aid stands, and that in our organ-short world we probably do have a duty to donate.
- ch. 25 "13. Rick, Morty, and the Cure for Unhappiness" **·** Epicurus — Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia); Death Is Nothing to Us; The Meaning of Life — The chapter diagnoses Rick's 'Wubba Lubba dub-dub' ('I am in great pain, please help me') as chronic Epicurean suffering and prescribes the tetrapharmakos, the four-part cure. Don't fear the gods: Epicurus's indifferent atomist gods versus Rick's atheism, his panic prayer in 'A Rickle in Time', and Toxic Rick's 'If god exists, it's me' as ego rather than argument. Don't fear death, since 'where death is, I am not', though infinite replacements make Rick and Morty fear each other's death rather than their own. The good is easy to get, so booze, Eyeholes, and Szechuan sauce must yield to water, friends, and family; and the terrible is easy to endure, as when Rick stops resenting Birdperson's wedding and finally turns himself in for his family.
- ch. 26 "14. Jerryboree!" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Immanuel Kant, René Descartes — Bad Faith; Respect for Persons — Arguing that even the interchangeable Jerrys of Jerryboree deserve better, the chapter uses Stephen Darwall's distinction between recognition and appraisal respect: Jerry lacks both, while Rick has appraisal self-respect (he loves his genius) but squanders recognition self-respect by portal-hopping away from every consequence. Jerry's spinelessness is then Sartrean bad faith, from celebrating being 'assigned a function' in 'The Wedding Squanchers' to needing the parasite Sleepy Gary to vouch for his very existence in 'Total Rickall' and lying to Keara in 'The ABCs of Beth'. The chapter closes with Thomas Hill's Kantian case that servility disrespects the moral law in oneself, quoting Kant's worm maxim against Jerry's failed him-or-me ultimatum in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption'.
- ch. 27 "15. Loving Your Pet Is Better than Utilitarianism" **·** David Hume, Peter Singer — Utilitarianism; Is–Ought Problem; Animal Liberation — Against Peter Singer's utilitarian case in Animal Liberation, spare Snuffles because he can suffer regardless of intelligence, the chapter argues utilitarianism fails because it quantifies the unquantifiable, happiness. It turns to Hume: intelligence cannot ground moral worth, since smart Rick enslaving a microverse would then be our moral superior; Hume's guillotine separates descriptive from moral claims so that metaphysics no longer decides who counts as a moral object; and Hume's real ground is sentiment, dogs loving across species as the tail-wagging Snuffles does. So the morally right response to 'Lawnmower Dog' is not Jerry's abuse or even Rick's intelligence helmet but simply loving the pet.
- ch. 28 "IV God, Grandpa, You’re Such a Dick!" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "16. He’s Ethickle Rick!!!" **·** Thomas Hobbes — The Social Contract; Ethical Egoism; The State of Nature — The chapter reads the Galactic Federation as Hobbes's Sovereign: Earth covenants in for security and gets an interplanetary TSA, pill-currency debt, and the surveillance droid Conroy, while the Citadel of Ricks tours Hobbes's three commonwealths in 'The Ricklantis Mixup', aristocratic Council, brief democracy, and Evil Morty's monarchy, where the Sovereign's rules cannot by definition be unjust. Against this, Rick embodies Hobbes's psychological egoism ('the object to every man is his own pleasure'), hiding his motives in the Riq IV hostage gambit and the Szechuan-sauce confession. Yet the chapter argues Rick's egoism is oddly ethical: in an infinite multiverse resources are not scarce, so refusing to surrender freedom to any Sovereign and competing for everything is the right way to live, with 'A Rickle in Time' and the self-sacrifice of 'The Wedding Squanchers' as its tested limits.
- ch. 30 "17. Who Is “Rick” Anyway" **·** Saul Kripke, David Lewis — Naming and Necessity (rigid designators); Possible Worlds — Starting from the mangled sentence 'Rick is the Rickest Rick who ever Ricked', the chapter asks what the name 'Rick' refers to in a multiverse. It contrasts Saul Kripke's view, names rigidly designate the same person across imagined counterfactuals, which would absurdly make the Council of Ricks one many-located Rick, with David Lewis's counterpart theory, each possibility a real world of world-bound duplicates. The show sides with Lewis: the Council says 'Rick C-137', C-137 works like a distinguishing last name, and Morty's 'I eat breakfast twenty yards away from my own rotting corpse' in 'Rixty Minutes' is true only because the corpse belongs to a Morty just like him. The chapter ends by noting Lewis never handled inter-reality travel, so which Summer C-137 Morty now refers to remains open.
- ch. 31 "18. What Makes Rick Tick" **·** Ethical Egoism; Anarchism — Surveying Rick's values area by area, a many-worlds multiverse, atheism ('There is no God, Summer'), scientism, egoistic ethics, hatred of all government, and rap as today's Romanticism, the chapter rejects absurdism, existentialism, nihilism, and even Max Stirner's individualist anarchism, which it says fits the Citadel of Ricks rather than the loner Rick. Its thesis is that Rick is an Ayn Rand Objectivist: Rand's ideal man of reason, independence, and rejection of altruism, collectivism, and mysticism, with Jerry as the pity-parasite anti-ideal exposed in 'The Whirly Dirly Conspiracy'. It warns that infinite choice risks the paradox of hedonism, pointing to Rick's half-hearted suicide machine after Unity, and ends that only chosen constructive goals, perhaps a kinder Rick, could save him, if some other universe didn't already have that Rick.
- ch. 32 "19. The Citadel of Ricks Is Untruth" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Socrates — Authenticity; Socratic Method (elenchus) — The chapter reads Rick C-137's war on the Citadel through Kierkegaard's claim that the crowd is untruth: the Council of Ricks is the leveling public, envying and punishing the passionate individual ('You're a rogue Rick, irrational, passionate'), as Rick J-22's breakdown over Simple Rick's wafers in 'The Ricklantis Mixup' dramatizes, while our Rick stays himself by refusing consensus. From Philosophical Fragments, via Socrates's maieutic midwifery, it draws Kierkegaard's ethics of selfhood: one person can only be the occasion for another's self-knowledge and must then push them away to become individuals. That is exactly Rick's advice to Beth in 'The ABCs of Beth', to leave Jerry, saddle her universe, and become herself, since only Beth can make Beth.
- ch. 33 "20. Getting Your Shit Together Stoic Style" **·** Epictetus — The Dichotomy of Control; Stoicism; The Unexamined Life — The chapter argues Rick is at his best an Epictetus-style Stoic: in 'A Rickle in Time' his total certainty keeps the split timelines perfectly synced, enacting 'choice alone is vice, choice alone is virtue'; his 'love is a chemical reaction... focus on science' speech in 'Rick Potion #9' treats passion as an impression outside the sphere of control; and his 'don't think about it' dismissal of the Hitler-cured-cancer reality applies the dichotomy of control to an unmasterable multiverse. Epictetus's model of hardship as training is vindicated by Cronenberged Jerry, whose struggle preserves his dignity in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption', and the chapter closes with the Stoic promise Rick's life shows: not pleasure but contentment.
