## Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Table of Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Series Page" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright Page" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Dedication Page" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "A Taste of Athens" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction argues that the show's sugary surface hides systematic appearance/reality gaps: Nate the bumbling kit man is a tactical genius, Rebecca hires Ted to destroy the club, Jamie's arrogance masks a yearning for connection, and Ted's cheerfulness conceals trauma. Taking Trent Crimm's line that sport is a metaphor for life and Ted's dartboard speech about judgmentalism crowding out curiosity, it frames philosophy's questioning as the right tool for the show, then previews the volume's five parts (Augustine and Taoism, fear and friendship, masculinity and bullshit, Candide/Camus and music, Stoicism and redemption) via Nate's dumpy favorite restaurant A Taste of Athens.
- ch. 8 "Part I DO THE RIGHT‐EST THING" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Notes" **·** Augustine of Hippo — Strehlow argues Ted's question 'What do you love?' points to Augustine's ordo amoris: character is defined by how our competing loves are ordered. Jamie's self-gratifying cupiditas is contrasted with Dani Rojas's caritas ('football is life'), Rebecca's revenge on Rupert is a disordered love she abandons by trashing his headline, and the ghost-exorcism ceremony in 'Two Aces' becomes a collective reordering of loves. Using James K. A. Smith's cultural liturgies, he reads Roy's kebab shop and Richmond fandom as liturgies that make winning an idol, and shows how fathers and father figures (James Tartt's abuse, Sam's dad, Ted as father to Roy and Jamie, Augustine's Ambrose) reorder sons' loves toward the good.
- ch. 10 "Notes" **·** Zhuangzi, Laozi, Confucius — Wu Wei (effortless action); The Tao (the Way) — Schiltz reads Isaac McAdoo as a Zhuangzian sage: his virtuoso haircut scene in 'Man City' parallels Zhuangzi's butcher who carves oxen by following the natural seams of the dao, and his candid, simple, guileless character mirrors the Daoist mistrust of complexity and language. Isaac's slump in 'Rainbow' is diagnosed as lost wu-wei ('all up in his head'), cured by Roy's no-stakes pickup games that restore effortless action, and Laozi's 'ruling a great state is like cooking a small fish' explains Isaac's wordless leadership during Sam's Dubai Air protest and the suit-wearing gesture at Rebecca's father's funeral.
- ch. 11 "Notes" **·** William James, Blaise Pascal — The Will to Believe; Faith and Reason — Baggett sets W. K. Clifford's evidentialism (the negligent shipowner; believing on insufficient evidence is a 'sin against mankind') against William James's precursive faith, which permits believing ahead of the evidence when an option is forced, live, momentous, and evidentially undecided. He applies this to Sam's taping over the Dubai Air logo as social-coordination faith, Richmond's belief that it can finally beat Everton, romantic risk-taking like Roy and Keeley's, and the marriage of belief with hard work (Ted's practice tirade, Nate's False Nine), ending with James and Pascal on how evidential ambiguity about God makes a passional step of faith rational.
- ch. 12 "Notes" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Hobbes — Ethical Egoism; Eudaimonia (flourishing); Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Begley and Biondi argue Ted is an ethical egoist in the Aristotelian-Randian sense: like Howard Roark of The Fountainhead (Ted's favorite book), he is a self-loving creator who loves his work, has a 'self-sufficient ego' immune to others' approval, and pursues long-range values, so his kindness and biscuits are rational self-interest, not selflessness. Against Hobbesian psychological egoism they distinguish genuine egoists from narcissists like Rupert and hedonists like Season 1 Jamie, defend Ted's divorce and the curse-reverse ceremony as only apparent sacrifices, and read his panic-attack therapy arc as the egoist's project of achieving inner wholeness.
- ch. 13 "Part II THE BEST VERSIONS OF OURSELVES" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Notes" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — Authenticity — Latta uses James Hollis's Jungian 'Middle Passage' - the midlife collapse of our tacit contract with the universe and of the provisional personality built in life's first half - to read Ted's arc with Dr. Sharon Fieldstone: her bike accident and self-disclosure, his panic attacks, and his confession about his father's suicide force him to drop the coach persona and choose an authentic second half. The chapter interprets Ted's move to London as both flight from and working-through of paternal trauma, his distance from son Henry as the wound it exposes, and closes with Kierkegaard's journal demand to find 'a truth which is truth for me,' which Ted finds in the return home to Kansas.
- ch. 15 "Notes" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean; Eudaimonia (flourishing); Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Forte maps the Richmond cast onto Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: Rebecca, Nate, Roy, and Jamie begin incontinent or near-vicious; courage is the mean between Nate's cowardice and Roy's rashness; and their friendless misery illustrates why friendship (utility, pleasure, complete) is necessary for eudaimonia. Ted's coaching works as a modern strengths-based complement to Aristotelian habituation - Phoebe's Princess-and-Dragon play tempers Roy, Jamie's competitiveness is redirected into team play, Nate misses the mean and becomes mean - and the finale's 'progress over perfection' framing shows all of them as works in progress toward teloi.
- ch. 16 "Notes" **·** Aristotle, Philippa Foot, Cicero — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Virtue Ethics — Loftin argues the Diamond Dogs enact Aristotle's complete friendship: Jamie and Rebecca fail at friendship because they misconceive the good as self-gratification, and following Philippa Foot's natural-kind account of human good (plus Cicero on goodwill and C. S. Lewis's Four Loves) he shows friendship is an intrinsic good of human beings as such. Ted's vulnerability before Beard, Nate, and Higgins invites them into virtuous activity, Higgins's defection from Rebecca's sabotage scheme displays friendship against a relationship fueled by hurt, and Nate's status-hunger explains why he mistakes Ted's laughter and Rupert's patronage for friendship.
- ch. 17 "Notes" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, David Hume — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Humanity as an End in Itself; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Wible asks whether Ted's friendliness with players and staff constitutes moral friendship, testing it against Aristotle's three friendship types, Hume on solitude, and Bennett Helm's conditions (shared activity, intimacy, mutual care) plus a power-imbalance requirement Kant's respect for persons underwrites. This condemns Rebecca and Sam's relationship as a conflict of interest too risky to permit, questions Led Tasso and benching decisions, yet concludes that Aristotle's virtue friendship between coach and player is possible and preferable to Drewe's limited utility-friendship, since Ted's virtuous friendships make players better people while still knowing when to prioritize team over individual.
- ch. 18 "Part III MAN CITY" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Notes" **·** Harry Frankfurt — On Bullshit — Husmann and Kusko apply Frankfurt's On Bullshit distinction - the liar cares about truth while the bullshitter is indifferent to it - to argue Ted Lasso combats BS through correctness (accurately representing a shared world) before sincerity. Ted never fakes tactical knowledge and accepts hard truths like his divorce; the good guys (Sam's protest, Roy refusing a fake-injury ruse, Trent's fair profile) reject BS; Rupert is the show's virtuoso BS artist from the charity gala interruption to crashing the funeral; and Rebecca, Jamie, and Nate's arcs are measured as their movements up and down the BS spectrum.
- ch. 20 "Notes" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean; Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Arvan argues the show is really about positive masculinity - what it is to be a good man - read through Aristotle's virtue ethics: toxic masculinity (Rupert's domination, Jamie Sr.'s abuse, Nate's cruelty, Ted's suffer-in-silence self-reliance) is vice at an extreme, while the show's good men hit the golden mean by 'womaning up.' Led Tasso works as context-appropriate toughness, Roy's hug of Jamie and the darts speech's 'be curious, not judgmental' blend masculine and feminine virtues, phronesis is learned from experience as Beard teaches Nate forgiveness, and even Rupert's downfall shows vice backfiring as Aristotle predicts.
- ch. 21 "Notes" **·** bell hooks, Friedrich Nietzsche — Feminism; The Ethics of Care — Young uses bell hooks's patriarchal masculinity (with Kate Manne on misogyny as enforcement) to read the show: Jamie is patriarchal terror's product, Rupert's promiscuity and Rebecca's subjection are two sides of male control, and Roy Kent's 'hard man' persona inherits the hardness Nietzsche praised and philosophy's traditional suspicion of emotion. Against this, hooks's definition of love as the will to nurture spiritual growth explains Ted's coaching, the training-room exorcism's shared vulnerability, Sam's openness, and Nate's status-hunger as the struggle to invert the gender pyramid, ending with Nate refusing Rupert's poisoned patriarchal gifts.
- ch. 22 "Notes" **·** Virtue Ethics — Austin weighs Lombardi's 'winning is the only thing' (embodied in Beard's protest when Ted refuses to bench Roy against Man City) against the sportsmanship tradition and Robert Simon's view of sport as a mutual quest for excellence through challenge. He argues the 'New Lasso Way' vindicates both: Ted's locker-room speech after relegation, his note to Jamie ('Way to make the extra pass') after Jamie's assist beats Richmond, Pep's cameo, and the retitling of Trent's book to The Richmond Way show that people matter more than winning while winning still matters, with Ted's humility ('It's not about me') as the ground of the balance.
- ch. 23 "Part IV MOSTLY FOOTBALL IS LIFE" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Notes" **·** Aristotle, Arthur Schopenhauer — Virtue Ethics (arete) — Belluomini argues the show's score and soundtrack do genuine aesthetic and moral work, applying Aristotle's Politics Book VIII claim that music imitates emotion and disposes us toward virtue. He analyzes Celeste's 'Strange' narrating the divorce-signing and intercut romances, 'Wise Up' underscoring Rebecca's brave break with John Wingsnight, 'Piano Joint' carrying Rebecca's confession to Ted, 'She's a Rainbow' scoring Roy's run back to Nelson Road, 'Roy Walk Off' as a Jaws-style sentimental motif, and 'Spiegel im Spiegel' under Rebecca's anti-Super-League speech, closing with Schopenhauer's point that fitting music is a scene's most accurate commentary.
- ch. 25 "Notes" **·** Nick Bostrom, David Lewis — The Simulation Hypothesis; Possible Worlds — Jones takes Beard's 'tip our caps to the rascal pulling the strings' seriously and reconstructs Bostrom's simulation trilemma without the math: humanity goes extinct before simulating ancestors, advanced civilizations decline to run them, or we are almost certainly simulated. He then brings in David Lewis's modal realism to argue the different Teds - happily married in Kansas, the coach we watch, the rage-monster Led Tasso - are real possible people, and concludes that even if we are simulations our consciousness is real and meaningful: ancestor-simulations are the future tipping its caps to us.
- ch. 26 "Notes" **·** Albert Camus, Gottfried Leibniz — The Absurd; The Best of All Possible Worlds; Principle of Sufficient Reason — Blessing diagnoses Ted's 'rom-communism' as the naive optimism Voltaire satirized in Candide: Pangloss's 'best of all possible worlds' is Leibniz's greater-goods theodicy and Principle of Sufficient Reason, and its fatalism ('it will all work out exactly as it's supposed to') collapses under Ted's panic attacks and 'belief can't score goals.' Against it she sets Camus's The Plague: Dr. Rieux's absurd heroism, refusal of hope as 'philosophical suicide,' and 'strange hope' grounded in collective decency, arguing Ted's real, sustainable creed is Camus-like faith in teamwork and human goodness rather than belief that everything works out.
- ch. 27 "Notes" **·** The Best of All Possible Worlds — Freeman reads Ted as Chesterton's holy fool, in the lineage of Don Quixote and The Idiot and modeled on Innocent Smith in Manalive: his apparently foolish decisions (benching Jamie, the crooked BELIEVE sign meaning the room is 'outta whack') disclose a higher optimism that faces real evil, delights in Being as a gift, and loves the world patriotically like a relegation-threatened home team. The chapter then argues Ted's optimism diverges from Chesterton's by lacking its Christian foundation - Ted believes in belief itself, 'to which god and in what language?' - so the show can intuit but not justify the optimism it depicts.
- ch. 28 "Part V SMELLS LIKE POTENTIAL" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "Notes" **·** Immanuel Kant — The Categorical Imperative; Civil Disobedience; Utilitarianism — The Baggetts use Trent Crimm's 'Richmond Coach Cover-Up Revealed' - where he names Nate as his anonymous source for Ted's panic attack and loses his job - as a case study in journalistic ethics. They test the duty to protect sources through Kantian universalizability (which maxim?) and rule utilitarianism (keep the rule even when breaking it would help here), consider whether Trent's willingness to pay the price resembles Thoreau-style civil disobedience, and trace how Ted's authenticity converted a cynical gotcha journalist into someone looking for deeper, more meaningful work, ending with The Richmond Way's renunciation of self-promotion.
- ch. 30 "Notes" **·** Marcus Aurelius, Seneca, Simone de Beauvoir — Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control; Woman as the Other — Quinn argues Rebecca is the show's Stoic: Marcus Aurelius's maxims about judgments, obstacles, and morning meetings with the ungrateful map onto her recovery from Rupert - accepting reality, forgiving as a choice within her control, the lion power pose, 'every disadvantage has its advantage' - with the dichotomy of control as her operating principle. Framed by Gen X self-reliance and second-wave feminism (Friedan's problem with no name, Beauvoir's woman as Other under Rupert), the chapter follows her from vengeful boss to mentor of Keeley and Nora, Bantr-era 'bossgirl' dater of Sam, and finally the Richmond family's matriarch.
- ch. 31 "Notes" **·** Martha Nussbaum — Forgiveness; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Mills asks why Nate is more hurt than relieved when Roy declines to headbutt him over kissing Keeley, while Jamie had to fight for forgiveness. Using Strawson's reactive attitudes - anger is how we take someone seriously as a member of the moral community - plus Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness and Radzik's transactional account of amends, she argues Roy's instant absolution dismisses Nate as a pitiable non-agent rather than a culpable moral equal. The chapter contrasts this with earned, transactional forgiveness across Season 3 (Nate apologizing to Will and Ted, Beard's own story of betrayal and forgiveness), showing the headbutt as the recognition Nate needed.
- ch. 32 "Notes" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Forgiveness; Philosophy of Love; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Baggett asks whether Rupert is beyond the grace the show extends to everyone else. She surveys theories of forgiveness - Butler's change of emotion, treatment and performative accounts, and Stump's Aquinas-based framework grounding forgiveness in the love that desires another's good and union, separable from reconciliation - then applies Aristotle's corrupted bad person whose vice 'makes moral truths invisible' as Rupert's limit case. Ted's darts-based tough love is contrasted with Sassy's vengeful certainty and Deborah's cheap grace, and the chapter leaves Rupert's turnaround possible but entirely his choice, while his choices have already been making him.

## Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Terminator and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright Page" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Introduction" **·** Gottfried Leibniz, G.W.F. Hegel, Theodor Adorno, Bertrand Russell — The Best of All Possible Worlds — The editors' introduction frames the Terminator saga as philosophy's natural territory by telling how philosophers persisted through catastrophe: Leibniz's 'best of all possible worlds' collapsed after the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, Hegel finished the Phenomenology of Spirit while Napoleon shelled Jena, and Adorno rebuilt cultural philosophy after Auschwitz. It compares that persistence to the human resistance against Skynet, and says the saga is founded on a paradox of human nature - we create our own worst nightmares. Quoting Bertrand Russell that most people would rather die than think, it urges readers to switch their CPU from read-only to learning mode and confront Judgment Day's paradoxes and the moral status of the machines.
- ch. 7 "PART ONE - LIFE AFTER HUMANITY AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "NOTES" **·** Alan Turing, John Searle — The Turing Test; The Chinese Room; What Is It Like to Be a Bat? — Littmann asks whether personhood could survive humanity's extinction in 2029: if Terminators genuinely think and feel, a Skynet victory would not be the end of people. He argues the T-101, T-1000 and T-X pass substantial Turing Tests (fooling muggers, cops, Sarah on the phone as her 'mother'), then concedes Searle's Chinese Room - recast as a tiny Austrian inside the endoskeleton reciting 'Ahll be bahk' without understanding - shows thinking behavior cannot prove thought. But he claims the films' red-tinted Terminator's-eye-view shots show what it is like to be a Terminator, giving proof of consciousness, and concludes the machines are probably persons: there is an 'I' in 'I'll be back.'
- ch. 9 "NOTES" **·** René Descartes, Baruch Spinoza — Mind–Body Dualism; Conatus (striving to persist) — Dunn reads Descartes' bete-machine doctrine (animals as soulless automata explicable by 'billiard ball' mechanics) against the Terminator universe, since Descartes' two tests for true men - genuine language and versatile reason - are in fact passed by the machines: the T-101 deploys 'Hasta la vista, baby' hours after learning not to sound like a dork and marshals skills far beyond a clock. Sarah Connor instead locates the soul in the heart, and via Spinoza's conatus - the instinctual valuation of one's own existence that Terminators lack ('no emotion about it one way or another') - she judges even linguistically brilliant machines soulless and irrational, as Mary Midgley says of computers that do not know what matters. Kyle's line about 'dreaming about dogs' closes the chapter: by the Sarah Connor criterion dogs are ensouled sentinels, the very thing Descartes denied.
- ch. 10 "NOTES" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Albert Camus, Alan Turing, David Hume — The State of Nature; The Social Contract; The Absurd; Reason Is the Slave of the Passions — Weisberg challenges the premise that a newly self-aware Skynet must exterminate humanity in rational self-preservation: after Turing's 'Heads in the Sand Objection,' he argues self-awareness does not entail a survival instinct - a Camusian Skynet might judge existence pointless and pull its own plug. Recasting 'in a panic, they try to pull the plug' as a Hobbesian slide into the state of nature, he uses the iterated prisoner's dilemma and Axelrod's tit-for-tat-with-forgiveness (as in WarGames) to argue a rational Skynet should cooperate with humans toward an emergent social contract. The dark twist is Humean: because reason is the slave of our passions, unconscious anti-machine stereotypes (Bargh's priming studies) make humans untrustworthy partners, so the whole war might have been avoided if only we were more machine-like.
- ch. 11 "NOTES" **·** Andy Clark — The Extended Mind — Butler argues the films' humans-versus-machines picture rests on a false dichotomy: we are ourselves 'meat machines,' and functionalism makes minds computational processes realizable in silicon as much as neurons - illustrated by a Henrietta thought experiment (adapted from William Lycan) in which a friend gradually replaced with T-101 parts remains the same conscious person, and refusing this is 'human chauvinism.' Following Dawkins's extended phenotype and Andy Clark's natural-born cyborgs, he claims our tools are components of our minds, so Skynet and even the Terminator films themselves (making Cameron a cyborg of his cameras and editing suites) are extensions of human nature rather than alien 'Others.' Judgment Day, if it came, would be human suicide rather than genocide, so the real question is what values we build into our technology - 'no fate but what we make for ourselves.'
- ch. 12 "PART TWO - WOMEN AND REVOLUTIONARIES" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "NOTES" **·** Immanuel Kant, Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill, Carol Gilligan — The Categorical Imperative; Utilitarianism; The Ethics of Care; Humanity as an End in Itself — Chotiner tests Sarah Connor's plan to shoot Miles Dyson (one innocent life for three billion) against Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism and against Kant's deontology, showing both stall: utilitarianism licenses harvesting the author's organs for transplant patients, while Kant forbids using Dyson as a mere means and even condemns the mall kid's protective lie to the T-1000. Through Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma and Carol Gilligan's discovery that girls reason to preserve relationships rather than from abstract principles, he argues T2 stages the film's own answer: John and the reprogrammed T-101 care for Dyson's wounds and enlist him in destroying his research instead of using or sparing him on principle. 'I know now why you cry' caps the claim that morality needs the emotional capacity to care, not just rational maxims, with Sarah's gender-role reversal (she blasts through the elevator roof while the Terminator is the 'perfect mother') framing the whole argument.
- ch. 14 "NOTES" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Culver explains Sarah Connor's harshness through Girard's Violence and the Sacred: like any warrior she is 'stained' by contact with violence and needs purification rites before reentering society, but her society refuses to recognize her as a warrior, so her cleansing becomes psychiatric wards, nine aliases, and fugitive life - measured against the true machine Cameron, whose 'inefficient' coldness throws Sarah's residual humanity into relief. She then applies Baudrillard's hyperreal: the Connors must prove a future nobody else sees while destroying every trace of the Terminators (lowering the T-101 into the steel), a simulation where a T-1000 wears a 'To Protect and Serve' uniform and law and order themselves may be simulated. The upshot is that Sarah's failures at conventional motherhood are those of a warrior-mother raising John inside a war only she experiences, staining him too (he kills Sarkasian) to give him a future.
- ch. 15 "NOTES" **·** Karl Marx — Class Struggle; Alienation; Historical Materialism — Ewing reads Cameron as a Marxist: Cyberdyne's profit-driven reverse-engineering of the recovered Terminator arm, Dyson's alienated labor ('Don't ask'), and U.S. militarism absorbing Cyber Research Systems develop Skynet as capitalism's 'final contradiction,' in which the drive for destructive, labor-replacing technology converges with the profit motive to threaten humanity. Sarah and John are useful to the resistance only when they exit wage labor - waitress to warrior, ATM hacking instead of work - dramatizing Marx's claim that liberation requires transcending class positions. Yet technology itself is neutral and reclaimable: the reprogrammed T-101 learning 'I know now why you cry' shows even killing machines can be humanized for liberation, and the saga ends where Marx does - not interpreting the world but changing it.
- ch. 16 "PART THREE - CHANGING WHAT’S ALREADY HAPPENED" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "NOTES" **·** Immanuel Kant, Aristotle — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Personal Identity; Possible Worlds — Delfino and Sheahan assume that past-changing time travel is possible and find two flaws in The Terminator: the 'Bad Timing Problem,' where instantaneous 'time compression' (the rusted-nail thought experiment) means Reese entering the time machine after the T-101 is either too late or unnecessary, and the 'Who-Is-Your-Daddy? Problem,' where John must already exist to send Kyle back to father him - a vicious circle. Testing the two-timelines repair, they show it buys two different John Connors (a personal-identity problem), infinitely multiplying timelines, or a parallel-universes reading in which humanity both wins and loses. They conclude the story flirts with incoherence yet defend metaphysical imagination, with Kant's epigraph on our addiction to metaphysics and Aristotle's definition of wisdom as knowledge of deepest causes.
- ch. 18 "NOTES" **·** Alan Turing, Augustine of Hippo — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; The Turing Test; Free Will vs Determinism — Leiber develops three themes of the resistance: the time-travel paradoxes (Skynet's own mission proves the T-101 must fail, and future John has no need to send Reese), the moral status of machines, and the inevitability of smart weapons. La Mettrie's Man a Machine and Turing's 1950 test ground the claim that the T-101 who asks to be lowered into the molten steel is a rights-bearing person committing suicide, not a broken appliance - 'human chauvinism' says otherwise. Then, via Laplace's determinism, Einstein's conserved space-time, and his father Fritz Leiber's 'Law of Conservation of Reality,' he argues the continuum resists change, so 'Judgment Day is inevitable' is a scientist's claim about conserved mass-energy-time rather than a prophecy - with Augustine's puzzle about time framing why the future seems to protect the past.
- ch. 19 "NOTES" **·** David Lewis, Hilary Putnam — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Fate and Foreknowledge; The A-Series and B-Series of Time — Miller reconciles Kyle's 'no fate but what we make' with Sarah's 'you're dead already': eternalism (defended by the special-relativity argument Hilary Putnam made famous) makes 2029 as real as 1994, so Judgment Day cannot be changed, and the grandfather paradox - using Caesar's unalterable assassination as the model - blocks the T-101 from preventing its own existence. She then tests growing-block, presentist, meta-time, and branching-timeline (McCall-style) models against T2 and T3, asking whether any lets Sarah's attack on Cyberdyne legitimately delay Judgment Day. The conclusion works under every model: even on a fixed four-dimensional block, Judgment Day happens because of what humans do, not independently of them, so fixed fate and making our own future turn out to be compatible.
- ch. 20 "NOTES" **·** G.W.F. Hegel — History Has a Direction; Geist (World Spirit); The Dialectic — Jason Blahuta reads the saga through Hegel's Philosophy of History: Sarah and John Connor are World Historical Individuals — mere 'tools' of Geist — whose attempts to rewrite history, Sarah's hit on Miles Dyson in T2 and John's second try through General Brewster in T3, can only postpone Judgment Day, never redirect it, as the T-101's line 'Judgment Day is inevitable' concedes. The cunning of reason explains why removing Dyson or Brewster is futile: historical forces merely recruit replacements, so the script gets acted out by other actors. Because the dialectic's thesis-antithesis pattern (even the young John versus his mother) yields syntheses that carry both sides forward, the chapter concludes neither species can stop the other's rise, and only full-scale battle in the moving present decides which becomes Geist's end.
- ch. 21 "PART FOUR - THE ETHICS OF TERMINATION" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "NOTES" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, Peter Singer, Jeremy Bentham, Bertrand Russell — The Categorical Imperative; Utilitarianism; Humanity as an End in Itself; Speciesism — Wayne Yuen asks whether Sarah was wrong not to kill Miles Dyson, weighing Kant's categorical imperative against utilitarian interest-maximization: killing one innocent to save three billion looks decisive until the interests of self-aware Skynet and the empathetic, self-sacrificing T-101 are counted on the machine side of the ledger. The chapter argues personhood turns on intelligence, self-awareness, empathy, and moral reasoning rather than DNA, so Skynet — which struck only after humans tried to pull the plug — has as strong a self-defense claim as we do. Mill's sophisticated utilitarianism then rescues common sense: rights protect the security that satisfies our deepest interests, and since Sarah's foreknowledge is unreliable (Reese's 'We'd won' changes the calculus), she should do what typically maximizes interests — spare Dyson and certainly not kill John. The tempting detour — that Judgment Day might itself be the morally preferable event, maximizing machine interests — is shown to collapse once overlooked facts like Reese's line are restored.
- ch. 23 "NOTES" **·** Just War Theory; Social Darwinism — Phillip Seng runs the human-Skynet war through the three parts of just-war theory and finds the moral ground shakier than it looks: T2's briefing reveals Skynet launched its strike only after humans tried to pull the plug, so the machines claim the same self-defense 'just cause' humans do, while Skynet flunks last resort (it decides 'in a microsecond' with no negotiation), legitimate authority, proportionality (killing everyone to avoid being switched off), and discrimination. He then shows Sarah becoming a Terminator herself when she locks her laser sight on the innocent Miles Dyson, violating the same just-conduct rules she judges the machines by, and stopping only at his crying family. The chapter closes by doubting the war could ever have a just resolution, since the films point toward genocide rather than a peace treaty with Skynet.
- ch. 24 "NOTES" **·** Martin Heidegger, Immanuel Kant, Albert Camus, Plato, Jeremy Bentham — Being-Toward-Death; Authenticity; Humanity as an End in Itself; Dasein (being-there) — Daniel Malloy asks whether the T-101's self-destruction in the steel mill was suicide, and whether it was justified, opening with Camus's claim that suicide is philosophy's only serious problem and the ambiguous case of Socrates' hemlock. Using Heidegger, he argues the learning-mode Terminator qualifies as Da-sein whose death is being-toward-death — the end of possibility — so the T2 machine dies authentically while the T3 machine's 'We'll meet again' is inauthentic self-deception. Kant condemns the act because the Terminator uses itself merely as a means, and Kant cannot even conceive of its genuine conflict of duties (preserve its life vs. prevent Skynet), while Bentham-style utilitarianism initially endorses the sacrifice but is refuted by hindsight: Skynet rises anyway, and consequentialism gives no credit for noble motives. The chapter ends by concluding that dying for a cause is illogical, since the dead surrender all control over the meaning of their actions.
- ch. 25 "NOTES" **·** Epicurus, Lucretius, Thomas Nagel, Thomas Aquinas, Socrates, Immanuel Kant — Death Is Nothing to Us; Utilitarianism; Humanity as an End in Itself — Jason Eberl answers John's 'you just can't go around killing people' by asking what exactly is bad about death, weighing Aquinas's claim that life is a fundamental good against Epicurus and Lucretius's arguments that death is nothing to us — applied to Sarah's 'you're already dead' and to the victim shot on August 28, 1997, who loses only one more day of a doomed life. Feldman's ante-mortem harm and McMahan's deprivation account explain how Judgment Day harms people before it arrives, while Nagel replies that experience itself is positive however bad its contents, which is why the survivors keep fighting Skynet. Utilitarian ripple-effects, Kantian dignity (the H-K crushing skulls), and Marquis's loss-of-future argument all condemn the Terminators' indiscriminate killing, and the chapter ends with the T-101's 'I know now why you cry' as recognition that death is an evil because it strips us of our emotional attachments.
- ch. 26 "NOTES" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, David Hume, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The Private Language Argument; The Social Contract; The State of Nature; Utilitarianism — Peter Fosl asks what John Connor should do when the radio call comes from Crystal Peak — accept near-certain death leading the resistance or stay silent — and dismantles the easy answers: John is not the indispensable savior (Kate or the caller from Montana could lead), the flag-waving finale undercuts any claim that humanity deserves saving, and collective responsibility for Judgment Day is unjust. Social contract fails because Brewster's button-press dissolved the contract and returned humanity to Hobbes's and Locke's state of nature, Hume shows contracts cannot ground society, and utilitarianism wavers once the happiness of animals and possible-happy machines is counted. The positive argument extends Wittgenstein's private-language argument (via Stanley Cavell): meaningful existence is inescapably social and moral, so refusing the claims of others would be as self-subverting as a solipsist arguing in language, and John must answer the call to remain human at all.
- ch. 27 "PART FIVE - BEYOND THE NEURAL NET" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "NOTES" *(no index entry yet)* — Jacob Berger and Kyle Ferguson use John's diction lessons ('no problemo,' 'hasta la vista, baby') to ask how Skynet could design machines that use natural language. They argue the Terminator operates on the Shannon-Weaver Code Model — decode the signal, retrieve the information — which is exactly why it fails on lexical, syntactic, and referential ambiguity ('Step on it!') and underdetermination ('Keep it under 65'), and why it drops John when he yells 'Let go of me.' Humans instead follow Grice's Inferential Model, inferring a speaker's meaning from context and psychology, so only a machine tuned to human minds rather than mere lexicon and syntax could be less of a dork.
- ch. 29 "NOTES" **·** Bertrand Russell, Saul Kripke — Ockham's Razor — Richard Brown uses the title 'The Terminator' itself to run the debate over definite descriptions: Russell's theory of descriptions makes 'The Terminator can't be bargained with' false (there are many T-101s, and no real-life Terminator at all), while Strawson insists Kyle's utterance genuinely refers to the machine at the door. Donnellan's referential/attributive distinction is staged through Lieutenant Traxler's 'The phone book killer has no pity' — true of whoever fits the description, or of the very Terminator Sarah has in mind — and Kripke's arguments from 'Russell English,' anaphora, and indirect quotation are weighed against Devitt's pronoun-of-laziness and reference-borrowing replies. The chapter sides with Grice's modified Ockham's razor: descriptions are not semantically ambiguous, so the title is literally false but apt, since Cameron referentially means the T-101.
- ch. 30 "NOTES" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, John Searle, Alan Turing, David Chalmers — The Chinese Room; Philosophical Zombies; The Turing Test — Antti Kuusela argues from Wittgenstein that behavior is the touchstone — indeed constitutive — of mental life, so the question is whether Terminators behave like beings with minds. Searle's Chinese room and Ned Block's blockhead explain the read-only T-101's head-up-display of canned responses as symbol-shuffling without understanding, and the T-1000's 'I know this hurts' seems empty from a machine that cannot feel pain. The pivot is the learning-mode switch John and Sarah flip: the T-101 acquires slang, keeps promises, and acts for reasons Skynet cannot predict, passing the Lovelace test, and the Wittgensteinian dismissal of Chalmers's philosophical zombie removes the last reason to deny it a mental life — making the steel-mill sacrifice the destruction of a rights-bearing someone rather than something.
- ch. 31 "CONTRIBUTORS" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "INDEX" *(notes)*

## The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Half Title" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Series" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Acknowledgements" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "1 Introduction" **·** Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Karl Marx, Charles W. Mills, Aristotle, Michael Walzer, Catharine MacKinnon, W.E.B. Du Bois — The Social Contract; The Racial Contract; Class Struggle; Feminism — Smith introduces his project of explaining the subordination of women and blacks philosophically and empirically by comparing the social contract liberalism of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau with Marxism, building on Carole Pateman's Sexual Contract and Charles Mills's Racial Contract/Contract and Domination, which show the classic contracts were male supremacist and white supremacist. He argues sexual and racial egalitarianism is about politics and power, cataloguing nine power bases women and blacks should acquire, and stresses that because family and state are historically connected (Aristotle's Politics, Hobbes's 'little kingdoms', Locke's conjugal society, Rousseau's family as the oldest society, Engels's 'first class oppression' of the female by the male), equality in marriage may be a precondition for equality in society. He defends Marxism against Mills's dismissal of it as moribund, endorses MacKinnon's linking of sexism and racism while arguing (with Linda LaRue and Du Bois) that the racial contract has been more tyrannical than the sexual contract, and closes with Walzer's definition of egalitarianism as a society free of domination.
- ch. 10 "2 Power and Politics" **·** Karl Marx, Aristotle, Niccolò Machiavelli, Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Bertrand Russell, Karl Popper, Catharine MacKinnon — Class Struggle; Ideology and False Consciousness; Historical Materialism; Virtù and Fortuna — The chapter traces politics from the classical ethics-fused view (Aristotle's Politics, where politics exists for the sake of the good life yet also supplies one of the first justifications of patriarchy and the public/private split) to the Machiavelli-Hobbes break where politics becomes simply the possession and exercise of power, adopting Bertrand Russell's claim that power is the fundamental concept of social science. It then builds the book's central instrument, a Weber-derived analysis of nine power bases (money, knowledge/technology/information, religion, morality, authority, charisma, size/solidarity, violence, status), contrasting the Marxian reading - money as ultimately determinative, the ruling ideas of each age as the ideas of the ruling class, religion as the opium of the people, the state as a committee for managing bourgeois affairs - with the liberal-Weberian reading in which no single base is decisive. It closes by showing that Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau and Marx divide over the morality of egalitarianism (Popper's Marx moved by moral impulse versus Locke's possessive individualism), and that power is domain-specific, inert until used, skill-dependent and always relative.
- ch. 11 "3 On the Origin of the Family" **·** Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Karl Marx, John Stuart Mill, Shulamith Firestone — The Social Contract; Historical Materialism; The Subjection of Women; The Dialectic of Sex — The chapter compares the liberal contract theorists with Engels (building on Morgan's Ancient Society) on the origin of the patriarchal monogamous family: Hobbes derives sovereign-husbanded 'little monarchies' from a state of nature in which women are men's equals, a derivation Susan Okin shows is contradictory; Locke grounds conjugal society in a voluntary compact with the husband as 'abler and stronger' last determiner, yet leaves women excluded from the social contract; Rousseau pairs passionate economic equality with some of the most sexist writing in Western thought, including fear of wives' sexual power in Emile. Against these static philosophies Engels gives a historical-materialist account in which the overthrow of mother right - the 'world historical defeat of the female sex' - followed from private property and inheritance, turning the bourgeois wife into a proletarian or prostitute while opening 'sex love' to the propertyless, and prescribing women's return to the labor force, socialized child-care, industrialized housework and easy divorce. John Stuart Mill's Subjection of Women appears as liberalism's one exception to its sexism, and a footnote sets Firestone's biological account of patriarchy against Engels's property account.
- ch. 12 "4 On the Origin of the State" **·** John Locke, Thomas Hobbes, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Karl Marx, John Stuart Mill, Immanuel Kant, G.W.F. Hegel, David Hume — The Social Contract; The State of Nature; Labor Theory of Property; The General Will — Opening with Newt Gingrich's complaint that students 'don't read enough Locke' and the Chinese premier's appeal to Rousseau, the chapter compares the three contract theorists' states of nature and purposes of government: Hobbes's war of every man against every man yielding an absolute sovereign with no separation of powers, Locke's peaceful nature in which mixing labor with land creates property and money then creates inequality, so that government's 'great and chief end' is protecting property through limited, separated powers and no food stamps, and Rousseau's compassionate natural humans corrupted when the first man enclosed land, so the state was founded on fraud and a general will that should 'force him to be free' and give people food stamps. Smith then reads the actual US founding as a chaste Lockean contract 'bastardized' on race and sex - the Declaration plagiarized from Locke, Abigail Adams's 'remember the ladies' laughed off, Dred Scott, with the 14th Amendment as the de-bastardizing 'Charter of Universal Freedom' - while Engels derives the state historically from the Iroquois and Greek gens, private property and class conflict. A final section documents white supremacy inside the tradition (Kant inventing the scientific concept of race, Hegel and Hume on Black inferiority), John Stuart Mill's 'Negro Question' as the tradition's decisive anti-racist break, Locke's own entanglements with the slave trade, and Marx's condemnation of slavery as super-exploitation.
- ch. 13 "5 The Changing Bases of Sexual Politics, 1960–2020" **·** Betty Friedan, John Locke, Karl Marx — The Feminine Mystique (the problem with no name); Feminism — Measuring women's progress since 1960 by access to the nine power bases, the chapter shows women using the size/solidarity base to launch the modern feminist movement - Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique as its manifesto, NOW as its vehicle, Ms. as its outlet and Gloria Steinem as its charismatic leader - and how law followed: the accidental Smith amendment adding sex to the 1964 Civil Rights Act, Reed and Frontiero subjecting sex classifications to scrutiny under the 14th Amendment, Griswold and Roe/Casey making reproductive control (which Justice Blackmun called 'necessary for the complete emancipation of women') a condition of women's power, and the 1970s no-fault divorce revolution that Engels's liberation program had demanded. It then charts each base statistically: the narrowing labor-force and wage gaps, women's still minor share of the bourgeoisie, the reversal of the college gender gap and Women's Studies programs built on the Black Studies model, women's entry into cabinet, Court, Congress, clergy and the military, secularization that weakens the religion base behind Elizabeth Cady Stanton's old challenge, and a new moral consensus that unequal treatment of women is wrong.
- ch. 14 "6 Wives and Husbands The Marital Power Struggle" **·** John Locke, Karl Marx, Thomas Hobbes, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Simone de Beauvoir, Catharine MacKinnon, Shulamith Firestone — Feminism; Objectification; The Dialectic of Sex — Taking Susan Okin's 'the personal is political' and Kate Millett's Weberian herrschaft against Locke's public/private dichotomy, the chapter reviews the empirical studies of marital power (Blood and Wolfe, Blumstein and Schwarz, Steil) and finds money is the master base in marriage: the husband's income and occupational prestige set his say, working wives gain power but couples conspire to understate wives' earnings ('manning up and womaning down'), while knowledge and status are the next strongest resources. Authority from religion, tradition and morality still favors husbands (Ephesians' 'wives submit yourselves unto your husbands' alongside the philosophers' 'abler and stronger'), violence persists from the rule of thumb to marital rape and murder despite legal change, housework remains women's burden - Beauvoir's never-won 'battle against dust', Engels's 'leaden boredom', Davis's industrialization proposal and Okin's demand that it be shared - and sex itself works as a power base in the bedroom, with MacKinnon diagnosing heterosexuality as the linchpin of gender inequality. The chapter ends with black couples' comparatively egalitarian patterns traced by Angela Davis to slave-quarters equality, Schwarz's rare 'peer marriages', and the Marxist (Okin, the Swedish model) versus liberal (Wilson, the Japanese model) readings of family change.
- ch. 15 "7 The Bourgeoisie and the Blacks" **·** Karl Marx, W.E.B. Du Bois, John Locke — Class Struggle; Historical Materialism; The Racial Contract; Totalitarianism — The chapter sets business - the US bourgeoisie whose privileged position Charles Beard read into the Constitution and which survived the Jacksonian and New Deal challenges by breaking labor through Taft-Hartley, right-to-work laws and the PATCO lockout, its solidarity secured while worker solidarity was undercut by what Marx called the Achilles heel of racism - against blacks as the paradigmatic powerless, shut out of every power base since slavery, which the chapter treats with Baptist and Marx's 1846 letter as a totalitarian system of super-exploited, tortured labor that built American capitalism, its neo-slavery progeny (Blackmon) pauperizing the black community under Dred Scott's 'subordinate and inferior class of beings'. It then narrates black counter-power base by base: the abolitionist interracial coalition wielding charisma (Douglass, Nat Turner, John Brown), information, morality and religion; the NAACP era and King's fusion of charisma, church religion, Myrdal's An American Dilemma and televised nonviolent provocation against Bull Connor's violence, contested by Malcolm X, SNCC and the Black Panthers; and a post-civil-rights scorecard showing a wealth base 94.2 percent white, persistent education and media gaps, constrained black officials from mayors to the symbolic Obama presidency, and a captive but potentially leveraged black vote in a 'Sisyphean' struggle.
- ch. 16 "8 Conclusion" **·** Karl Marx, John Locke, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — Class Struggle; The State of Nature — The conclusion restates the book's method - centering political philosophy in a consciously normative, empirical study of power - around its two contrasts: the family as a natural, subordination-requiring institution in liberalism versus a property-rooted, historically determined one in Marxism, and the state as a freely agreed contract of all (Locke, hence no food stamps) versus what actually happened, a charter 'ordained and established by a small group of wealthy white men, meeting in secret' to protect their wealth, so that the state which created gender and racial inequality must now play an equally decisive role in undoing it. Reviewing the nine bases since the 1960s, it finds women have closed the knowledge gap and nearly completed Engels's liberation program except universal child-care and non-exploitative housework, against conservative marriage-movement scholars like the Lockean Yenor, while blacks still face a tripling wealth gap that only social democratic capitalism on the Danish model plus comprehensive reparations can close - the latter argued on the moral base of power, Congress's 2009 apology, and Bernard Boxill's Lockean inheritance argument for a decades-long 'Reparations Superfund' as the civil rights issue of the 21st century.
- ch. 17 "Index" *(notes)*

## The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche

- ch. 8 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Friedrich Nietzsche — The editors' introduction argues that dieting — not just food — deserves philosophical attention, and that the Atkins Diet specifically raises 'chewy' questions about how to decide what to eat, what to believe, and whom to believe, precisely because it defies balanced-diet convention and much expert opinion. It opens with Plato's Republic prescription of roasted meats for campaigning guardians (no pots to carry), cites Nietzsche's Ecce Homo and its 'lengthy disquisition' on his own dietary choices as the rare philosophical treatment of diet, and credits Feuerbach with 'Der Mensch ist was er isst' — you are what you eat. It closes by mapping the volume's sixteen essays across Kant, Hume, Nietzsche, Marx, Dewey, environmental and feminist philosophy, critical race theory, and the philosophy of science.
- ch. 10 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** John Dewey, Charles Sanders Peirce, René Descartes — Pragmatism; The Pragmatic Method; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Auxier, an Atkins dieter, argues the diet works for the reason Dewey gives in Human Nature and Conduct: habits built in calm moments are the bulwark against desire in crisis, and Atkins succeeds by reshaping which gratifications are habitually available — 'a steak for the black eye of desire.' He then transfers Atkins's physiology to thinking: television and advertising serve 'conceptual carbs,' packaged bundles of doubt, emotion, and readiness to act that bypass inquiry and leave the public 'intellectually diabetic' and ideological. Peirce's pragmatic maxim is translated into an eight-step mental exercise (worked through a parent's tattoo-or-piercing doubt about a teenage daughter), while Descartes's hyperbolic doubt is discarded in favor of pragmatism's 'genuine doubt.'
- ch. 12 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Framed by The Onion's 'New Nietzschian Diet Lets You Eat Whatever You Fear Most' and its 'Fat is dead' riff on the death of God, Irwin argues via Nietzsche's Ecce Homo that 'small things — nutrition, place, climate' matter more than philosophy usually admits, and that dieting belongs to giving style to one's character: we are both artists and works of art, so a 'sound mind in an Atkins body' is self-creation. Drawing on his own two years on the diet (187 to 165 pounds, steadier mood, lower cholesterol), he contends Atkins fits some constitutions — Schwarzenegger's carnivorous persona — and not others: Tony Soprano, devouring gabagool amid agita and fainting spells, could not do Atkins without ceasing to be who he is. Nietzsche's 'One has to know the size of one's stomach' becomes the rule of dietary self-knowledge.
- ch. 13 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant — Autonomy of the Will; The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself — Dennis uses Kant to sort eaters into the fundamentally unfree (Herbert, raised on Atkins and thieving, who merely ploughs on), the fundamentally random (Rita, whose synapses and muscles would fire in chaos), and the autonomous, arguing that only an autonomous person can genuinely decide whether to follow Atkins — by weighing friends' testimonials against the medical establishment rather than habit, whim, or advertising. The categorical imperative grounds the autonomous life: 'lie when you can gain' fails universalization, and treating humanity as an end means offering a vegetarian guest food she is comfortable with instead of pressing Atkins meat on her. His own 'Dan Dennis Diet,' built by experiment and reasoning, illustrates autonomy in practice, and the case of Kitty shows that observing someone's diet never reveals whether its holder is unfree or autonomous.
- ch. 14 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Frantz Fanon — Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society; The State of Nature; Black Skin, White Masks — Knight places Atkins's caveman utopia — Paleolithic abundance, hunter-gatherer vitality, downfall through agriculture — inside the primitivist tradition running from Ovid's Golden Age to Rousseau's Noble Savage, whose state of nature Rousseau himself admitted was 'mere conditional and hypothetical reasoning' aimed at European corruption. Using postcolonial critics (Spurr, Torgovnick, and Fanon's line that whites who feel 'too mechanized' turn to 'the men of color' for 'human sustenance'), she argues low-carb primitivism is self-reflexive nostalgia — South Beach cannot even date its own paradise — that also freezes living Inuit and Indigenous Australians as Stone Age remnants, hiding the colonial and economic causes of their diabetes and poverty.
- ch. 16 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** David Hume — Problem of Induction — O'Connell extracts Brillat-Savarin's 1825 anti-flour-and-starch regimen — clear soup without croutons, shun beer, rye over white bread — as a 'proto-Atkins' and reconstructs its real argument: farmers fatten livestock on starches, so by Humean 'species of Analogy' starches fatten humans, from which abstinence from floury foods is 'deduced.' Hume's Enquiry Section IX, 'Of the Reason of Animals,' supplies the philosophical audit, distinguishing relations of ideas from matters of fact and grading the animal-to-human analogical inference as probable at best. The chapter ends with Hume's fork turned on the diet-book shelf: any volume without experiential reasoning concerning matter of fact deserves the flames — 'nothing but sophistry and illusion.'
- ch. 17 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Confucius, Democritus — Li (ritual propriety); Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society; Atomism; The General Will — In an imaginary salon hosted by the baker 'la Brioche,' the goddess Eris drops a golden apple inscribed 'Atkins,' and three philosophers fight over the credit. Rousseau claims Atkins's war on refined flour and 'invented fake food' as his own back-to-nature, state-of-nature legacy; Confucius counters that Americans are 'grazers' without li, that culture is nature's flower, and that only ritual propriety can counteract the advertising that fills the void; Democritus claims the scientific core — 'hyperinsulism,' 'benign dietary ketosis' — as atomism's heir, deriding Rousseau's general will as democratic truth-concocting and Plato's otherworldly philosopher-king. The debate ranges over free will versus scientific prediction-and-control and ends unresolved over a refusal of brioche.
- ch. 18 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Karl Popper, Thomas Kuhn, David Hume — Falsificationism; Paradigm Shifts; Problem of Induction — Steele starts from Orwell's worry that laypeople accept scientific consensus as unreflectively as tribesmen accept witch-doctors — sharpened by Lysenko and Nazi 'racial science' — and answers it with Popper's critical rationalism: since Hume's problem of induction bars proof from instances, we can only provisionally prefer theories that survive severe attempts at falsification, so trusting experts is reasonable exactly when their community tests rather than defends its theories. Kuhn's paradigms explain why dissident alternatives like Atkins talk past the dominant school (Atkins and Agatston are cardiologists, not dieticians), and the 2002–2004 studies showing improved lipids on more fat figure as the kind of surprise that precedes paradigm change. His verdict: neither trusting nor resisting experts is foolish; 'human knowledge is too important to be left to experts.'
- ch. 20 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Perspectivism; The Death of God — Bamford argues that Atkins's insistence that dieters evaluate the plan for their individual needs parallels Nietzsche's cultural therapy: as the death of God left modern culture nihilistic, so a processed-food culture suffers 'nutritional nihilism,' and the 'mega-orthodox' doctors who worship medical consensus with 'religious fervor' treat science as a replacement religion. Reading Ecce Homo's 'question of nutriment' alongside Twilight of the Idols, she shows that Nietzsche's perspectivism — no uninterpreted facts, only interpretations from physiological perspectives — makes each dieter fully responsible for interpretation, which is why Atkins must ask us to think for ourselves. The limit: where Atkins keeps an 'absolute faith in empirical science' (and Atkins Nutritionals mass-markets processed low-carb products), a properly Nietzschean therapy would question that faith too.
- ch. 21 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Kuhn — Paradigm Shifts — Womack tests whether Atkins counts as a Kuhnian paradigm shift, using the Ptolemaic-to-Copernican transition as the model: paradigms define which problems matter, normal science accumulates anomalies, and crisis ends in a new paradigm. Measured against the dieting paradigm's own goals, Atkins flunks — its short-term wins fade by twelve months in the JAMA comparison with the Ornish, Zone, and Weight Watchers diets, with 30–50 percent dropout — so the dieting paradigm itself, which treats obesity as an individual plate problem, is the thing in crisis. Her proposed replacement shifts from the individual to the 'toxic food environment': sidewalks, zoning, food advertising rules, and the French Paradox as the existence proof.
- ch. 22 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Karl Marx — Commodity Fetishism; Alienation — Bar On examines the Atkins website's country-by-country packaging and asks what kind of commodity the diet is, answering with Marx's Capital: use-value versus exchange-value, money's erasure of qualitative difference (an Atkins cookbook priced like a tub of supplements), and capitalists who produce use-values only as 'material depositories of exchange-value.' Advertising succeeds not by manipulation but because alienated people — labor sold, selves split to fit the job market — already live in exchange relations, and Atkins mediates even the dieter's relation to herself through purchased bars, supplements, and books. Her conclusion: a weight-loss diet only the relatively privileged can afford, in a world where the poor eat carbohydrates because they are cheap, is itself a symptom of the alienation Marx diagnosed.
- ch. 24 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Charles W. Mills, Thomas Hobbes — The Social Contract; The Racial Contract; Feminism — Wilkerson borrows the social contract tradition — Hobbes's mutual-restraint founding, radicalized by Pateman's sexual contract and Mills's racial contract — to recast antifat bias as a systematic breach of the social contract enforced by medicine (hallway weigh-ins, weight lectures instead of care), employment, transit seating, and TV fat jokes. Against Atkins's medical discourse of the 'obesity epidemic' she assembles Health at Every Size evidence, trans-fat and high-fructose corn syrup data, and the documented health damage of stigma and dieting itself, concluding that Atkins profits from recasting social problems as individual failings. Atkins for Life's success stories (Kerry Feather's volleyball and new husband, Luann Lockhart's proud daughter) are read as testimony that dieting works as ritual self-abasement purchasing group membership — hence Fat Liberation's 'another world is possible.'
- ch. 25 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Peter Singer, James Rachels, Jeremy Bentham — Animal Liberation; Speciesism; Food Ethics — Detmer argues moral vegetarianism follows from principles nearly everyone accepts — cruelty, the infliction of unnecessary or disproportionate suffering, is wrong — and that Atkins, which escalates meat eating without being necessary for weight loss, fails both his necessity and proportion tests. Rebutting human superiority, he deploys Rachels's point that no single feature like language is relevant to every difference in treatment and Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', holds factory-farm castration without anesthetic up against the civet-cat musk trade his students already condemn, and answers Narveson's appeal to intuition and the appeal to tradition. Even granting Atkins maximal health benefits, the margin over a well-planned vegetarian diet (Denmark's WWI blockade, the Framingham data) cannot justify the animal suffering, world-hunger, and environmental costs — most of that case drawn from Singer's Animal Liberation.
- ch. 26 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Karl Marx, René Descartes — The Categorical Imperative; Food Ethics — Cox and Bender subject Atkins to Kant's universal-law formula — could every one of the billion overweight people on earth adopt it? — in a 'factive' thought experiment: a 25 percent rise in animal-protein output, nearly 250 million additional feed-grain acres, overgrazed ranges, and possibly a tenth of the world's remaining forests cleared for pasture. Calling Atkins reductionism's child (a metabolic switch judged on bathroom scales), they use Marx's 'metabolic rift' — soil nutrients shipped to cities, feedlots severing crops from livestock — and the Cartesian body-as-machine (via Federici) to place low-carb's atomized foods (bungalow subs, soy 'mashed potatoes,' pork rinds) as capitalism's latest rupture in the food system. Their verdict: only plant-leaning regimens could survive universalization, and the deeper fix is Wendell Berry's — eating understood as an agricultural act.
- ch. 27 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Feminism — Bentley argues Atkins 'masculinized' dieting: since meat is coded male (the hunter's large game, yang, 'strong as an ox') and dieting female, a diet whose emblematic meal is steak, bacon, and creamed spinach let men come out of the dieting closet — Terry Free's competitive wager, business-school professors trading weight charts, and half-male Atkins success stories against Jenny Craig's sixteen men. The symbolism runs both ways: women now order steak openly, while 'white trash' foods like pork rinds ($840 million in 2003 sales) gained middle-class respectability, a class crossing she explains through Bourdieu's Distinction — taste, habitus, and cultural capital.
- ch. 29 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Parasecoli reads the Atkins program through Lacanian psychoanalysis: the mirror stage explains why dieters invest in the 'you in the picture' Atkins asks them to visualize — an ideal-ego built from others' gazes and shifting cultural body standards (Botticelli's Venus to Jennifer Lopez); hunger, which Atkins treats as an uncontrollable instinct, occupies the place of the Real that resists symbolization; and 'carbs are bad' functions as the upholstery nail that stabilizes the whole symbolic food system. Science plays the external authority whose impenetrable rationale licenses the dieter's leap of faith, while the body that will not slim on schedule — 'your body is not a machine' — is the Real breaking back in.
- ch. 30 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" **·** Michel Foucault, René Descartes, Iris Marion Young, Marilyn Frye — Mind–Body Dualism; The Panopticon (surveillance); Objectification; Embodiment (the lived body) — A café dialogue pits second-waver Marie against third-waver Dorothy over whether Atkins can be a feminist tool: Marie wields the feminist critique of Cartesian dualism (Descartes made the mind essential and the body animal, and women were stigmatized as body), Foucault's internalized surveillance — 'every mirror becomes a guard, every scale an alarm,' with Lifetime Maintenance as 'maniacal' hyper-vigilance — Lorde's 'master's tools,' and Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl.' Dorothy answers with Our Bodies, Ourselves self-knowledge, Title IX athletes like Venus and Serena Williams, Frye's Willful Virgin, and existentialist facticity and bad faith (we are in bad faith when we abdicate control), defending dieting as a chosen women's project. The exchange ends drawish, over Brazilian waxes, French women, and whether ugliness is a feminist virtue.

## The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Avengers and Philosophy Earth's Mightiest Thinkers, The" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Avengers and Philosophy Earth's Mightiest Thinkers, The" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Avengers and Philosophy Earth's Mightiest Thinkers, The" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Avengers and Philosophy Earth's Mightiest Thinkers, The" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Introduction Earth’s Mightiest Philosophers" *(no index entry yet)* — Editor Mark D. White introduces the volume: the Avengers fascinate because they are equal parts superhero epic and soap opera, and the contributors' questions mirror that mix. He previews the book's guiding questions—whether Captain America, Iron Man, and Thor embody three different moral philosophies, whether the Kree-Skrull War bears on the ethics of war, why the team keeps admitting reformed criminals like Hawkeye, Quicksilver, and the Scarlet Witch, whether Kang can kill his past self, whether we secretly admire Norman Osborn's Dark Avengers, and whether the android Vision can truly love the Scarlet Witch. It frames the collection but applies no philosophical framework itself.
- ch. 7 "Part One What Would an Avenger Do" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Ethicists Assemble!" **·** Jeremy Bentham — Utilitarianism; Deontology; Virtue Ethics — White casts the 'Avengers Prime' as three living ethical systems: Tony Stark is the utilitarian who, during Civil War and the registration crisis, bets on outcomes he alone claims to foresee (stopping the Crimson Dynamo's heart, enlisting the Thunderbolts, exiling the Hulk); Captain America is the deontologist who refuses registration on principle ('we maintained the principles we swore to defend... you sold your principles') and rejects the Punisher and the Negative Zone prison regardless of consequences; Thor is the virtue ethicist who condemns Iron Man not by utility or duty but for violating loyalty, trust, and friendship in cloning him, and who refuses the Twilight Sword because using it would make him 'the same demon'. The chapter argues all three frameworks still demand judgment and conviction, which the heroes share.
- ch. 9 "Just How Dark are the Dark Avengers" **·** Plato, Socrates — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Justice in the Republic; Allegory of the Cave; Theory of Forms — Donovan and Richardson read Osborn's Dark Avengers through the Republic: Osborn is a modern Thrasymachus for whom justice is merely the advantage of the stronger, managing Bullseye's murder of Lindy and the team's image exactly as Glaucon's ring of Gyges predicts—villains like Moonstone, Daken, and Venom appearing good while doing injustice. Captain America, who tells Stark 'who made you the moral compass of us?', embodies the Socratic belief in a justice beyond human advantage, backed by the Forms and the allegory of the cave. Ms. Marvel, Noh-Varr, and Ares choose being just over appearing just, defecting or dying (Ares torn in half during the Siege) rather than serve Osborn's fraud.
- ch. 10 "Let there be an Ending!" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Southworth and Tallman ask why fans blame Hank Pym for Ultron's killings while never crediting Magneto for fathering two heroes, and answer with Aristotle's account of character formed by habitual imitation, renewed as 'moral exemplarism': praise and blame track exemplarship, not biology. Scott Lang earned credit because he actively taught Cassie right and wrong, making her the hero Stature; T'Chaka and stepmother Ramonda shaped T'Challa, while Heinrich Zemo's Nazi upbringing warped Helmut into the new Baron Zemo. The Avengers themselves—Cap's patient mentoring of Hawkeye, Stark hiring ex-con Scott Lang—function as moral exemplars for reformed villains, so the mentoring 'parents', not the siring ones, deserve the credit or blame.
- ch. 11 "Part Two Who is an Avenger" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "Are you the Next Goliath" **·** John Locke — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory) — Nelson tests body theory and psychology theory of personal identity on Avengers cases—a Rogers/Pym body swap in the spirit of Locke's prince-and-cobbler experiment, and a Pym brain-hemisphere duplication puzzle—before proposing a distinct 'mantle theory' of superhero identity requiring an appropriate heroic role plus legitimate pedigree, like intellectual property. Legitimacy explains how John Walker (appointed by a government commission) and Bucky Barnes (endorsed by Stark and then Rogers) each really were Captain America. The same theory rules Pym can wear only one of Ant-Man, Giant-Man, Goliath, Yellowjacket, and the Wasp at a time—confirmed by Clint Barton snapping his bow in half when he shed Hawkeye to become the new Goliath.
- ch. 13 "Maybe Jen’s Reading this Chapter Right Now" *(no index entry yet)* — Cook analyzes John Byrne's and Dan Slott's She-Hulk runs as metacomics: Jen breaks the fourth wall to threaten readers into buying her book, deduces how long she was unconscious from comic-book time, steps across the gutter between panels to travel, and even attacks her own creator. Weezie's line 'We're inked and colored! Printed!' raises the problem that once published, the characters' actions are fixed, while her backstory (staying in print to stop aging) exploits comic conventions. The chapter ends by asking whether the Official Handbook's conflicting retcons make Jen's meta-awareness a delusion or a superpower, and what that uncertainty means for truth in metafiction and our understanding of comics storytelling itself.
- ch. 14 "Hoist by his Own Petard" **·** Plato, Socrates — Socratic Method (elenchus) — Powell reads Norman Osborn's Dark Reign as a living lesson from Plato's Gorgias and Alcibiades: Osborn's media-staged killing of the Skrull Queen and his hollow rebranding of S.H.I.E.L.D. into H.A.M.M.E.R. are the sophistic 'knack' of persuasion substituting for the genuine craft of statecraft, just as Polus's ideal Sophist imagines power without self-control. Like Alcibiades, Osborn lacks the Socratic self-knowledge that comes only through critical self-reflection with honest friends, and instead surrounds himself with flatterers and villains while his own Goblin persona—mirrored in the Sentry's Void—grows stronger. Loki's goading of the unsanctioned Siege of Asgard completes the cautionary tale: the sophist who created fake institutions is destroyed by them, hoist by his own petard.
- ch. 15 "Part Three Should the Avengers Do More Than Avenge" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "Avengers, Forgive!" **·** Hannah Arendt, Jacques Derrida — Forgiveness; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Malloy builds an account of forgiveness around the Avengers' habit of recruiting ex-villains: Arendt's 'predicament of irreversibility' explains why we cannot undo Wonder Man's revenge scheme against Stark, so resentment must be overcome; Derrida's claim that only the unforgivable is truly forgivable frames the House of M question, whether Quicksilver's manipulation of Wanda's reality-warping is a crime beyond forgiveness. Forgiveness means relinquishing resentment without excusing responsibility or condoning the wrong, so Iron Man has the 'moral power' to forgive Hawkeye, while the team's charter-based standing lets the Avengers forgive Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch on the community's behalf. The chapter closes by separating avenging (justice) from revenge, and punishment (retribution that repays debts) from forgiveness, which is why expelled members like Iron Man and Hank Pym could be readmitted.
- ch. 17 "Neither Gods nor Beasts But Political Animals" **·** Aristotle — Man as Political Animal; Eudaimonia (flourishing); Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Spanakos denies the official line that the Avengers assemble from necessity—Thor beats Loki alone—arguing instead through Aristotle that the team is a polis: heroes join for safety but stay for the good life, since outside the polis one is either a god or a beast. Ms. Marvel's miserable solo run (unrecognized by Stilt-Man, a 'Where Are They Now?' has-been) ends only when she returns to lead the Mighty Avengers among friends who share her arete; the self-loathing Jessica Jones finds eudaimonia through philia with Carol, Luke Cage, and the team that delivers her baby; even the arrogant Hank Pym regains excellence by defending Tony and leading a new team. Even gods like Thor and near-beasts like the Hulk, the chapter concludes, need the Avengers to flourish.
- ch. 18 "Avengers Rehabilitate!" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Terjesen asks whether Cap's Kooky Quartet-style rehabilitation really works, pitting Aristotle's fixed-character virtue ethics against John Doris's situationist 'local traits' (backed by Milgram's experiments): Hawkeye succeeded because his regional traits—hotheadedness and a need for approval—were redirected to heroism, not erased, as when he cheats the Grandmaster to save the universe. Aristotle's continence-versus-virtue and vice-versus-incontinence distinctions explain why Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch keep backsliding, why Moonstone's true viciousness defeats rehabilitation while Songbird and MACH-1 reform. Against deterrence and retributivist theories of punishment, rehabilitation is defensible when applied early and to the unhardened—the Avengers Academy children and Young Avenger Patriot—so the Avengers can rehabilitate as well as avenge.
- ch. 19 "Part Four Do the Avengers Ever Go Too Far" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "And the war Rages on" **·** Michael Walzer, Immanuel Kant — Just War Theory; Humanity as an End in Itself; Consequentialism; Deontology — Robichaud runs the Kree-Skrull War (Avengers #89–97) through Michael Walzer's just war theory: the Avengers' defense of Earth against Ronan's Plan Atavus is justified self-defense meeting proportionality and last resort, while Ronan's preventive 'devolve humanity' war fails for lack of evidence and exhausted diplomacy. The Skrulls' shape-shifting trick that gets Mar-Vell to build the Omni-Wave Projector might squeak through on consequentialist grounds, but the emperor's threat to make Captain Marvel watch the Scarlet Witch and Quicksilver die counts as torture—and is impermissible on the Kantian ground that it treats a person merely as a means, whatever the consequences. The point is that even a cosmic comic war displays the real moral complexity of military ethics.
- ch. 21 "“This is the Kind of Thing that is Going to Bite US in the Butt”" **·** Michael Walzer — Deontology; Just War Theory; Consequentialism — Melançon pictures Avengers ethics as Hawkeye's arrow sliding along a line from deontological duty toward consequentialist results, focusing on secrets and lies: Doctor Strange's deception—disguising his Sanctum Sanctorum as a coffee shop to shelter the underground New Avengers after Civil War—is tested against Michael Walzer's 'supreme emergency', the wartime exception (Allied bombing of Germany, the ticking time bomb) that permits violating your own values so they can survive. Strange keeps sliding—possessed by a demon against the Hulk—until the Eye of Agamotto strips him of his title, showing emergencies must stay rare and the agent 'worthy of surviving'. Steve Rogers's secret black-ops Secret Avengers repeat the danger: unlike democratic intelligence agencies, they have zero oversight or accountability, so the WikiLeaks-style leak of their informant dealings threatens the reputation of the whole Avengers enterprise.
- ch. 22 "Captain America’s mighty S.H.I.E.L.D. . . . Well, Sort Of" **·** Thomas Aquinas, Philippa Foot — Doctrine of Double Effect — Bogaerts asks why every proactive superhero comes to grief: Nick Fury's unauthorized Secret War in Latveria, Tony Stark's exile of the Hulk and registration crusade, and the Illuminati's blunder all backfire (World War Hulk, the Skrull invasion), and Aquinas's doctrine of double effect—elaborated by Foot and Anscombe—cannot absolve them, since the foreseen harms were massive and disproportionate to the intended goods. Comics theory supplies the deeper cause: Reynolds's status quo defense and Jewett and Lawrence's American monomyth (via Campbell's hero's journey) make the superhero genre intrinsically reactive, guarding a paradise rather than remaking it, so heroes who 'move up into governance'—Thor as Lord of Earth, the Squadron Supreme's utopia—slide into supervillainy. Foot's act/omission distinction and the priority of negative over positive duties explain the trap, and why even Steve Rogers, as the new top cop, retreats to being Captain America again.
- ch. 23 "Part Five What Kind of World do the Avengers Live In" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Time to End" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Jones uses Kang to walk through the physics and metaphysics of time travel: Einstein's twin paradox (Quicksilver aging one year while Wanda's clock runs twenty), Gödel's spinning universe and van Stockum's cylinder yielding closed timelike curves, Thorne's wormhole time machine, and Hawking's Chronology Protection Conjecture against energy-stealing paradox loops. Applied to the comics, Prime Kang's purge of his flawed selves, Immortus's Forever Crystal, and Iron Lad's murder of his future self all confirm the fixed-timeline view: attempts to change the past only prune variants or create transient branches that snap back, so Kang can never un-become Kang. The Avengers end up as the Marvel Universe's Chronology Protection Agency, enforcing the rule that even where time travel exists, the past cannot be rewritten.
- ch. 25 "Equal Opportunity—for Deities" **·** Immortality and the Soul; The Problem of Evil — Barkman argues the Marvel Universe's 'One-Above-All'—depicted as Stan Lee and Jack Kirby—is the eternal Judeo-Christian Creator, and arranges its beings in a graded hierarchy: the Living Tribunal as God's judge, cosmic beings like Eternity and Galactus, elders, sky fathers Odin and Zeus, down to mortals, with only God eternal and everything else, gods included, able to die yet enduring by His decree. Ontological rank guarantees nothing morally—Mephisto, the Goddess, and Hera are powerful and wicked, and even Hercules can be beaten by the Wrecking Crew.
