A free-will theodicy answers where evil came from: 'no other gods before me' never denied other gods' existence but commands loving the Good above all, which mortal Avengers like Thor, loving justice perfected by sacrificial love, manage as well as any deity.
- ch. 26 "Love American Style" **·** Peter Singer, Charles Sanders Peirce — Philosophy of Love; Speciesism; The Pragmatic Method — Klayman asks whether the android Vision can love the human Scarlet Witch, working through C.S. Lewis's four loves to show affection, friendship, Eros, and charity are all open to human-android pairs, with their marriage best read as Eros—preoccupation with one irreplaceable self rather than sexual desire. Peter Singer's attack on speciesism is extended into 'organicism', the prejudice that dismisses synthetic beings: the Vision suffers, has interests, and laments that 'we artificial life-forms are still the least accepted', so denying androids love is arbitrary bias. Peirce's pragmatic maxim settles the question by practical effects—the Vision's care, kindness, attentiveness, and intimacy with Wanda just are loving—whether the lover is flesh or machine.
- ch. 27 "The Way of the Archer" **·** Laozi, Zhuangzi — Wu Wei (effortless action); Taoism (Daoism); The Tao (the Way); Zhuangzi's Perspectivism (butterfly dream) — White reads Clint Barton through the Tao Te Ching and Chuang Tzu: Hawkeye's instinctive archery—'use your bow gently, naturally, instinctively'—is wei wu wei, while his bragging, his glory-chasing failure against Iron Man, and his attempt to become Goliath all violate it by striving against his own nature, until the Kree-Skrull War teaches him the bow is his way. Chuang Tzu's butcher carves the lesson that the effortless path (the straightforward shot) is the skilled one, and Lao Tzu's sage-leadership—lowering oneself, deflecting praise—is exactly how Captain America handles Clint's insurrections. Lao Tzu on sages putting themselves last illuminates Hawkeye's sacrificial death and his legacy passed to Kate Bishop, while the butterfly dream frames his resurrection and the House of M's rewritten reality: with no way to compare the states, life and death are both to be welcomed as parts of the Way.
- ch. 28 "Appendix Why are there Four Volumes of Avengers" *(no index entry yet)* — A fan-guide appendix, not a philosophical essay: it untangles the Avengers' publication history to show which comics the book's chapters draw on—the original 1963–1996 volume, the thirteen-issue Heroes Reborn relaunch ('never cited in this book—for a reason'), the 1998 volume ending in Avengers Disassembled, then New Avengers, Young Avengers, the Civil War split, Mighty Avengers, Osborn's Dark Avengers, and the Heroic Age's fourth volume alongside Secret Avengers and Avengers Academy. It makes no philosophical argument; its point is navigational, mapping the canon that the essays' examples come from.
- ch. 29 "Contributors Avengers Academy" *(notes)*
- ch. 30 "Index From Jarvis’s Secret Files" *(notes)*

## The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Unknown" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Unknown" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "Unknown" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 5 "Unknown" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 6 "PROLOGUE “WHAT’S THAT SUPPOSED TO MEAN ”" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Will to Power — The prologue closely re-watches Bob Dylan's 1965 Newport 'going electric' set and argues that the famous booing began for mundane musical reasons — the bassist missing the change to the five chord in 'Maggie's Farm' and an under-rehearsed band — not ideological betrayal by folk purists. It contends that the audience collectively transmuted a flawed performance into an epochal myth of folk-vs-rock rupture, and that this shared fiction, not how the music actually sounded, is what mattered culturally. Framed by the Nietzsche epigraph on self-overcoming, it reads Dylan as a catalytic, quasi-messianic figure who performed the 'necessary murder of the old order' (culminating in the 1966 'Judas!' shout), enjoyed even the booing as part of the cultural drama, and refused every label by calling his new style 'vision music.'
- ch. 7 "I. “STANDING IN THE GATEWAY”" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "CHAPTER 1 “LET’S GET REAL, REAL GONE FOR A CHANGE”" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, William James — The Dialectic; Authenticity; Geist (World Spirit); Zen Buddhism — The chapter argues that Elvis's Sun recordings — the staged rupture in 'Milkcow Blues Boogie' ('That don't move me. Let's get real, real gone for a change') and the accidental 'acting the fool' emergence of 'That's All Right' — enacted an epistemological revolution: a leap out of modernity's rationalized, disembodied mode into repressed bodily affect, defining American cool as affective authenticity against Bill Haley's affected performativity. Elvis's immersion in a Black Memphis neighborhood and his emulation of Black performers made him a catalyst for racial-musical integration and the 'visceral empathy' that prepared desegregation, while the panic of critics (Sinatra, the Times, Congressman Celler) is reread via Hegel's 'tarrying with the negative' as the resistance Geist needs for its self-overcoming. Creative novelty is described with Whitehead's and William James's metaphors — the 'lure of feeling,' sudden phase transition, radical empiricism in what Elvis kept or dropped onstage — with his 'did it make me feel good' studio criterion and a Zen-like mushin statesmanship of loosing egoic control in the band.
- ch. 9 "CHAPTER 2 “A CREATIVE TENSION”" **·** William James, René Descartes — Authenticity; The Dialectic; The Cogito — The chapter traces the Beatles' rise as a case study in how novelty enters culture: Lennon and McCartney polarize into transgressive truth and melodic beauty, their 'creative tension' producing an emergent whole greater than either (the 'holding a mirror' songwriting method, their fused harmonies, the Decca audition versus Hamburg swings between commerce and authenticity). Hamburg is the underworld initiation where 'Mach Schau!' humiliation, absurdist humor read as Freudian catharsis, and Preludin-fueled marathon sets broke them out of English propriety into ecstatic physicality, before Epstein's suits and George Martin's harsh Abbey Road critique dragged the pendulum back toward rational professionalism. Against the Cartesian thesis that humanity is defined by the thinking mind ('I think, therefore I am'), the chapter reads 'Please Please Me,' Beatlemania's screaming crowds (citing Ehrenreich on female assertiveness and solidarity), and Rubber Soul as successive dialectical phase transitions integrating affect with intellect — a rock-and-roll answer to rationalized modernity, in James's wave-crest image of novelty flung ahead of history.
- ch. 10 "CHAPTER 3 “LOOKING FOR THE INNER HEAT”" **·** Thomas Kuhn, G.W.F. Hegel, Jean-Paul Sartre, William James — Paradigm Shifts; Authenticity; Existentialism — The chapter reads Dylan's self-becoming as a chain of identity-emulations and overcomings — Hank Williams, Woody Guthrie, Ramblin' Jack Elliott — with Jon Pankake's folk-police critique and the Mike Seeger epiphany acting as Kuhnian anomalies that force a paradigm shift from folksinger to songwriter, each gatekeeper playing the 'Hegelian negative' Dylan needed. It argues Dylan fused folk, beat poetry, and rock and roll into an 'archaic revival' of mythic, enchanted consciousness against modern rationalization, rejecting the Sartrean/beat existentialism of a meaningless world in favor of co-creating meaning, and treating authenticity as the refusal of fixed identity (the Zimmerman-to-Dylan renaming, 'I'm gonna get me a new Bob Dylan'). The Newsweek exposé, Irwin Silber's open letter, and Johnny Cash's guitar-gift blessing stage his passage from 'King of Folk' to electric rock, with the little-known 1962 cut of Presley's 'That's All Right' showing that going electric was a return home — folk having been, in Dylan's words, 'just an interruption.'
- ch. 11 "II. “YOU REALLY DON’T KNOW UNTIL YOU STEP INSIDE”" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 12 "CHAPTER 4 “A REVELATION TO BEHOLD”" **·** William James, Aristotle, G.W.F. Hegel — The Will to Believe; The Four Causes; Truth as What Works; The Leap of Faith — Argues that the Beatles' devotion to rock and roll was a literal religious phenomenon rather than loose metaphor: Lennon's first hearing of Elvis is analyzed as a William James-style conversion, the Radio Luxembourg broadcasts were treated 'like scripture,' Hamburg was a 'baptism by fire,' and Epstein's new suits at the Cavern were announced as 'a revelation.' Drawing on James's Varieties of Religious Experience and Pragmatism, the chapter reads Beatlemania's screaming crowds as collective ecstatic ritual and the 'toppermost of the poppermost' chant as the will-to-believe making its own truth, in the way James says truth 'happens' to an idea. Aristotle's four causes supply the metaphysical frame — the 'magic' of Liverpool and the sacred quality fans reported are formal-final causation against the material-efficient causation of disenchanted modernity — while the band's double irony ('tarrying with the negative,' after Hegel) let them hold skepticism inside belief, as in Lennon's 'flaming pie' origin parody and the 'more popular than Jesus' episode.
- ch. 13 "CHAPTER 5 “AN EXTREME SENSE OF DESTINY”" **·** Aristotle, William James, Heraclitus, Thomas Kuhn — The Four Causes; The Will to Believe; Fate and Foreknowledge — Reads Bob Dylan's 'extreme sense of destiny' as lived Aristotelian final causation: Dylan's passivity about fame ('It happened like anything else happens'), his 'Jack Fate' persona, and the odyssey of 'goin' home' all treat his future self as the telos drawing him forward rather than his past pushing him. William James's Will to Believe ('faith creates its own verification') explains the self-fulfilling portents Dylan found in Gorgeous George's wink, his felt succession to Woody Guthrie, and his premonition of Joan Baez, while the chapter insists this destiny is not fatalism since Dylan could have ignored the signs and 'gone off another way.' It closes by taking Dylan at his word that 'Bobby Zimmerman' died when his namesake was killed in a 1961 motorcycle crash — a Jungian synchronicity that seals the shamanic death-and-rebirth 'transfiguration' Dylan claims for himself, where Heraclitus's river captures that the old self cannot be recovered.
- ch. 14 "EPILOGUE “THROUGH THE MIRROR”" **·** William James — The epilogue reads the three pairwise meetings — Elvis and the Beatles at his Bel Air home in 1965 ('Long live the King!'), Dylan turning the Beatles on to cannabis on August 28, 1964, and Dylan's refusal to ever meet Elvis, memorialized in 'Went to See the Gypsy' — as mirrors through which each figure's transformation passed to the next. Its central argument is that the 'marijuana summit' was an epistemological watershed: following Terence McKenna's claim that a culture's sanctioned drugs select its ways of knowing, cannabis (against caffeinated, speed-fueled rationalism) opened the affective, intuitive mode that became the counterculture, audible in Lennon's turn from 'Help!' to 'Come Together.' The song's gypsy and 'pretty dancing girl' are finally read as the Jungian anima, the archetypal feminine drawing the West back to embodied, enchanted experience — a book-length thesis the epilogue attributes to the 'radical empiricist' lineage of James, Jung, Bergson, and Whitehead.
- ch. 15 "BIBLIOGRAPHY" *(notes)*
- ch. 16 "ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS" *(notes)*
- ch. 17 "NOTES" *(notes)*

## The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke

- ch. 1 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Dean Kowalski's introduction pitches the volume: philosophy's big questions about what is really real, how we ought to behave, and what we can know brought to Sheldon's spot on the couch. It previews the essays to come — Aristotle weighing Sheldon's way of life, Hobbes applauding the roommate agreement, Kant deriding 'un-unravelable webs' of lies — and frames the book's running thought that comic-book and sci-fi geekery can be put to serious philosophical use, while even Sheldon cannot escape the 'inexplicable need for human contact.'
- ch. 8 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Virtue Ethics (arete); Aristotle on the Soul — Greg Littmann tests Sheldon's geek existence against Aristotle's ideal of living well: since humanity's distinctive function is reason (the DVD-player-and-screwdriver argument), a life devoted to thought like Sheldon's — down to his fantasy of being a thinking satellite in orbit — has genuine Aristotelian worth. The chapter argues Aristotle could even bless geek obsessions, because poetry explores universal hypotheticals (Terminator causal loops, Superman's laundry) and adventure fiction purges emotion much as tragedy's catharsis does. But Sheldon's arrogance ('Captain Arrogant'), rigid clinging to his spot on the couch, and selfishness toward Leonard and Howard would earn failing marks in virtue, so the modern geek gets a mixed yet partly vindicating report card.
- ch. 10 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Kowalski maps Aristotle's three kinds of friendship onto the gang: pleasure-friendships (Halo and paintball nights, and Raj's fury when Howard abandons their kite fight for a jogger), utility-friendships (Sheldon's failed Friendship Algorithm bid on Kripke for lab access, and the roommate agreement's Friendship Rider invoked over the CERN trip). Complete friendship — mutual care for the other's own sake between moral equals — looks closest in Leonard and Sheldon, yet Sheldon's pancake-breakfast apology collapses the moment Leonard refuses to take him to Switzerland ('Drat. No Frodo for you'), exposing contractual utility where genuine care should be. The chapter concludes no pairing in the show achieves Aristotle's rare complete friendship, and asks whether similarity is really required for true 'besties.'
- ch. 11 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete); Man as Political Animal — Sayles sorts the show's technology use by Aristotle's doctrine of the mean: healthy supplements (Raj webcamming his parents in India, Sheldon and Amy's video dates) versus unhealthy substitutes (Penny's Age of Conan spiral into unwashed hair and sick days, Sheldon living as a 'mobile virtual presence device,' one-sided 'virtual vengeance' videos against Penny's Wi-Fi theft and Kripke's helium prank). Since the mean is relative to the person and situation rather than a mathematical midpoint, moderation must be found case by case, and man as a social being must keep his social skills exercised. The chapter finds Penny and Amy — not the four scientists — best model balanced technology use.
- ch. 12 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Philosophy of Disability; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Clifton asks whether fans are moral monsters for laughing at behavior that looks autistic, running Sheldon through the DSM criteria for Asperger's syndrome: missing Penny's sarcasm about doctors who 'remove shoes from asses,' hedging the bath-item Christmas gift, and inflexibly clinging to nonfunctional routines like Saturday-night laundry. Setting the writers' stated intentions aside as one fallible piece of evidence (the intentional-fallacy debate), he weighs the medical model of disability (leveling and normalizing) against the social-constructivist model in which disability is a misfit between trait and environment. Because Sheldon has built a world — theoretical physics, accommodating friends, the comic book store — where his traits are advantages, even an 'alpha nerd' leader, they constitute an 'enability' rather than a disability, and the laughter is morally innocent.
- ch. 14 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Gottfried Leibniz, Hannah Arendt, Martin Buber — The Problem of Evil; Will to Power; The Banality of Evil; The Best of All Possible Worlds — Smith weighs Sheldon's vendetta against Wil Wheaton — the skipped 1995 Dixie Trek convention, the fake dead 'Nana' that won the Mystic Warlords tournament ('Game over, Moon Pie!'), the bowling-alley sabotage of Leonard and Penny — against theories of evil: Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds theodicy (with Voltaire's Candide objection), Buber's claim that the lie is the specific evil humanity introduced into nature, and Arendt's banality of evil at Eichmann's trial, which shows Wil's deceptions are bad moral choices rather than evil. Nietzsche's will to power would instead admire Wil, and even Khan-style revenge, as proto-Übermensch exploitation. The chapter closes by reading Sheldon's 'Comic Book World paradigm' (the Green Goblin to his Spider-Man) through Ricoeur's view that evil is grasped through myths and symbols: Star Trek and comics are the symbolic framework by which he interprets wrongdoing he cannot otherwise fathom.
- ch. 15 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Aristotle, John Stuart Mill, Jeremy Bentham, Plato — The Social Contract; The State of Nature; Higher and Lower Pleasures; Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — The Bocks test three answers to the good life against the show: Howard as hedonist (laser-obstacle-strip-chess, the 'whore of Omaha') read through Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures, and Aristippus; ethical egoism via Glaucon's ring of Gyges and Howard's offer to Skype rather than visit the deported Raj; and Hobbes's state of nature and social contract read into Sheldon's roommate agreement, whose lack of a Hobbesian sovereign leaves 'I settle all ties' arbitrary and rule-following too thin for ethics. Aristotle's virtue and practical wisdom crown Leonard — the nucleus of the social group, as Amy says — as the closest thing to the phronimos. The gang's sabotage of Dennis Kim with a manufactured girlfriend closes the chapter by asking who really ruined whose life.
- ch. 16 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Lawhead reconstructs Sheldon's 'fundamentalist scientism' — an inverted pyramid of knowledge with fundamental physics as the load-bearing point — and tests it through 'Sheldonology,' a mock special science that predicts Sheldon's behavior from the Parking Principle and his seven-restaurant dinner rotation. He grants Sheldon that a grand unified theory would be maximally general (against Amy's claim that neurobiology could 'subsume' physics as rank psychologism), but argues that a successful brain simulation would just be a system that does physics, and that the special sciences trade generality for usefulness — so choosing Sheldonology over fundamental physics to find a Sheldon-approved restaurant is perfectly rational. Science thus contains an ineliminably pragmatic element, deflating Sheldon's haughty derision of Howard, Raj, and the humanities.
- ch. 18 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Karl Popper, Thomas Kuhn — Falsificationism; Paradigm Shifts — Jones explains the Leonard–Leslie breakup ('Tell me, Leonard, how would we raise the children?') as a genuine clash of research commitments: string theory with its demanded extra dimensions versus Leslie's loop quantum gravity. Along the way he uses Popper's falsifiability and Kuhn's paradigms — the 1998 dark-energy discovery as falsification at work, Sheldon's alien-parasite hypothesis as paradigm-protecting refusal to accept that Amy is aroused by Zack — and the Dirac-to-Anderson antimatter story alongside Sheldon's North Pole monopole expedition to weigh theoretical against experimental science. Leonard emerges as the Feynman-style skeptic ('At best you can say, hey, my idea has internal logical consistency'), which is exactly what Leslie cannot forgive.
- ch. 19 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, René Descartes — Is–Ought Problem — Pigliucci argues the gang is funny because their scientistic worldview misfires in ordinary life: Howard's Drake-equation-derived 'Wolowitz coefficient,' Sheldon's friendship algorithm that Howard must rescue from an infinite loop, and Leonard's 'bio-social exploration' kiss experiment with Leslie all fail because courtship and friendship resist quantification. Tracing scientism's appeal to the Cartesian method of reductionism, he criticizes E.O. Wilson's Consilience, Sam Harris's science of morality (defending Hume's distinction between empirical facts and values), and the Churchlands' eliminative materialism — the tequila sunrise and the rock wall's qualitative feel escaping the neuro-reductive gaze. Sheldon's chocolate-based operant conditioning of Penny and the Tuskegee syphilis study show why science needs ethical evaluation from outside itself.
- ch. 20 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Alvin Plantinga, John Locke, Peter van Inwagen — Faith and Reason; The Watchmaker Argument (design) — Barkman and Kowalski mine the Cooper household for science-and-religion lessons: Mary's 'Third-World demon' diagnosis of Raj raises religious diversity (exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism), her 'But intelligently designed by a creator, right?' prompts an assessment of Behe's irreducible complexity against Darwinian counterexamples like the flagellum-turned-syringe and a warning against god-of-the-gaps reasoning. Her claim that 'all that science stuff comes from Jesus' occasions Plantinga's argument that Darwinian naturalism undermines trust in our cognitive faculties, plus origin-of-life and fine-tuning probability arguments, tempered by Kitcher's caution that such estimates rest on unknown background conditions. Van Inwagen on why Genesis need not teach literal science, and Locke's advice to proportion belief to evidence, frame the mutual education Mary and Sheldon owe each other.
- ch. 21 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, John Locke — Language Games; Tabula Rasa — Pötzsch reads Sheldon as the early Wittgenstein trapped in the Tractatus's picture theory — taking Penny's 'How've you been?' as a question about existence and replying 'I can't be impossible, I exist' — living among speakers of the later Wittgenstein's language games, where meaning is use within forms of life and social conventions (the tea that must be an invitation, the pizza-for-helping-moving protocol). Family resemblance, the childlike learner whose slate of social convention is blank (the Lockean tabula rasa applied to Sheldon's social mind), and lying as a language game Sheldon plays badly — the fake cousin Leopold Houston's fabricated Facebook trail, the orangutan hair — all dramatize the passage from logic-bound to use-based meaning that Sheldon, like Wittgenstein, may eventually make.
- ch. 23 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, Democritus — Possible Worlds; Problem of Induction — Mackonis shows Sheldon is wrong about being wrong: Stuart's tomato counterexample ('it's very wrong to say it's a suspension bridge') refutes his claim that wrongness admits no gradation, and closeness to truth is cashed out with possible-worlds similarity — vegetable theory sits one small alteration from actuality, echoing Sheldon's own many-worlds refusal to dance in any of them. The Raj exchange ('So you were wrong' / 'I didn't say that') motivates many-valued logics in which degrees of truth let both be partly right, while the 'Cooper-Wrongness Paradox' argues that if Sheldon always knew when he was wrong, he could never know that he was wrong. Hume's problem of induction then shows his post-Toby confidence in his other beliefs can never be inductively verified, only sometimes falsified, and his French-sprinkled 'victory' over an exhausted Stuart is sheer logical fallacy.
- ch. 24 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Isaiah Berlin, Richard Rorty — Two Concepts of Liberty — Lowe stages a 'Tolerance Bowl' between Sheldon's scientism and Mary's fundamentalism, opened with Berlin's liberal answer to pluralism — everyone entitled to their opinion, yet Sheldon insists 'evolution isn't an opinion, it's fact' and Mary's tolerance becomes its own tyranny. Davidson's argument that there is no very idea of a radically different conceptual scheme shows mother and son argue from shared concepts (DNA, intelligent design), but both remain metaphysical realists who cannot brook disagreement, while Rorty's 'the world does not speak' antirealism encourages fallibilist tolerance only to congeal into a 'what-we-have' dogma of its own that cannot account for genuine plurality. Nobody wins the bowl: each worldview makes tolerance hard in its own way.
- ch. 25 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato, Augustine of Hippo, Gilbert Ryle — The Categorical Imperative; The Noble Lie; Deontology — Fallis uses Sheldon — a lousy liar with an elaborate theory of lying — to probe the philosophy of lying: Kant's absolute prohibition (even 'out of frivolity'), Bok's presumption against deceit, Plato's noble lies reserved for philosopher kings, and Nietzsche's self-deceiving overmen, whose counsel explains the 'un-unravelable webs' of fake Facebook and blog evidence for the imaginary cousin Leopold Houston. Ryle's knowing-how versus knowing-that split explains how Sheldon can state the rules ('casually, no rapid breathing') yet botch the performance, while the Bazinga! pranks and the insincere courtroom apology break the Augustinian definition that lying requires intent to deceive. Grice's norms of conversation then ground the author's own definition — lying as intending to violate the norm against saying what you believe false — until a hypothetical, convention-oblivious liar like Kripke forces him to concede a counterexample and admit he was wrong.
- ch. 26 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Nel Noddings, Plato — Virtue Ethics (arete); Caring as the Ground of Ethics; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Barkman diagnoses four mama's boys: Raj's selective mutism under his parents' webcam meddling, Sheldon's comfort-seeking from a fundamentalist mother ('Soft Kitty,' mandatory grace), Howard's learned helplessness with his foghorn mother, and Leonard raised as Beverly's lab subject, his hugging machine echoing the wire-mother monkey experiment. Plato and Aristotle ground the charge of injustice — receiving less than one's station deserves, and wrongs against intimates are 'more terrible' — so parents bear special obligations their neglect breaches, a contemporary point pressed in the care-ethics tradition of Noddings. Cognitive-dissonance theory and Putman's Aristotelian 'psychological courage' prescribe honest self-reckoning for mothers and sons alike, with Leonard furthest along after confronting Beverly in 'The Maternal Congruence.'
- ch. 28 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Evans defends the Penny–Sheldon friendship as genuine by three universal marks — mutual care (two Saturnalia-miracle hugs), intimacy (keeping Penny's community-college secret; friends who direct and interpret each other's conduct), and shared activity (singing 'Soft Kitty' in the round) — and then argues its deep differences are not an obstacle but the engine of moral growth. Against Aristotle's similarity-based complete friendship, oriented to a shared eudaimonia, he offers a modern pluralist account: Sheldon's self-aware jokes, dancing, and social awareness and Penny's physics lessons show each growing toward the other's way of flourishing without becoming alike, which a friend as similar as Amy could never force.
- ch. 29 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Judith Butler, Simone de Beauvoir, John Stuart Mill, Plato — Gender Performativity; One Is Not Born a Woman; Woman as the Other; The Subjection of Women — White and Fisher run the show's women (and men) through feminist philosophy: the sex/gender distinction from Plato's Republic Book V and Mill's Subjection of Women through Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' and Butler's antiessentialist performativity. Penny's hyper-femininity reads as Butlerian parody that satirizes the script, the Penny–Bernadette–Amy lineup exposes the custom that smarts and beauty must trade off, and Elizabeth Plimpton and Leslie Winkle ('come for the breasts, stay for the brains') break it — while the four guys fail every 'real man' stereotype beside Penny's muscle-bound exes like Zack. Gender emerges as an artificial label that limits everyone, and seeing that would be the show's ultimate change through parody.
- ch. 30 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom

- ch. 1 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** The Meaning of Life — Editor Peter Fosl's introduction argues that a box-office-disappointment stoner comedy is genuinely philosophical: the film confronts sex, violence, and death (Donny dies, Maude conceives, marmots are drowned), stages class war between the unemployed Dude and the capitalist 'achiever' Big Lebowski, and sets the Dude's pacifist abiding against Walter's Vietnam warrior ethic and European nihilism. People are drawn to the Dude as an exemplar of stoic, nonmaterialistic abiding, and the essays draw on thinkers from Aristotle and Epicurus to Derrida and Butler; Ethan Coen's Princeton philosophy thesis on Wittgenstein anchors the film's pedigree.
- ch. 8 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Jacques Derrida, Aristotle, Friedrich Nietzsche — Deconstruction; Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Zeccardi and Ma deconstruct the film's hierarchical dichotomy between Walter's rule-obsessed ethical generalism (Shabbas rules, 'MARK IT ZERO!') and the nihilists' particularist 'Zere ARE no ROOLZ', using Derrida and Culler's method of undermining the opposition the text privileges. Each extreme fails: Walter's principles collide in the beeper dilemma, and active Nietzschean nihilism makes the nihilists unpredictable cowards. The Dude emerges as an Aristotelian agent of virtue whose phronesis perceptively weighs contextual facts (Smokey's disputed toe, the carpet-pissers' false assumption) against principles, making 'What would the Dude do?' a question about character rather than rules.
- ch. 10 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Bertrand Russell, Gottlob Frege — Jackson models the Dude as a formal system whose axioms are bowling, White Russians, and the rug, so that the counterexample to 'Jeffrey Lebowski = Jeffrey Lebowski' precipitates a foundational crisis just as Russell's paradox shattered Frege's set theory and non-Euclidean geometry unsettled Euclid's fifth postulate. Gödel's incompleteness theorems then show the Dude's system was never complete: no matter how many axioms (rugs) he regains, true-but-unprovable statements remain. His final reply is to adopt 'the Dude abides' as a new self-referential axiom asserting its own consistency — which, by Gödel's second theorem, a consistent system cannot do; hence 'fuck it, let's go bowling'.
- ch. 11 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill, Epicurus, Thomas Aquinas — Eudaimonia (flourishing); The Hedonic Calculus; Higher and Lower Pleasures — Eberl asks whether the Dude's 'pure abiding' is happiness: he runs Bentham's utility calculus on Dude-style pleasures (bowling's fecundity, the rug's purity, attending Marty's dance quintet for long-term rent goodwill) and Mill's higher/lower pleasures (Maude's vaginal art versus Logjammin'). Aristotle's verdict is that the Dude is not flourishing — his pleasures are incomplete, losable (the burned Torino), and he neglects his rational, social nature — yet Aristotle also ranks friendship with Walter and Donny highly, and Pieper's leisure, built on Aquinas's contemplation, gives the Dude's leisure a partial defense: he is incomplete but not bad, and he 'lives' while achievers merely make a living.
- ch. 13 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Epicurus — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Death Is Nothing to Us — O'Loughlin reads Walter biting off a nihilist's ear and the Dude refusing to walk out on league play as concrete realizations of ancient friendship: Aristotle's eudaimonia requires friends as 'second selves' whose shared activity (bowling in the friends' company) structures the excellent life, while Epicurus's Garden ordered life around simple pleasures and ataraxia, with friendship supplying pleasant memory and a kind of immortality after death. Because we moderns claim friendship's value without practicing its costs, the Dude's priorities look comic yet pierce us — and Donny's death, the Ralph's coffee can, and 'let's go bowling' become Epicurean commemoration rather than irreverence.
- ch. 14 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Epicurus, Lucretius, Seneca — Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia) — Rempel argues the Dude is a modern Epicurean parable: Epicurus's ataraxia is freedom from disturbance achieved by limiting desires to the natural and necessary — simple food, shelter, a few friends — so the Dude's 69-cent check, whale-song baths, and contentment with four dollars ('almost five') express 'enough is enough'. Maude's easily-had, non-binding seduction fits Epicurus's classification of sex as natural but not necessary (Lucretius: choose the joys of Venus without penalty), while Walter's million-dollar ringer scheme and his 'sick Cynthia thing' personify vain, insatiable desires — 'contented poverty is an honorable estate', so the Dude may be the wealthiest man in Los Angeles County.
- ch. 15 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Zhuangzi, Laozi, The Buddha, Confucius — Wu Wei (effortless action); The Tao (the Way); Buddhism — Lynch tests the fan claims that the Dude is 'the Duddha' or a practicing Daoist: the Dude has wu wei in his effortless arts of bowling and abiding and shares Zhuangzi's withdrawal from society (the Nixon bowling poster, learning from drunks, Donny's ashes scattered with naturalistic acceptance), but lacks Daoist metaphysics, the Dao's inexpressibility, and any articulated views. The Buddha parallels are real — nonattachment, practice over theory (the poisoned-arrow parable), compassion for Bunny — yet Gautama's radical discipline and middle path are the opposite of the Dude's laziness, so Dudeism emerges as an undisciplined American cousin, and the Dude follows 'just his way and his alone'.
- ch. 16 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Aquinas, John Locke, Michael Walzer — Just War Theory — Taking the film's opening 'This will not stand' seriously, Svolba and Betz read the Dude and Walter's rug campaign alongside the 1991 Gulf War through just war theory: just cause exists (soiled rug, invaded Kuwait), but Walter's gun at Smokey's foul line violates last resort and proportionality ('You're not wrong, Walter, you're just an asshole'), Aquinas's right intention is compromised when the ransom errand is motivated by the twenty grand, and Locke's case for right authority explains why justice cannot be left to 'fucking amateurs' like Walter, who overestimates injuries and retaliates disproportionately. Jus in bello discrimination fails everywhere — the neighbor's Corvette, the goons' mistaken Lebowski — and the escalation kills the innocent Donny.
- ch. 18 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Peter Singer — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Categorical Imperative; The Golden Mean; Authenticity — Jollimore and Jones diagnose three 'very unDude' vices: Walter's rule rigidity, which confuses Kant's hypothetical rules of games (don't cross the foul line) with categorical moral ones and needs 'rules all the way down' to ward off nihilism; the Big Lebowski's hypocritical inauthenticity, a fake achiever living on his daughter's allowance who collapses facedown before his own rug; and the exclusionism with which everyone shuts Donny out of the conversation. Against these the Dude exhibits Aristotelian virtue as good judgment (knowing when rules don't apply), the Golden Mean between Walter and the nihilists, and Singer-style inclusion — 'he's in bed with everybody' — making him an authentic man of humor and perspective.
- ch. 19 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Alasdair MacIntyre — Virtues, Practices and Traditions; Will to Power; Master and Slave Morality — Nicholas argues the film's supposed nihilists, Walter, and the Big Lebowski are all failed Nietzschean value-creators: Walter's arbitrary givings of value ('Donny was a good man... he was one of us') just enact nihilism, and the disabled achiever's money-and-plaques world mistakes symbols for value. He then uses Charles Taylor's three malaises of modernity — disenchantment, disengagement, atomism — to explain the Dude's world (even bowling stops mattering: 'Fuck the tournament'), and finds the way out in MacIntyre's notion of a practice: bowling's internal goods, standards of excellence, and community of giving and receiving tie the three friends to meanings outside themselves, resisting nihilism.
- ch. 21 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Absurd; Radical Freedom and Responsibility; Existentialism — Baird contrasts Camus's absurdity — the divorce between man and world demanding 'lucid indifference' and an absurd art that refuses counterfeit meaning — with Sartre's, where the world's meanings are contingent human projections and freedom entails absolute responsibility (Being and Nothingness sits by the Dude's bed). He argues the film is Sartrean rather than Camusian: the Dude weaves random events (the peed-on rug, the ransom) into the interpretation 'Bunny kidnapped herself', holding it provisionally as one story among possible ones, while Walter never takes responsibility for his Corvette-swinging choices. The viewers, knowing all interpretations are groundless, watch the absurd from the front row.
- ch. 22 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche — Despair (sickness unto death); The Myth of Sisyphus; Rebellion and Revolt; Eternal Recurrence — Brown and Fosl read the twin Lebowskis as America's post-1960s despair: the Big Lebowski is Kierkegaard's failed Caesar who despairs because he cannot rid himself of the self that did not become Caesar (a fake achiever living on an allowance), while the Dude is the failed leftist whose revolutions collapsed. Against nihilism Walter pulverizes with Nietzschean will, Kierkegaard prescribes the leap of faith, and Camus revolt — but the Dude offers a distinctly American answer, abiding repetition: rolling balls frame after frame like Camus's happy Sisyphus, repeating phrases and roles (Butlerian performativity) so that re-creating himself is his victory over meaninglessness, with No Country for Old Men as the dark twin where nihilism may be winning.
- ch. 23 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Sigmund Freud — The Unconscious; The Death Drive (Thanatos) — Hunt treats the film as a direct view of a single subject's unconscious, Freud-style: the Dude is the pre-Oedipal narcissist, the Big Lebowski the father toppled from his wheelchair-throne after the confrontation, Maude the mother, with a scattered superego distributed across the Stranger's moralizing and the Malibu sheriff's 'Stay out of Malibu!'. Donny and Walter figure oral and anal fixations, Jesus the threatening playground peer, and Bunny and the nihilists Freud's life and death drives — so Donny's death in the parking-lot melee lets the ego fuse death-drive energy into life, and the Dude's walk-away from the little Lebowski back to bowling and White Russians reads as repression into comfortable pre-Oedipal phantasy.
- ch. 25 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Plato, Aristotle — Subjectivity Is Truth; Allegory of the Cave — Drawing on fieldwork and surveys at the 2011 Tampa Lebowski Fest, Dufort and Lemire-Cadieux use Kierkegaard's Concept of Irony and indirect communication — contrasted with Plato's condemnation of mimesis in the cave and Aristotle's rehabiliation of it — to explain why Achievers who dress as rugs, memorize lines, and re-watch the film dozens of times find no objective message to decode. Kierkegaardian irony leaves each receiver to dig out a subjective existential truth through self-reflection and repetition, so that fans repeating the Dude's message become part of the irony itself: being an 'Achiever' achieves nothing objective and something deeply personal ('don't pee on other people's rugs').
- ch. 26 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** bell hooks, Miranda Fricker — Feminism; Epistemic Injustice; Objectification — Almassi grades the Dude as a halfway feminist ally: he divests from the Big Lebowski's patriarchal achiever-masculinity ('that and a pair of testicles'), respects Maude's conception project without paternalism (O'Neill's Kantian line between love and respect), and defends pacifist Smokey — yet his pacifism has stalled into passivity that King's active nonviolence would reject, he leaves Bunny's objectification unchallenged while 'Mr. Treehorn treats objects like women', and he only belatedly gives Maude the credibility Fricker's testimonial justice demands ('why don't you fucking listen occasionally?'). Using bell hooks's feminist masculinity and Larry May's progressive male standpoint, the chapter leaves the Dude five pins up with a spare still to pick up.
- ch. 27 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Bertrand Russell, Aristotle, Cicero — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics — Michaud asks whether the Dude's sloth is a vice and answers no: from Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness' he argues that overwork chiefly serves the rich — exactly how the Big Lebowski exploits the Dude as unpaid courier while sneering 'The bums will always lose' — and from Aristotle's and Cicero's moderatio he argues the Dude practices a mean between frantic work and paralysis, working hard when it matters (the drop, the rug). The fable of the ant and the grasshopper, retold, shows both die anyway, while the Dude 'works at being unemployed' and enjoys the time he has — sloth, ironically, does a kind of work.
- ch. 28 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** William James, Blaise Pascal, Bernard Williams, David Hume — The Will to Believe; Pascal's Wager — Malloy examines Walter's incorrigible leaps — Bunny kidnapped herself on no evidence, the toe is a fake ('I can get you a toe by three o'clock'), the Big Lebowski can walk — through Clifford's ethics of belief (the ship-owner who sinks his passengers) and James's 'Will to Believe' reply with its living, forced, and momentous genuine options, applied to Walter's 'dabbled' pacifism and his preference for Nazism's ethos over nihilism's nothing. Walter's conversion to Judaism for Cynthia raises whether practice can will belief, tested via Pascal's wager and James's objection, and the verdict borrows Bernard Williams: we cannot choose beliefs, but Walter's reckless policy of dismissing counterevidence makes him 'not just an asshole, he is also wrong'.
- ch. 30 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, John Locke, Edmund Gettier — The Gettier Problem; Language Games — In the method of ordinary language philosophy (Wittgenstein, Austin, Ryle), Stern and Wilkinson defend the Dude's retort to Jesus as no misuse of 'opinion': knowledge is justified true belief, undermined by Gettier-style epistemic luck, and opinions are beliefs supported only by subjective justification — like the taste of White Russians, Locke's secondary qualities — rather than public evidence. Jesus's claim that he and Liam will 'fuck you up' is a prediction that could in principle be publicly justified, but with no available evidence it is an unsupported opinion; Donny's gut-feeling Raiders pick shows opinions need not concern 'matters of opinion', and it is stubborn Walter who is truly 'opinionated'.
- ch. 31 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 32 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Plotinus, Charles Sanders Peirce — Augustine on Time — Smith turns Walter's 'Three thousand years of beautiful tradition, from Moses to Sandy Koufax — YOU'RE GODDAMN RIGHT I'M LIVING IN THE FUCKING PAST!' into a question in the philosophy of time: with Augustine's Confessions (the past exists only as a present of things past, in memory) and Plotinus's internalized time as 'the life of the soul in movement', Walter's Vietnam rages ('there isn't a literal connection, Dude'), his Cynthia show-dog errands, and his assumed Jewishness all show the past actively constituting his present. Peirce's 'method of tenacity' names his clinging to belief against doubt — an ailment the Dude secretly shares, given his own Port Huron past, drug-blurred memoir, and Creedence-soaked anachronism.
- ch. 33 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer, Maimonides — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons); The Meaning of Life — Rabbi Edelheit reads Walter as a figure of the Jewish philosophy of history: his 'I don't roll on Shabbas', Herzl's 'If you will it, it is no dream', the Baal Shem Tov's 'remembrance is the source of redemption', and the garbled Rambam fragment about aish all bind him to a historical community whose memory makes life meaningful — Gadamer's Truth and Method point that we belong to history before we understand ourselves, our prejudgments constituting our being. Against the nihilists' 'Vee belief in NOSSING', Walter's defiant living-in-the-past (Tevye, Sandy Koufax sitting out the World Series on Yom Kippur) is identity and meaning itself, even when Donny's ashes blow back in the wind and his grief can only speak in Vietnam's vocabulary.
- ch. 34 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 35 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

- ch. 1 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Jerry Walls's introduction opens with the film Shadowlands (the Oxford dons teasing Lewis about the fur coats in the wardrobe) to present Lewis as a part-time philosopher who taught philosophy at Oxford and presided over the Socratic Club. It previews the questions the Chronicles raise: truth versus illusion, whether might makes right, why be moral, what may be accepted on faith, whether more than one religion could be true, whether time flows differently in different worlds, and whether Eustace could become a dragon and still be the same person. It reassures Narnia fans that the essays enrich rather than ponderously distort ('gas') stories that should first be enjoyed on their own terms.
- ch. 11 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Stephen Webb argues that Lewis gives hearing, not sight, the fundamental role in knowledge: the Dufflepuds choose invisibility over ugliness, the crew in the Dark Island hear nightmares they cannot see, and in The Magician's Nephew Aslan is heard singing before he is seen. Against A.J. Ayer's logical positivism, Webb develops a 'vocative philosophy of sound' in which meaning lives in voices: Jadis's destructive Deplorable Word versus Aslan's world-creating song, Uncle Andrew's tone-deafness to warranted authority, and Shasta in The Horse and His Boy learning who he is from the voice in the dark that answers 'Myself.'
- ch. 13 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Socrates — Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); The Gettier Problem — Kevin Kinghorn uses virtue epistemology (Sosa, Code) to solve the puzzle of why Uncle Andrew alone hears only roaring when Aslan sings Narnia into being: he fails all four intellectual virtues. He does not value truth for its own sake (unlike Frank the Cabby), indulges wishful thinking (like Edmund defending the Witch for Turkish Delight, or imagining Jadis fancies him), lets fear dictate belief (terror of the animals he has vivisected), and lacks Socratic self-knowledge, which the dragonized Eustace painfully acquires. A closing reading of Prince Caspian has each character's ability to see Aslan track their earlier trust in Lucy's testimony: sin blinds, and faith produces its own authenticating evidence.
- ch. 14 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Philosophical Skepticism — Thomas Senor turns the Professor's trilemma about Lucy (lying, mad, or telling the truth) into a general account of when to believe incredible testimony: weigh the testifier's reliability against how well the claim fits your background beliefs. He shows why Lucy's siblings should have believed her second report of Aslan in Prince Caspian, since by then talking animals and a resurrected Lion no longer clashed with what they knew, and then applies the framework to 'Julia's' report of hearing God, arguing that believing, disbelieving, or withholding rationally depends on the hearer's own background commitments. A footnote explains why Hume on miracles does not fit Lucy's case, since she claims no violation of natural law.
- ch. 15 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** William James, Blaise Pascal, Augustine of Hippo — Pascal's Wager; The Will to Believe; Faith and Reason — Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.
- ch. 16 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Kuhn, René Descartes, John Locke, Immanuel Kant, Alvin Plantinga, John Dewey — Paradigm Shifts — Bruce Reichenbach recounts the failure of the Enlightenment quest for certainty from Descartes and Locke through Kant to the positivists, and argues that Lewis's Narnia instead models knowing as perspectival (the Stable door whose inside is bigger than its outside), value-laden (the Dwarfs' self-chosen dark paradigm that turns Aslan's feast into refuse and violets into stable litter), and personal (Lucy's unarguable knowledge that she has seen Aslan in Prince Caspian, read through Michael Polanyi's tacit knowledge). Kuhn's competing paradigms frame theism versus atheism, James's will to believe opens the chapter, and Plantinga's defeaters keep personal knowledge from collapsing into mere subjectivity.
- ch. 17 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Alasdair MacIntyre, David Hume, Aristotle, William Paley — Ethical Egoism; Philosophy of Love; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Laura Garcia assembles Narnian heroes: Jill, Eustace, and Puddleglum untying Rilian at likely lethal cost, Eustace hacking at the Sea Serpent, unarmed Shasta charging the lion to save Aravis, and Digory refusing the Witch's offer of the apple that could heal his dying mother. She asks whether egoist theories can explain such deeds and argues they cannot: Hobbes's disguised self-interest, Butler's and Paley's reward schemes, Hume's sympathy, and MacIntyre's identity-based interests all fall short. Only love of others for their own sake, and (for Jill and Digory) trust in Aslan's proven goodness, explains both the heroic choices and our admiration of them as supererogatory acts beyond the call of duty.
- ch. 19 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** John Stuart Mill, Epicurus, Aristotle, Karl Marx, Thomas Aquinas, Jeremy Bentham — Higher and Lower Pleasures; Eudaimonia (flourishing); The Golden Mean; Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia) — Devin Brown uses Eustace, who dodges work on Dragon Island until he wakes as a dragon and discovers he would rather be hungry among human friends than comfortable alone, to contrast Epicurean hedonism and Tom Sawyer's work-avoidance with Mill's higher pleasures and the 'Sherlock Holmes philosophy of work.' Weighing Aristotle's contemplative life against Lewis's love of quests, he reads Father Christmas's tailored gifts and 'everyone must do what he can do best' as an Acorn Philosophy of Vocation with a Marxian 'from each according to his ability' echo, condemns wrong livelihoods like Governor Gumpas's slave trade, and closes on leisure and Aristotle's golden mean, which Lewis turns into 'golden extremes.'
- ch. 20 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Aquinas, Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato — Natural Law; Moral Relativism; Will to Power — Tim Mosteller identifies Lewis's Tao from The Abolition of Man with Aquinas's Natural Law, an objective moral order knowable by all rational beings, and maps three responses onto Narnian characters: wholehearted acceptance (Peter, Lucy, Tirian, Reepicheep), selective 'Innovators' who pick and choose (Shift and Miraz, with Nietzsche's invented master-values as the philosophical extreme), and total rejection by 'Conditioners' (Ginger the Cat, who reverts to dumb beast, and Uncle Andrew, who loses the animals' speech). Individual laws are illustrated by Mr. Tumnus freeing Lucy, Aslan scratching Aravis for her gladness at the slave girl's beating, Nikabrik's treacherous Realpolitik, Lucy's eavesdropping spell in the Magician's book, and Jill's showing-off at the cliff.
- ch. 21 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, Plato — Virtue Ethics (arete); Cardinal and Theological Virtues; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Bill Davis argues that Narnia works as a classical moral-education environment: against Experiment House's science-worship, Narnia supplies the three ingredients Aristotle and Aquinas require, namely instruction, virtuous exemplars to imitate (Reepicheep's courage, Puddleglum's temperance), and habituation through repeated right action, which together transform Peter's indecision, Edmund's treachery, Lucy's envy, and Jill's timidity. What finally lasts beyond Narnia, he contends, is a transforming encounter with Aslan: Eustace's dragon skin torn off by the Lion, Jill's drink at the stream where 'there is no other stream,' and Digory's tearful confession. He closes by arguing today's self-esteem-based character education cannot replicate this, since it pursues virtue from love of self rather than love of the good.
- ch. 22 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates, Thomas Hobbes — Master and Slave Morality; Justice in the Republic; Moral Relativism — Janice Daurio sets Plato's Thrasymachus and Callicles and Nietzsche's immoralism against three Narnian immoralists: Uncle Andrew, who exempts 'profound students and great thinkers' from rules meant for little boys, servants, and women; Queen Jadis, whose Deplorable Word and 'What else were they there for but to do my will?' embody might-makes-right; and the Green Witch, who extends going beyond good and evil to going beyond truth itself. Following Lewis's moral realism (the Golden Rule and Natural Law as facts like gravity, with Hobbes's lesson that someone always turns up with more power), she shows the immoralists cannot live by their own creed, since Uncle Andrew resents being treated as Jadis's slave, and since Lewis ties real authority to service, as when humble Frank the Cabby is made king.
- ch. 23 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Alasdair MacIntyre, Plato — Virtue Ethics; Moral Relativism — Gayne Anacker defines moral imagination, the capacity to see one's values and life from fresh moral perspectives, and argues the Chronicles exercise it through three character types readers live through: flawed repenters (Edmund, Eustace, Bree, Aravis), the essentially good under trial (Lucy believing her Aslan sighting in Prince Caspian, Caspian's greed on Goldwater Island), and the fatally self-absorbed (Uncle Andrew, Shift), together with portrayals of worship and of true versus usurped nobility (Peter versus Miraz). Philosophically he contends the stories' effectiveness supports virtue ethics over action-centered modern theories, and that disagreement among ethical theorists is no ground for relativism: no one needs theoretical consensus to know Miraz is evil.
- ch. 24 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Martin Heidegger, René Descartes, Alasdair MacIntyre — Allegory of the Cave; Just War Theory; The Ethics of Political Violence — Wendy Hamblet asks whether Narnia feeds children a dangerous militaristic moral imaginary: Homeric warrior heroes, swarthy Calormene villains, voiceless animals excluded from moral concern, and battles that decide truth, in a lineage running from Plato's censorship of nursery stories through Descartes's modernity to Heidegger's seduction by Hitler's myths. On closer reading she finds Lewis undermining militarism: morally mixed characters, condemnation of aggression, despotism, and 'reasons of state,' and room only for just war and righteous self-defense. The finale is read through Plato's cave, as the Last Battle's worlds-within-worlds expose our political 'truths' as shadow-images that unscrupulous leaders manipulate when the god is absent.
- ch. 25 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Simone de Beauvoir — Woman as the Other; One Is Not Born a Woman; Feminism — Argues that Narnia is 'unfriendly to the feminine' by reading Susan's exclusion from Aslan's country at the end of The Last Battle ('no longer a friend of Narnia', too interested in nylons and invitations) as the fate of the one heroine who stays stereotypically feminine. It shows that the admired girls (Lucy, Aravis, Jill) succeed only by approximating a masculine standard of adventure, applying Beauvoir's point that measuring women against a male norm implies something wrong with femaleness itself. It further traces how evil in Narnia wears a feminine face: the Green Witch seduces Prince Rilian into Underland, the White Witch tempts Edmund and Digory where the girls resist, and the Witch's Lilith/Jinn lineage ties women to the Fall via 'Daughters of Eve'.
- ch. 26 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Socrates, Aristotle — Allegory of the Cave; Theory of Forms; Socratic Method (elenchus) — Takes Digory's dying remark 'It's all in Plato' as the key to the Chronicles. It compares the Professor's guided questioning of Peter and Susan about Lucy's wardrobe testimony to the Socratic method, though noting he supplies evidential maxims rather than eliciting a virtue-definition as Socrates does with Cephalus on justice. It maps Underland in The Silver Chair onto the Allegory of the Cave (Rilian bound in his silver chair like the chained prisoners, the Green Witch's enchantment that denies any world beyond), observing that the Witch 'plays Aristotle' by ridiculing Aslan as an invented perfect Form, while Puddleglum's 'stand by the play-world' speech echoes Socrates's reply to Glaucon that the ideal pattern is none the worse for being unrealizable. Finally it reads the 'real Narnia' of The Last Battle ('world within world, Narnia within Narnia') as Christian Platonism, with the nested heavens even raising Plato's Third Man problem.
- ch. 28 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** John Locke, René Descartes, Aristotle — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory); Ship of Theseus — Uses Narnia's magical transformations to probe personal identity, starting with the qualitative/numerical identity distinction illustrated by the look-alike twins Shasta and Corin in The Horse and His Boy. Aristotle's essential/accidental properties frame the question of what Eustace can lose and remain Eustace, including turning into a dragon, and Rabadash into a donkey, showing persons are not identical to their bodies. Descartes's soul argument and Locke's memory theory are tested and rejected, the latter because it cannot handle Rilian's enchanted amnesia, Shasta's forgotten infancy, or Susan's disowned memories without circularity. The chapter defends instead a first-person-perspective theory on which a person is constituted by, not identical to, a body, illustrated by the repeatedly repaired Dawn Treader and by the heroes surviving death in The Last Battle as restored points of view.
- ch. 29 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato — Master and Slave Morality; Tripartite Soul — Reads Eustace, Uncle Andrew, Experiment House, and Miraz's censored Narnia as Lewis's portraits of modern secularism, which treats the world as mere resource and dismisses the transcendent regardless of evidence. It argues that denying intrinsic value collapses into a Nietzschean master morality of power, visible in Uncle Andrew's use of the children as guinea pigs and the Lone Islands' slave trade, and exposes the secular 'conditioner's' self-exemption as a violation of the Principle of Relevant Difference. Against the Green Witch's debunking of Puddleglum's sun and Aslan as copies of a lamp and a cat, it deploys the Platonic-Cartesian copy/original model of ideas to argue transcendent ideas (eternity, perfection, necessary being) cannot be derived from lower material causes, suggesting instead that the material world is the 'shadowland' copy of a divine original.
- ch. 30 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Boethius — Fate and Foreknowledge; The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Starts from Narnia's time discrepancies (hours in the wardrobe, reigns of years that cost seconds in England, 1303 Narnian years in one) and shows Einstein's relativity makes different time frames plausible before admitting science cannot explain Aslan's 'I call all times soon'. It interprets that claim through Boethius's doctrine of God's timelessness, the eternal present embracing all moments as a simultaneous whole, and defends its compatibility with creaturely free choice: not even Aslan can override the Dwarfs' self-imprisoned perception or force Uncle Andrew to hear him. The chapter closes on the end of Narnian time in The Last Battle, Father Time making an end, and Aslan's timeless country as the fuller reality the temporal world shadowed.
- ch. 31 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 32 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, Augustine of Hippo — The Problem of Evil; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Frames the problem of pain with Hume's Dialogues (Demea and Philo) and reconstructs Lewis's answer as played out on Aslan: pain is God's megaphone that rouses Edmund on the Witch's frozen sledge and strips Eustace's dragon skin in the transforming embrace. Suffering also reveals hidden strengths, as when Aslan's pursuit goads Shasta into unexpected courage, modeled on Augustine's reading of the binding of Isaac as teaching Abraham, not God, what Abraham could endure. Aravis's claw wounds are treated as retributive punishment, tear for tear, exactly proportioned to the drugged slave's whipping, which the chapter defends via Lewis's retributivist theory against purely deterrent punishment. Because divine goodness aims at making creatures good rather than merely happy, Aslan can be both good and terrible, 'not a tame lion', since free will cannot be coerced into perfection.
- ch. 33 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Argues that Lewis is an inclusivist about salvation, not a universalist or pluralist: Shift and the self-enclosed Dwarfs are lost, and Aslan explicitly denies being one with Tash, yet Emeth's service to Tash is counted by Aslan as service to him ('all find what they truly seek'). Shasta's providential guidance by a lion he has never heard of, and Jill being saved by drinking from the one stream before knowing whose stream it is, illustrate that the water saves, not knowledge about the water. The chapter supports inclusivism over exclusivism with Lewis's Mere Christianity passages, the 'ought implies can' justice argument against condemning those who never heard the gospel, and Rabadash's healing in Tash's own temple as Aslan working through pagan means.
- ch. 34 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Forgiveness — Reconstructs Narnian atonement as the early Christian Ransom Theory: Digory's confession, remorse, and 'undoing' of his wrong in The Magician's Nephew, and Aslan giving his life as ransom for Edmund against the Witch's Deep Magic claim in The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe, ending with the Deeper Magic that cracks the Stone Table. It answers John Lucas's four objections (literal Satan, Satan's rights, God negotiating with evil, divine deception) by treating evil as self-chosen bondage whose doors are 'locked on the inside', arguing Aslan's sacrificial identification with wrongdoers displays a love that mere omnipotent force could not, and that wrongdoers like the Witch are not owed full disclosure. It also defends mercy's tension with strict justice, via the example of a deserving prisoner mercifully freed, and finds humor rather than crudeness in Peter Lombard's cross-as-mousetrap image.
- ch. 35 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** Elizabeth Anscombe — Faith and Reason — Debunks the 'Anscombe legend' that Lewis abandoned rational apologetics for children's stories after his 1948 Socratic Club defeat by Elizabeth Anscombe over the argument that naturalism is self-refuting. It shows Lewis revised and expanded the argument in the 1960 Miracles, incorporating Anscombe's reasons/causes distinction, and kept writing apologetic essays, while the Professor's trilemma about Lucy (liar, lunatic, or truthful) mirrors the Trilemma of Mere Christianity and shows Narnia using logic, not fleeing it. It rejects A.N. Wilson's identification of the Green Witch with Anscombe and argues the Chronicles teach that prudence and faith are compatible virtues: Edmund's rationalizing, Trumpkin's honest skepticism, and Puzzle's blind trust in Shift all show that fideistic faith is a vice, not what Lewis asks of children.
- ch. 36 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, Thomas Aquinas — Immortality and the Soul; The Problem of Evil; Karma and Rebirth — Observes that only Talking Animals enter Aslan's country when Narnia ends in The Last Battle, then critically examines Lewis's case against wider animal salvation: derivative immortality through human love (Sarah Smith's train of beasts in The Great Divorce), compensation of animal pain in an afterlife, Lewis's follow-Descartes claim that most animals are sentient but not conscious enough to feel pain or have a surviving 'self'. The chapter argues each point fails: the physiological evidence shows animals suffer, resurrection or God-given souls remain possible (Strawberry's transformation into a winged Talking horse), and a compensatory hereafter is still the most promising answer to why a loving God permits the fawn's miserable death. Aquinas's rational-creature hierarchy frames the Talking/Dumb divide, and the Hindu-Buddhist rebirth theodicy is considered and rejected as unbiblical.
- ch. 37 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
