Zelda is woman as Idea, traced to Platonic Forms: young, beautiful, virtuous, and radically passive (turned to stone in The Minish Cap, asleep through The Adventure of Link, imprisoned in nearly every game), an object that exists to motivate Link's heroism. Significantly, only the masculine-garbed Sheik and the pirate Tetra escape passivity, a shift the authors link to Miyamoto's design philosophy of 'reality over realism' and to changing conceptions of women.
- ch. 36 "20 - Getting to Know the World Next Door" *(no index entry yet)* — Roger Ngim reflects on the blurring boundary between games and the real world: the dying instruction manual, the Wii's naturalistic controller, and the fact that game spaces are 'gated communities' whose deliberate limits — impassable rivers, finite boards, unbreakable rules — are exactly what make them knowable scaled-down realities worth studying. Drawing on his UCSD course 'Playing by the Rules', he notes that even avid students resisted treating games as objects of scholarship, partitioning play off from their serious lives. He concludes that game studies is emerging as its own discipline, like film studies before it, as game structures colonize shopping, banking, television, and work.
- ch. 37 "Heroes of Hyrule" *(notes)*
- ch. 38 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 39 "The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 40 "The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All

- ch. 1 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Plato — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Justice in the Republic — Eric Katz reads Tolkien's One Ring as a modern retelling of Plato's Ring of Gyges: Glaucon's challenge in Republic II that no one, given impunity, would remain just. He traces each character's moment of choice - Gollum already corrupted and split into 'Slinker and Stinker', Boromir trying to seize the Ring at Amon Hen and dying redeemed, Galadriel passing the test ('I will diminish, and go into the West'), Tom Bombadil untouched, Frodo finally claiming the Ring at the Cracks of Doom while Sam rejects the vision of 'Samwise the Strong'. Katz argues Tolkien improves on Plato by showing, through living characters, that unlimited power corrupts the soul, and that the answer to 'Why be moral?' is 'to be yourself': those who refuse the Ring are exactly those who know their own limits.
- ch. 13 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Existential Risk — Theodore Schick takes Tolkien's remark that the Ring represents 'potency' externalized beyond its maker's control and applies it to emerging nanotechnology, genetics, and robotics. He sets Bill Joy's call for relinquishment against Eric Drexler's promise of universal assemblers, cell-repair machines, and soldier nanosuits, weighing the 'grey goo' risk against the Rings' own power to heal and preserve (Lothlórien, Bilbo 'well-preserved'). Against the Council of Elrond's solution of destroying the Ring, he argues our situation is disanalogous - Ring-making knowledge is now spread worldwide and there is no single device to destroy - so grass-roots social response, not bans, must tame the new technologies.
- ch. 14 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Karl Marx, Martin Heidegger — Commodity Fetishism; Alienation — Alison Milbank argues we are all in thrall to the Ring because it mirrors our own fetishism: she reads the film's lingering close-ups, Smaug-like hoarding, and Gollum's baby-talking self-division through Freud's theory of the fetish and Marx's commodity fetishism, with Sauron as the emptied idolater who poured his power into the thing. Against this she sets Middle-earth's gift economy - Bilbo's party, Galadriel's gifts, Sam's elven rope - glossed by Heidegger's 'Thinging gathers': Sam praises the rope by restoring it to its elven makers and its use. Tom Bombadil, who treats the Ring as 'a very pretty ring' and nothing more, and Frodo's final sacrifice model the unfetishized life; the chapter closes with Sam's homecoming, where chairs are only chairs and the family circle replaces the Ring.
- ch. 15 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Epicurus, Henry David Thoreau, Marcus Aurelius, Augustine of Hippo — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia); Walden (deliberate living); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Gregory Bassham distills six keys to happiness from Tolkien's hobbits and elves: delight in simple pleasures (Epicurus on natural pleasures, Thoreau's Walden simplicity), making light of troubles (Sam's star above Mordor, with Marcus Aurelius and Augustine on courage and hope), friendship (Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics read against Sam, Merry, and Pippin refusing to let Frodo go alone), good character, beauty and creativity (Lothlórien versus Mordor, 'flow'), and wonder (Tom Bombadil, Frodo's 'recovery' of fresh vision at Cerin Amroth). He argues Tolkien thereby becomes a philosophical guide, pointing from the Shire and Rivendell to a richer, more joy-filled life.
- ch. 17 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Philosophy of Love — Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum as two hobbits of the same nature and culture seeking the same happy life, so their success and failure are instructive for ordinary people like us. Gollum's happiness is solitary possession of the Ring - he murders Déagol for it and ends 'into the dust' - while Sam's is fellowship in the Shire with Rosie and Frodo, pursued through loyalty and giving (spending Galadriel's seed-box to restore the Shire). The pivotal episode is Gollum's trembling caress of Frodo's knee, 'the most tragic moment in the Tale', squandered when Sam's jealous rebuke drives him back to treachery. With Aristotle on friendship and self-love, the chapter concludes that happiness is achievable only in a social context and its key is love.
- ch. 18 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Hannah Arendt — Existentialism; Will to Power; Amor Fati (love of fate) — Eric Bronson places Tolkien among the 'sometimes merry' existentialists: Nietzsche's artist who says Yes amid catastrophe and needs 'the power to forget', Jaspers on machines estranging us from our past, and Arendt on Eichmann's obedient inhumanity and the few who create joy in dark times. The elves' songs in Rivendell and Lórien are joy born of sorrow and dispossession - Galadriel suffers because she remembers too much, trying to 'embalm time', while Arwen forgoes immortality for Aragorn. Her refusal of the Ring ('I will diminish, and go into the West, and remain Galadriel') embodies the existentialist affirmation: trust your own light, know what to remember and what to forget.
- ch. 19 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Will to Power; The Übermensch; The Death of God; Eternal Recurrence — Douglas Blount tests Nietzsche against Sauron, whose forging and grasp of the One Ring - even striving to supplant Ilúvatar - enacts the will to power, exploitation, the death of God, and the ideal of the Übermensch. He argues that in Middle-earth the naked will to power appears not as a brave new humanity but as plain evil, and that Tolkien answers Nietzsche not with argument but with a rival portrait: Gandalf's self-sacrifice on the Bridge of Khazad-dûm, Frodo's mercy to Gollum that becomes Middle-earth's salvation, and Sam's humble refusal of 'Samwise the Strong'. Judged by Nietzsche's own aesthetic criterion of taste, Tolkien's vision of community, humility, and abnegation is the more beautiful - and therefore the more compelling - portrait of reality.
- ch. 21 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Aristotle — The Problem of Evil — Scott Davison asks whether Tolkien's world is Manichean - two equal forces of Good and Evil - and answers no: the Ring is not 'altogether evil' in itself but animated by Sauron's infused will, and nothing, not even Sauron, is totally evil, since 'nothing is evil in the beginning'. Developing Augustine's account, he shows evil as parasitic privation - Ringwraiths wear robes 'to give shape to their nothingness', the Eye is 'a window into nothing' - and traces evil to inordinate desire: Sam stays content with his garden while Boromir, Saruman, Denethor, and Sauron reach for more than their place allows. Evil unmakes itself (Saruman dies by Wormtongue's knife), and because goodness is the world's default, there is always hope of overcoming it.
- ch. 22 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant — Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis); The Golden Mean — Aeon Skoble uses Tolkien's characters to defend Aristotelian virtue ethics against Kantian and utilitarian rivals. Sam's loyalty is a virtue because critically directed at a worthy friend while Wormtongue's loyalty to Saruman is not; Sméagol's instant murder of Déagol reveals prior vice that let the Ring corrupt him quickly, whereas Bilbo resists it for sixty years; Aragorn's temperance and teachableness contrast Boromir's resentment and pride. Working through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean (courage between cowardice and rashness), practical wisdom, and the phronemos as role model, he argues that rule-following cannot capture moral perception (do we owe truth to Black Riders?) and that utilitarianism absurdly requires Galadriel's foresight.
- ch. 23 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Socrates, Lucretius, Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre, Boethius, Aristotle, Bernard Williams — Death Is Nothing to Us; Immortality and the Soul; The Myth of Sisyphus — Bill Davis asks why Arwen would 'choose a mortal life' with Aragorn and why wise elves and men call death a gift. The Ringwraiths show that existence can be worse than death - undead kings whose frustrated nature is perpetual torment - while Socrates in the Apology, Lucretius, Sartre, and Camus supply reasons not to fear annihilation, and the elves' endless life raises Boethius's and Bernard Williams's problem of boring immortality (Camus's Sisyphus, Wowbagger the Infinitely Prolonged). He concludes that Arwen and Aragorn, uncommonly wise and loving, accept death as Ilúvatar's gift: she prefers a finite life of deep love, and they trust the old stories of a world 'remade' beyond the circles of Arda.
- ch. 25 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Karl Marx — The Death of God — Joe Kraus argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings in part as a protest against modernism - the post-WWI mood (Berman, Marx's 'all that is solid melts into air', Nietzsche's 'God is dead') that tradition is obsolete and whatever can be done must be done. The heroes win by remembering: Gandalf alone thinks to watch the Shire, Sam's book-learning about elves and the password 'Elbereth' saves the day at Cirith Ungol, while Saruman and Denethor fall into modern despair through the palantír and Pippin's stone dropped in Moria brings Gandalf down. The Ring itself is modernism's false promise of remaking the world, and Tolkien answers it with a fantasy where ancient lore has tangible power - sealed by Pippin's maturing into one of Middle-earth's great librarians.
- ch. 26 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Deep Ecology; Anthropocentrism — Andrew Light identifies a distinctive environmental theme he calls 'green time': Tom Bombadil and the ents embody nature's long rhythms and are largely indifferent to the War of the Ring - Tom would simply mislay the Ring, and the ents march to war only after Saruman strips Fangorn. Against readings that make elves or dwarves stand-ins for nature, he argues the text lets nature speak for itself, from a collective, ecosystemic perspective: the ents, 'made of the bones of the earth', decline with their forests and lost the entwives to the tilled land. Deploying Wittgenstein's point that we could not understand a talking lion, he concludes that Tolkien's personified nature trains us in the long view and humility needed for problems like global warming.
- ch. 27 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Augustine of Hippo — Fate and Foreknowledge; Autonomy of the Will; The Problem of Evil — Thomas Hibbs reads the Quest's ending as providential: the Ring is destroyed against Frodo's own will at the Cracks of Doom, through Gollum, exactly as Gandalf hinted when he said Bilbo was 'meant' to find the Ring, 'and not by its maker'. Providence first appears as chance - Bilbo's arrival, Aragorn's landing at the Pelennor, Gandalf 'sent back' until his task is done - and is discerned only in hindsight as the epic's dramatic unity. Against the worry that providence cancels freedom, he uses Kant on duty and dignity (Frodo's 'I will take the Ring', Sam's 'I must see it through', set against Denethor ruling his 'own end'), while noting Tolkien rejects Kant's autonomy/heteronomy split, and with Augustine he treats evil as parasitic, able only to mar itself ('Oft evil will shall evil mar').
- ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Dogen, The Buddha, Laozi — Buddhism; Yin and Yang; Zen Buddhism; The Tao (the Way) — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki compare Tolkien with Zen Buddhism and Taoism on four themes while insisting on the real differences. Tolkien's talking trees (Old Man Willow, Treebeard's 'half awake' forest) invite comparison with Buddhist universal sentience and Dogen's walking mountains, but Tolkien anthropomorphizes where Buddhism grants non-human modes of sentience; the hobbits' ties to the Shire echo dependent origination, though Tolkien's stewardship and preference for the domesticated Shire over sinister wild nature remain Western. Frodo's succession of mentors (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, and the unlikely 'Master Samwise') parallels the Zen master-student relation, while Tolkien's war of light against darkness - nine Walkers against nine Riders - is decisively not the Taoist balance of yin and yang, for Taoists destroying either cosmic force would itself produce evil.
- ch. 30 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Augustine of Hippo, René Descartes, Friedrich Nietzsche, Martin Heidegger, Martha Nussbaum — Allegory of the Cave; Authenticity; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Amor Fati (love of fate) — Lenore Wright reads Sam and Frodo's Quest through the two journey motifs of Western philosophy: the journey out (Plato's cave, structuring Augustine's Confessions and Descartes' escape from the senses' deceptions) and the journey inward (the cogito, self-transformation, with Nussbaum's claim that literature gives philosophy a body). Frodo's steps out of the Shire-cave - selling Bag End, 'I will take the Ring, though I do not know the way' - create the Fellowship and its freedoms, while Boromir attains self-knowledge only at death's door and Gandalf, Aragorn, and Sam are remade by the road. Against classical heroes like Theseus and Odysseus, Sam and Frodo are modern pilgrims - Nietzschean Yea-sayers becoming who they are, with Heideggerian 'potentiality-for-Being' - whereas Sméagol and Saruman live inauthentically, defined by their pasts.
- ch. 31 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Boethius — The Leap of Faith; The Consolation of Philosophy — John Davenport argues that The Lord of the Rings is neither mere adventure nor Christian allegory but an epic fairy tale whose 'eucatastrophe' - Tolkien's term for the sudden joyous turn, a miraculous reprieve - carries religious hope even though the book contains no churches or prayers. Drawing on Tolkien's 'On Fairy-stories', he makes Sir Gawain and the Green Knight the model for Frodo: Gawain accepts the girdle and is scarred yet reprieved, just as Frodo claims the Ring, loses a finger as Beren lost a hand, and is saved only because the mercy shown Gollum lets the Ring fall into the fire. Gandalf's return, Éowyn's healing, and the sapling of Nimloth extend the pattern; with Kierkegaard the deliverance is grace 'by virtue of the absurd', an echo of the eschaton answering Boethius's question whether our struggles have final significance.
- ch. 32 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "i" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Thanks" *(notes)*
- ch. 8 "I. Now Wait for Last Season" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "1. Juliana in Plato’s Cave" **·** Plato — Allegory of the Cave — Dennis Weiss argues the Amazon series is really about television and screened images: Juliana screening the Grasshopper newsreel in her basement replays Plato's Cave, except that the projected images, not the 'real' world of Nazi America, are what offer her 'a way out.' Following her from transfixed belief to doubt (calling the final film 'a nightmare' and choosing to trust Joe over the reel), and reading the show's media surfaces (Nazi commercials, 'Edelweiss,' the Riefenstahl comparison, Tagomi's cross-world vision), the chapter uses media thinkers like McLuhan, Meyrowitz, and Don Ihde to describe learning to see with 'compound vision' in a placeless, image-saturated culture.
- ch. 10 "2. Say Heil! to Architecture" **·** Walter Benjamin — The Aura of the Artwork — Reading the show's Nazi-remade monuments (the swastika on Mount Rushmore and the Statue of Liberty, the SS tower, VA Day spectacle) through Walter Benjamin's account of fascism as aestheticized politics that narcotizes the masses, the chapter argues architecture is what makes the alternate timeline legible to viewers. It then contrasts these fixed 'words in stone' with 'counter-monuments' that keep alternative memory alive: the clandestinely circulating newsreels, Frank and Mark's underground Hebrew prayer, and the fragile chrysanthemums Tagomi and Juliana exchange, with Tagomi's final vision of a Lolita-billboard San Francisco recognized through buildings alone.
- ch. 11 "3. Saving Hitler’s Life" **·** René Descartes — Mind–Body Dualism — The chapter claims the show takes dualism — the same physical world with different 'histories' as its mind — and multiplies it into many overlapping versions of each person: Juliana and Frank swap awe and fear between the first and ninth episodes' screenings, and the newsreel in which Joe executes Frank shifts how they see the real Joe. Its centerpiece is the finale, where viewers find themselves rooting for the Nazis Smith and Wegener to keep Hitler alive and prevent a worse war, forcing the audience to confront its own shifting allegiances and how easily fascism could take root in America.
- ch. 12 "II. The World Dick Made" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "4. Cruel Optimism and the Good Nazi Life" **·** Bertrand Russell — Applying Lauren Berlant's 'cruel optimism,' the chapter argues John Smith and Frank Frink are ruined by the very 'good life' they pursue under the Reich: Smith sustains the system of suburban family, VA Day rituals, and housewife-training daughters until Thomas's Dejerine-Roussy diagnosis makes the eugenic order threaten his own son, while Frank clings to settling down with Juliana and keeps choosing escape over resistance even after his sister's murder. Bertrand Russell's definition of the good life as 'inspired by love and guided by knowledge,' together with Henri Lefebvre's need/desire contrast and Jonathan Crary on television's anti-nomadic passivity, supplies the measuring stick this world fails to meet.
- ch. 14 "5. In the Neutral Zone, a Libertarian’s Home Is Their (High) Castle" **·** John Locke, Thomas Hobbes, Robert Nozick — Natural Rights; The State of Nature; The Minimal State — The chapter reads Dick as a left-leaning libertarian for whom the deepest evil of the High Castle world is the loss of privacy: Arnold's surveillance unit and the Kempeitai's wiretaps illustrate Locke's self-ownership and natural rights, while the Neutral Zone poses the Hobbesian question of whether even an oppressive state beats the state of nature, and the 'libertarian minimal state' names what the Reich destroys. On this reading the American Nazis like John Smith were internal collaborators all along — 'it already happened here' — and ethics lies in refusal, as when Tagomi declines to sign the order sending Frank to his death.
- ch. 15 "6. The Self-Willed and Ignorant Law" **·** Plato — The Philosopher King — Marc Cole argues the Reich's and Japan's governments have the structure of Plato's Republic: supreme power in a political expert who is above the law and manages citizens' work, breeding, education, and music from cradle to grave — in some ways more controlling than the Nazis, since Plato abolishes the family outright. John Smith's son Thomas, condemned to death by a law blind to particular circumstances, embodies the Statesman's 'self-willed and ignorant' law, and after weighing the doctor/patient defense of rule by expertise, the chapter sides with democratic republics and warns that multiplying laws and state management inches us toward Plato's republic or the Reich.
- ch. 16 "7. What if Your Hero Is a Fascist" **·** Karl Marx — Ideology and False Consciousness — Bruce Krajewski provocatively argues that Dick and his works promote fascism rather than warn against it, citing Dick's Exegesis confession that 'my real idol is Hitler' and his fascist epistemology on which what we believe becomes objective truth. Reading the opening credits' overlays (Nazi eagle on the American eagle, 'Edelweiss,' swastikas in Times Square ads) as capitalism colonizing the swastika, and noting the 'structuring absence' of the communists who actually fought fascism, he treats the show's success amid the alt-Right moment as evidence that Dick's projected fascist America is already arriving.
- ch. 17 "III. Captives of Unchance" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "8. Is It Free Will If You Pay for It" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Fate and Foreknowledge — John Karavitis contrasts the novel, where Frank, Juliana, and Tagomi treat the I Ching oracle as alive, infallible, and inescapable even though its hexagrams are cast at random, with the TV series, where Tagomi's 'Fate is fluid, destiny is in the hands of men' asserts that choice shapes reality. After reviewing Laplace's demon, quantum uncertainty, and Libet's experiments, it concludes that the show's world, unlike the novel's fatalism, teaches us to act as the authors of our own futures, with John Smith's self-made rise the starkest exercise of free will.
- ch. 19 "9. Could the Axis Have Won the War" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Compatibilism — Miguel Paley maps the three classic positions on metaphysical freedom onto the show: Frank the determinist (Laplace's demon; d'Holbach's claim, illustrated by the LSD interrogation, that the mind is as bound to causality as Connolly's falling body), Juliana the libertarian (Corliss Lamont's burden-of-proof argument, with Wegener's hesitation over the microfilm as deliberation a determined world would render pointless), and Tagomi the compatibilist (W.T. Stace's point that Juliana boards the bus freely though caused, while Frank is stripped by the Kempeitai unfreely though caused). Tagomi's 'Fate is fluid, destiny is in the hands of men' sums up compatibilism, and the chapter ends on what the answer means for holding Nazis responsible.
- ch. 20 "10. Defying Fate" **·** Theodor Adorno, Epictetus, Seneca, Marcus Aurelius — Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control — Benjamin Evans reads Frank as fate's plaything, Tagomi's hydrogen-bomb gambit as an attempt to steer an uncontrollable web of events, and Hitler's claim that destiny belongs only to 'some men' as political exploitation of fate-talk. Stoicism (Zeno through Marcus Aurelius) explains Ed's serenity-prayer acceptance and the sinister Nazi version in which the 'natural order' means wolves eating sheep, but the chapter's verdict follows Adorno's studies of astrology and the occult: believing in fate seeds authoritarian submission, so Juliana letting Joe sail to Mexico — trusting her own judgment over the prophetic film — is the show's Adornian heroism.
- ch. 21 "IV. Flow My Tears, the Ethicist Said" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "11. Is Resistance to Fascism Terrorism" **·** Jürgen Habermas — The Ethics of Political Violence — Corey Horn tests whether the American Resistance counts as terrorists, first against the US Justice Department definition and then Jeremy Waldron's four conditions of coercive terror: Lem's gunpoint demand of Joe and Juliana meets only two conditions, while the Reich's torture of the factory courier and the atomic destruction of Washington meet all four. Jürgen Habermas's distinction between political terrorism with an end goal and purely fear-driven global terrorism then lets him conclude that the Resistance is at most political terrorists whose violence is really a just continuation of war against an occupier — the same act that gets relabeled justice once the revolution wins.
- ch. 23 "12. Are We Really Sure They’re Wrong" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Thomas Aquinas — Natural Law; Just War Theory; Moral Relativism — Timothy Hsiao argues we cannot condemn the burning of the disabled or Smith's son's mandated euthanasia by appealing to Nazi values, since cultural relativism would make the Resistance the real wrongdoers; the horror we feel presupposes an objective natural law known to reason, the violation of which grounded the Nuremberg trials. From Augustine's 'an unjust law is no law at all,' the chapter then tests the Resistance's armed rebellion against the five just-war conditions — proper authority (the Resistance as agent of the moral law), just cause, reasonable chance of success (the newsreels as grounds for hope), proportionality, and last resort — and finds it justified.
- ch. 24 "13. But Why Is Our World Better" **·** Utilitarianism; Moral Luck — Tim Jones asks why Juliana and Tagomi are right to call the Allies-win world 'better' when our world also holds the Red Army's mass rapes in Berlin, Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and the Czech expulsions — a German widow or hibakusha who found Axis-victory reels could call them 'a better world' without being evil. His answer is a numbers-of-victims argument: Juliana's world duplicates our atrocities (the Heisenberg Device on Washington mirrors Hiroshima) and adds unique ones like the Nazi genocide in Africa, so our world is better for the most people — though its victims deserve the empathy and remembrance Obama showed at Hiroshima.
- ch. 25 "14. Reel Lucky" **·** Thomas Nagel — Moral Luck — Elizabeth Rard uses Thomas Nagel's moral luck to show that Juliana's heroism and John Smith's Nazi career are largely products of circumstances beyond their control — Trudy's death in front of her, being born German twenty years before the war — while Frank's interrupted assassination of the Crown Prince shows luck intervening mid-action. The twist is that the Grasshopper newsreels would give High Castle characters what we lack: evidence of how the same people act under different luck, so their characters could be ranked across timelines in a way largely immune to luck, where we must judge from actual conduct alone.
- ch. 26 "V. A Maze of What-ifs" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "15. Farts, Butterflies, and Inner Truth" **·** Laozi — The Tao (the Way); Yin and Yang; Taoism (Daoism) — Franklin Perkins reads Frank's fear that his jewelry business might start World War III — 'you can't fart without changing the balance in the universe' — as the butterfly-effect problem of acting inside a complexity we cannot grasp, from the Roosevelt assassination down to Tagomi's Colt .44. Against the Germans' fatal flight into abstraction (Volk, Blut, Ehre), the chapter presents the I Ching, read through Chinese correlative cosmology of the Tao and yin-yang, as a manual for mole-like, concrete, adaptive interpretation in which each casting (hexagram 11's 'wall falls back into the moat,' the purple knee bands) means only through creative engagement, ending with hexagram 61: our world arose as contingently as a throw of the yarrow stalks.
- ch. 28 "16. How Close Is That World to Our World" **·** Robert Nozick, Edmund Gettier, Alvin Goldman — Possible Worlds; The Gettier Problem — Brett Coppenger treats the show as a nearby possible world identical to ours until the 1930s, then uses Gettier-style cases — Joe Blake forming justified true beliefs while driving through Alvin Goldman's Barn Façade County — to show such beliefs can still fail to be knowledge. Robert Nozick's truth-tracking conditions, defined via what happens in the closest possible worlds, handle the barns but generate 'abominable conjunctions' (knowing Jones killed the Crown Prince while not knowing the Crown Prince was killed), and the chapter closes on the thought that the large stock of shared knowledge is exactly what makes that dystopia feel only a few big events from our world.
- ch. 29 "17. When Worlds Diverge" **·** David Lewis — Possible Worlds — Ananya Chattoraj tests David Lewis's modal realism — possible worlds as real, spatiotemporally and causally isolated, each actual to its own inhabitants — against Tagomi's journeys: the TV Tagomi's silent bench appearance leaves his world a genuine Lewisian possible world where 'actual' just means 'where we live.' But the novel's Tagomi talks with the policeman, a passerby, and a coffee-shop patron, creating two-way spatial and causal relations that break Lewis's isolation criteria, so the book's two realities are better seen as 'island worlds' of one larger world with Tagomi as the bridge.
- ch. 30 "VI. A Video Darkly" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "18. How to Deal with Reality when We’re not Built To" **·** Bertrand Russell — Philosophical Skepticism — The Zawadzkis and Cisowski argue Dick's deliberate confusion enacts what psychology and radical skepticism say about cognition: our 'cognitive miser' brains build simplified models, and the films shatter them, producing Leon Festinger's cognitive dissonance — Frank's chain of external justifications for his rebellion, Joe and John facing excuses they cannot so easily make, Tagomi's overload after killing the two Nazi agents. Following Karl Jaspers, such limit situations can force a leap into a new mode of thinking (Tagomi's transport to a world where the killings never happened), with radical skepticism — Bertrand Russell's five-minute hypothesis — and the I Ching as vehicles for dealing with a reality we are not built to handle.
- ch. 32 "19. What if Evil Had Won" **·** Hannah Arendt — The Banality of Evil — Verena Ehrnberger reads the High Castle world through Hannah Arendt's Eichmann report: Smith's 'It was necessary work. We did it,' Kido's 'The law is the law,' and the surveillance room named Iwazaru ('speak no evil') show evil as thoughtless, self-protecting obedience rather than sadism, embodied in the disturbingly loving Smith family. The real conflict, on this reading, is not Resistance versus Reich but obedience versus the few — Tagomi, Wegener, Juliana, eventually even Smith — who dare to think and feel for themselves, and the chapter weighs the security obedience buys against the freedom and humanity it costs.
- ch. 33 "20. The Spirit of Abstraction" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, W.E.B. Du Bois — Double Consciousness — Christopher Ketcham uses Gabriel Marcel's 'spirit of abstraction' — granting an abstract category arbitrary primacy over actual persons — to explain both Nazi anti-Semitism in the novel (Loetze's chatter, Baynes surgically remaking himself to pass as Swedish, Wyndam-Matson manufacturing stories that beat the merchandise) and America's own version from slavery through Plessy v. Ferguson's whiteness-as-property. Jean-Paul Sartre's Anti-Semite and Jew supplies the hater's passion-as-faith against the rational man's groping for truth, and W.E.B. Du Bois's double consciousness names the victims' divided self-image, while Marcel's claim that peace derived from war 'contains war in a latent condition' reads the show's cold peace as war continued by lies.
- ch. 34 "21. After Death It Can Get Worse" **·** Epicurus — Death Is Nothing to Us — Sam Director asks whether Amazon's unauthorized changes to Dick's novel posthumously harmed him, and against Epicurus's Letter to Menoeceus claim that the dead no longer exist to be harmed, he defends harm as desire-frustration that need not be experienced (Childan's unknown counterfeit antiques, Juliana's deception by Joe) and can involve desires reaching past death (Baynes's Operation Dandelion warning dying with Tedeki). Since Dick delighted in the Blade Runner footage and wanted science fiction to thrive, the chapter concludes the TV adaptation fulfilled rather than thwarted his desires — he is no worse off, maybe better off.
